Resident Evil movie director says he was not prepared for fan backlash

BBC News Fri, 18 Sep 2026 12:58:55 GMT

One of the hottest horror directors on the planet adapting the world's most popular scary video game series?

On paper Zach Cregger and Resident Evil are the perfect unholy alliance.

The film-maker was widely praised for his original, imaginative work on horror hits Weapons and Barbarian and is a long-time fan of the video game series.

But in the lead-up to the film’s release, Cregger’s spent a lot of time defending himself against complaints he’s cashing in on the Resident Evil name.

Speaking to BBC Newsbeat, the director says he was "not prepared" for what came his way.

First launched in 1996 on the original Sony PlayStation by Japanese developer Capcom, Resident Evil was a sensation.

Rather than casting players as super-powered characters, as was the case with most video games in the 90s, it forced them to survive with limited resources.

Thanks to smart reinventions and remakes, the series has managed to stay relevant, selling a total of 213 million copies since its debut.

Some of its characters are among the most well-known in video games, and there are whole communities dedicated to discussing the lore of their universe.

Cregger's Resident Evil follows the story of Bryan, an original character played by Austin Abrams who worked with the director on Weapons.

He's a courier who agrees to deliver a package to a hospital in Raccoon City - a key location from the games.

As Bryan makes his way to the drop-off, it becomes apparent he is caught in the middle of some sort of viral outbreak, with the infected becoming monstrous creatures.

When the first trailer appeared online, many users swamped comment sections to complain about what they'd seen.

Where were the beloved characters? The familiar monsters?

Cregger says he had little interest in simply retelling the story of the Resident Evil games, but that didn't seem to calm some fans.

"I think I was naive," he says.

"I think I was expecting people to be excited to see a Resident Evil movie that felt in the spirit of the games.

"What I was trying to do is make a movie that really honoured the experience of playing them."

According to most reviews, Cregger has achieved what he set out to do.

In its three-star review, NME asked whether it was "the first great horror movie game adaptation".

"For a large chunk of the film's runtime, the answer is a resounding yes," wrote reviewer Jordan Bassett, who said Bryan's encounters become repetitive as the film wears on.

Doug Jamieson, of The Jam Report, awarded four stars and said Cregger "understands adaptation as translation rather than imitation".

In an eight out of 10 review, Looper critic Alastair Ryder wrote: "Zach Cregger has done the best job I've seen of translating the experience of playing a video game and making it feel cinematic."

The verdict from fans remains to be seen, but Resident Evil looks to be on track to have a successful opening weekend at the box office.

It follows recent video game adaptations such as the Minecraft and Super Mario Bros films, which were poorly reviewed but hugely popular.

This isn't the first adaptation of Resident Evil, which was brought to cinema screens in 2002 - the first of six films overseen by writer-director Paul WS Anderson.

His wife, Milla Jovovich, starred in each one, and while they have grown a cult following they were never a hit with critics.

A 2021 "reboot" heavily based on the games and a 2022 Netflix series also failed to impress.

The live-action rights to Resident Evil are owned by German production company Constantin Film - a fact fans have blamed for the perceived low quality of previous adaptations.

Reports online suggest the company's agreement with Capcom prevents Constantin from setting its films in the same timeline as the games.

Cregger told Newsbeat he'd had no contact with the game developer while working on the film.

"Nobody from Capcom ever reached out to me, ever, in any way," he said.

Constantin Film declined to comment, but BBC Newsbeat has been told there was co-ordination between the developer and the film's producers behind the scenes.

Cregger says it's "probably" impossible to please everyone, but it was never his intention to recreate the game on-screen.

"If I had delivered a faithful retelling of one of the stories in the games, I feel like those people would probably be upset with me for that too," he says.

"Because I would have messed it up somehow, inevitably.

"So all I can do is just tell the story that I think is going to be the very best story.

"If somebody's going to have a problem that it doesn't do exactly what they had in their mind of what a Resident Evil movie is, I can't say anything to that."

MI5 accepts it gave evidence based on lies in neo-Nazi spy case

BBC News Fri, 18 Sep 2026 12:30:16 GMT

The security service has accepted it gave evidence based on lies to three courts and that senior MI5 officers were repeatedly dishonest.

It is the first time MI5 has accepted that lies were told to the courts while defending a violent neo-Nazi spy whose abuse was uncovered by the BBC.

The lies were revealed by the BBC in February 2025, which the security service then vehemently denied.

Tim Otty KC, representing MI5, announced the position during a High Court hearing in London on Friday.

He said "MI5 accepts without reservation" the findings of a damning report which concluded that it gave evidence based on "lies" about having kept to its core secrecy policy - known as 'neither confirm nor deny' (NCND) - about the agent status of the neo-Nazi informant.

The security service claimed it had maintained NCND and, consequently, the courts allowed it to keep information secret from a woman who was abused by him.

But what MI5 said was untrue. The security service had in fact disclosed the man's agent status in phone calls to me, as it tried to persuade me not to investigate him in 2020.

A panel of three senior judges - England and Wales' most senior judge, Lady Chief Justice Baroness Sue Carr, President of the King's Bench Division Dame Victoria Sharp and Mr Justice Chamberlain - is considering what action to take over the false evidence.

In particular, it will decide whether to initiate contempt of court proceedings against certain MI5 officers or MI5 itself. Any such move would be unprecedented.

The report, by then-deputy investigatory powers commissioner Sir John Goldring, found that one senior MI5 spy - known as Officer 2 - lied repeatedly, while another - Officer 3 - misled his own colleagues and lied about what he was told.

He also found there were "serious and systemic failures in MI5's conduct" throughout the case.

Otty said MI5 "fully accepts and acknowledges the gravity of the issues raised" in the report, published in July, and they must never happen again.

He added that MI5 had committed to a major programme of reform under the leadership of director general Sir Ken McCallum.

Otty argued against contempt proceedings being brought, saying it would not be in the public interest given Sir John's detailed investigation, MI5's apologies, and its commitment to a programme of reform.

He said Officer 2 had resigned from the service and that Officer 3 had been suspended and was facing disciplinary proceedings, which could lead to his dismissal.

Lawyers for both officers also argued against launching contempt proceedings.

Matthew Butt KC, for Officer 2, said the officer accepted that his conduct had fallen "below the standard expected of him", for which he apologised and expressed regret.

But he said he denied acting dishonestly or having interfered with the administration of justice, and did not accept the report's findings.

Aaron Watkins apologised on behalf of Officer 3 and accepted his conduct "undoubtably" contributed to the courts and parties involved being misled, but denied it had been the result of dishonesty.

He said the evidence presented by Sir John fell short of the threshold for contempt of court, and said such proceedings would not be in the public interest because there had already been a thorough investigation.

Meanwhile, lawyers for the BBC said the corporation considered the threshold had been met and said there was a "very clear public interest" in doing so.

Jude Bunting KC said providing false evidence was "a particularly serious affront to the administration of justice" and noted that while MI5 now offered a sincere apology to the court, its response when the lies were first exposed was "not consistent with transparency or responsibility".

At the conclusion of the hearing, the Lady Chief Justice said it had been a "serious day addressing serious matters".

She said a judgment will be issued at a later date.

The case centres around the foreign neo-Nazi misogynist - an MI5 informant known as Agent X who used his security service role as a tool of abuse.

He coercively controlled his partner, known by the alias Beth, and attacked her with a machete. MI5 then helped him go abroad to continue intelligence work while under police investigation.

The government took the BBC to court in 2022 in a failed attempt to block its investigation into X, but won him legal anonymity. Beth then sued MI5 at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, and in 2024 she sought a review of a ruling at the High Court.

Arguing for secrecy in all three courts, the security service told judges that it had always stuck to its core secrecy policy and never told anyone whether X was an agent, including me. The courts were told this in a sworn statement from a senior officer, a deputy director called Witness A.

The courts accepted MI5's arguments. This meant Beth and everyone else was banned from ever officially being told X was an agent and denied access to the key evidence. She was left at a serious disadvantage and may have lost the case.

Officer 2 had tried to cover up for the man, falsely saying he was not an abusive misogynist nor a real extremist.

Following the court decision in late 2024, I challenged MI5 and said they had lied to the courts. MI5 aggressively maintained its position that its NCND policy had been maintained until I produced evidence proving it was untrue, including a recording of one of the calls with Officer 2.

Because of the BBC's revelations, two official inquiries took place which absolved MI5 and its officers of deliberate wrongdoing, claiming the false evidence was down to mistakes and poor memories.

But, in July 2025, a panel of senior High Court judges ruled that the investigations carried out by MI5 suffered from "serious procedural deficiencies" and that "we cannot rely on their conclusions".

Sir John's investigation was ordered by the prime minister in September 2025 after MI5's explanations about what happened were rejected as deficient and unreliable.

Charlotte Kilroy KC, for Beth, said contempt proceedings should be brought against Officers 2 and 3, as well as the Director General of MI5 Sir Ken McCallum in his capacity as the person with corporate responsibility for the organisation.

In written submissions, she said the false evidence "did not emanate from one individual, or a "bad apple'" and was "sustained and long-lasting".

She added: "There have been repeated efforts to prevent the truth emerging. The reality of the dishonesty and false evidence that has taken place has only emerged because MI5 was faced with incontrovertible proof of its wrongdoing."

She told the court that the "function" of the Goldring report was to allow it to consider whether to bring contempt proceedings, meaning the report was never meant to be the final word.

"Contempt proceedings are essential", she said.

Shots heard as police start moving migrants from Ceuta beaches

BBC News Fri, 18 Sep 2026 11:59:42 GMT

Police have begun moving hundreds of migrants in Ceuta to a new tented site in the port area of the Spanish territory in north Africa.

Officers struggled to contain crowds of people jostling to secure a place at the site after weeks of living on the beaches. Shots could be heard, with reports that police fired into the air.

Several hundred migrants have now reached the camp, which has a capacity for 1,700 people.

Most of the 72,000 migrants who breached the border from Morocco in July have returned. Ceuta's authorities have estimated that 13,000 remain in the enclave, but the Spanish central government has said it is lower.

The operation began at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Friday, with more than 3,000 migrants being transferred, according to the Spanish government-owned news agency Efe.

During the process, some migrants broke through the cordon along the designated 2km (1.2 mile) route to the port. Video shows young men running in the darkness as police tried to maintain control.

More than 170 police officers have been deployed, including drone technicians, Efe reported. It added that the situation was later "brought under control quickly", and the operation was able to continue.

The operation is part of the government's attempt to concentrate the migrants in facilities where they can be identified and cared for while their administrative status is individually determined.

The chaotic scenes will do little to dampen opposition criticism in Spain of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has faced strong criticism over his handling of the crisis.

Since the migrant influx, residents of the 18.5 sq km (7.2 sq miles) territory have expressed safety concerns. Some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.

Ceuta's Mayor Juan Jesus Vivas told lawmakers in the European Parliament earlier this month that the migrants had turned Ceuta into a "pressure cooker".

"The city is completely different than it was before this event, Ceutans have lost their joy and their lifestyles have been completely shaken up," the conservative mayor said.

The opposition also accused Sánchez of knowing about the influx of migrants in advance. Sánchez has insisted that it was impossible to predict, but according to government documents, its intelligence services had warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before the events happened.

Ester Muñoz of the conservative People's Party said the government was "directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died".

Sanchez has blamed trafficking gangs and has also said the crisis was sparked by hoaxes and rumours spread by social media.

Ceuta was "a humanitarian crisis and also an administrative challenge within the city itself", the prime minister said.

The incident has also created diplomatic headaches for Sánchez.

The prime minister is at odds with Italy, with the two countries earlier this week extending temporary border controls imposed on each other. He is also trying to maintain his bilateral relationship with Morocco.

The influx of migrants in late July came after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta cannot be summarily returned to Morocco.

After the ruling, some social media accounts spread misinformation and offered to help migrants cross the Spanish border for hundreds of pounds.

Thousands of people then flooded across the border fence and swam around the ocean barriers. At least 100 people died during the crossing, according to local authorities.

Lindsay Clancy holdout juror says he had no doubt she deliberately killed her children

BBC News Fri, 18 Sep 2026 11:49:46 GMT

The lone holdout juror in the trial of Lindsay Clancy has said he "didn't have any doubts" that she was criminally responsible for killing her three children.

"Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned it," Michael Desronvil said in a statement to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

The judge declared a mistrial on 4 September after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict following nearly 40 hours of deliberating.

Clancy admitted to the killings but her lawyers argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors said the killings were calculated.

Warning: This article contains distressing details

The 36-year-old was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after strangling Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home before jumping out of the second-floor window.

To find Clancy guilty, jurors had to be unanimously convinced beyond reasonable doubt that she intentionally killed her children and that she did not do so as a result of postpartum psychosis, a rare and serious condition.

The jury - nine women and three men - considered a range of options including not guilty by reason of insanity, manslaughter and first-degree murder.

Several jurors have said following the mistrial being declared that the panel was ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.

Desronvil said he believed the evidence presented in court showed she had planned the killings.

"I didn't have any doubts," he said in a statement to CBS on Thursday.

"As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented."

Paula Devlin, one of the other jurors, told CBS Mornings that the panel had spent several days trying to convince Desronvil to change his mind.

"We all worked together to convince ourselves once we got to that point where it was 10 to 2," she said.

The jury foreperson, a retired fifth-grade teacher, described not being able to reach a verdict as "awful" and an "emotional rollercoaster".

She told NBC that Desronvil had "admitted he had reasonable doubt", but as she started filling out the verdict sheets, he apparently said: "But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity."

Another juror told local CBS station WBZ-TV that most of the jurors had been "very firm in their stance" from the start and "the stand-alone juror was not the only one that was unwilling to see things from the other side".

But they added that because Desronvil would not "follow" his reasonable doubt nor offer logical reasoning for his position, they felt Clancy had not received a fair trial.

The identities of all 11 jurors have not been officially disclosed but in the US, once a case is over, any juror can choose to speak publicly about a case and their deliberations.

Patrick Clancy, the children's father and Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband, is due to speak publicly about the case in an interview with the CBS programme 60 Minutes on Sunday.

In it, he is expected to discuss his grief, his memories of his children and the conspiracy theories that have flooded social media since the trial began.

He said he still speaks to his children "all the time", describing it as "a way I stay connected to them".

During the trial, Clancy's defence team had attempted to use her being put on more than a dozen medications in the lead-up to the killings, as well as seeking help from a suicide hotline and an emergency room, as evidence of her psychosis.

Postpartum psychosis can involve hallucinations and delusions, and her lawyers argued that she was unable to understand the nature of her actions or distinguish right from wrong.

A forensic psychiatrist who testified for the defence said Clancy experienced a "command hallucination" and a "delusion of influence" when she killed her children.

However, her psychiatrist testified for the prosecution that Clancy did not show signs of psychosis during their sessions, while another psychiatrist noted that the condition was not currently recognised by the American Psychiatric Association.

Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible for the jury to find her guilty. The defence did not have to prove her mental illness or lack of criminal responsibility.

The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial.

Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has said he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors to avoid a second trial.

He told ABC's Good Morning America that he was upset that the lone juror would not acquit Clancy.

He said the holdout "would not apply the law of reasonable doubt" as instructed by the judge, adding: "That's not right. And that's why I was upset."

The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts.

We bought our £242,000 home without a deposit - here's how

BBC News Fri, 18 Sep 2026 10:43:03 GMT

Until last year, Conroy, 32, and his partner Amber, 28, saw little prospect of owning their own home. They were renting in central Manchester where they work and could not afford to save up for a deposit.

Then they came across a relatively niche, and some experts say riskier, type of mortgage that offered a solution.

The Track Record mortgage from Skipton Building Society covers 100% of the value of a property, with the borrower paying nothing upfront.

Borrowers must meet strict eligibility checks and pay a higher interest rate - in Conroy and Amber's case 5.33% fixed for five years - but they were happy to do this. And in August they bought a four-bed home for £242,000 in Swinton on the edge of Manchester.

"I don't think it's dawned on us it's really ours," says Conroy, a video editor.

According to the Bank of England, the share of UK mortgages with deposits worth less than 10% of the property's value is currently the highest it has been since 2008 when such loans were widely available.

The average deposit for first-time buyers is currently around 20%.

It comes as lenders such as Lloyds, Santander, Skipton and Yorkshire Building Society have launched a raft of new mortgage deals over the last few years covering upwards of 95% of the value of a property, and in some cases as much as 100%.

They say they want to help first-time buyers get on the housing ladder as property prices continue to rise and while saving for a deposit remains a struggle.

But these loans tend to charge higher rates, aren't available for all types of property or borrower, and come with risks customers should be aware of.

Conroy and Amber, a solicitor, have a 25-year loan with monthly repayments of £1,500 - roughly what they were paying in rent.

He says they feel comfortable with the higher cost because they "earn quite well" and expect their salaries to rise.

But he is aware there is a greater risk of falling into negative equity with a no- or low-deposit mortgage. That is when the value of a property falls below the value of the loan still owed on it - leaving the borrower with potentially painful costs if they suddenly have to sell.

Conroy says they plan to overpay their mortgage for the first five years to build up more equity in their home.

"There is always the element of a gamble with the property market," he says.

"But I have researched the area we moved to and don't think house prices are going to drop."

Twenty-seven-year-old Bronya and her partner George, 29, also used a low-deposit mortgage to buy their four-bedroom house in Rhuddlan, North Wales in August.

Lloyds lent them £258,000 - roughly 98% of the property's value - over a 33-year term and they only had to put down £5,000 as a deposit.

The couple pay an interest rate of 5.89%, fixed for five years, equating to monthly repayments of £1,400 - about the same as what they paid to rent a one-bed flat before.

Bronya, a civil servant, says they could have put down a bigger deposit but wanted to use their savings for a renovation project costing upwards of £20,000.

They are aware of the risks of negative equity but believe the refurbishment will boost the value of their home.

"We also plan to stay here our whole lives," George adds, explaining that they are prepared to ride out any dips in the property market.

Widespread uptake of low-deposit mortgages by borrowers who could not afford them was seen as a major factor in the 2008 global financial crisis.

But today's deals have much stronger affordability checks and do not pose the same risks, says David Hollingworth, associate director at brokers L&C Mortgages.

Borrowers of Skipton's zero-deposit mortgage, for example, have to prove they have kept up with their rent for at least 12 consecutive months and credit payments for the last six months.

And Lloyds won't issue one of its £5,000 deposit mortgages for new-build properties and shared ownership homes.

Hollingworth says lenders are recognising that some people have "good affordability but may be struggling to save for a deposit while paying a rent and dealing with cost of living pressures".

Following a recent rule change, he adds, lenders are also offering more "flex" on how much someone can borrow as long as it's within their means.

Nevertheless, he urges borrowers to use common sense.

"Think carefully - what do monthly payments look like? Are you aware that interest rates could go up?"

See the dazzling images that won Astronomy Photographer of the Year

New Scientist September 17, 2026

The astonishing diversity of the cosmos is on display in the 2026 Astronomy Photographer of the Year competition, organised by the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London. From our own solar system to distant nebulae, these images showcase the many wonders we can observe from the ground on Earth.

The overall winner (above), The Quiet Predator, was taken by Ali Alobaidly in Kuwait. It shows a dense nebula 650 light years away, in the constellation Cepheus. This cloud of dust, called the Shark nebula, contains a few bright stars that make their surroundings glow blue. The nebula is so dark and distant that it took Alobaidly more than 28 hours of observing to create this image.

The runner-up in the competition (above) is Beyond the Wormhole, taken by Kfir Simon in Israel. While the image may evoke a hole in space-time, it actually depicts the centre of the Helix nebula, which is about 650 light years away in the constellation Aquarius. Beyond the central star that formed the nebula when it shed its outer layers thousands of years ago, extraordinarily distant galaxies shine through the dust and gas.

Advertisement

In the Our Moon category, Venusian Pearl on the Moon (above) took the prize. Petr Horalek took this photograph in the Czech Republic as the moon passed in front of Venus in the middle of the day. He captured this relatively rare event, called an occultation, just as Venus slipped behind the crescent moon.

The runner-up in the Our Sun section is, unsurprisingly, an image of the sun. However, Anatomy of the Chromosphere (above), captured by Peter Ward in Australia, isn’t a simple photograph. It represents two different wavelengths of light, one of which captures emission from hydrogen along the sun’s edges, represented in red, while the other shows emission from calcium, shown in lilac. Together, they reveal the structure of the sun’s chromosphere, which is the layer just above its visible surface, but below its corona.

Comet C/2025 A6 (Lemmon) jets across the sky in this highly commended image by Julien DeWinter and Landon Boehm, taken from Texas. When it was captured, in October 2025, the comet was almost at its closest point to the sun, about 101 million kilometres from Earth. That proximity to the sun caused remarkable activity on the comet, creating two long plumes, one made of dust and the other of electrically charged plasma.

With a more earthly setting, the winner of the Skyscapes category is Botswana Star Trail, taken by Stefano Pellegrini. It captures the movement of stars above a grove of baobab trees over the course of 340 camera exposures, each lasting 30 seconds.

The winning images from the competition will be exhibited at the National Maritime Museum in London from 18 September.

Robots clash in first naval engagement between uncrewed sea drones

New Scientist September 17, 2026

In the first-known naval engagement between uncrewed vessels, a Ukrainian robot boat sank a Russian opponent in the Black Sea.

The action between the remote-controlled uncrewed surface vessels (USVs), or sea drones, took place earlier this month. A video released by the Ukrainian Navy shows its USV, identified as a Sargan-3000, firing a 12.7-millimetre heavy machine gun at the Russian vessel, which appears to be of the Orcan type, until it sinks.

Both sea drones are propelled by water jets. The Sargan is around 7 metres long with a top speed of over 80 kilometres per hour, while the Orcan is about 5 metres long and can reach 64 km/h.

Advertisement

Fully autonomous drones have killed human soldiers for the first time

This is the first-known clash of its type in the history of naval warfare, according to independent naval expert H. I. Sutton. But it didn’t come as a surprise.

“It was inevitable that there would be USV-on-USV combat,” says Sutton. “We have seen the same in the air, and on the ground.”

Ukraine developed USVs after scuttling its only major warship early in 2022 to prevent its capture. In October 2022, Ukraine carried out a successful attack with seven sea drones, damaging a Russian frigate and a minesweeper at the Sevastopol naval base in Crimea.

Since then, Ukraine has moved from improvised USVs based on speedboats and jet-powered watercraft to advanced designs, including the Magura and Sea Baby series. In conjunction with shore-based anti-ship missiles and aerial drones, Ukraine’s uncrewed vessels have sunk or damaged a third of the Russian Black Sea fleet. The remainder is now largely confined to port behind booms and other defences.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Initially, Ukraine’s USVs carried explosive charges for one-way attacks. More advanced versions are now armed with surface-to-air missiles, with one Ukrainian USV being the first ever to shoot down a helicopter, in 2024. Others are fitted with machine guns and unguided rockets. Some Ukrainian USVs are miniature aircraft carriers, launching aerial drones.

Sutton says the action is likely to drive further evolution of USVs on both sides. This first robot naval action is unlikely to be the last. “Probably in future we will see Ukrainian USVs interdicted by Russian ones close to Russian naval bases,” says Sutton.

In this sense, this archaeological finding connects very directly with challenges that people continue to face today.”

Ancient Chinese legal texts describe cutting off a person’s nose as one of the “Five Punishments”, along with decapitation, limb amputation, castration and facial tattooing. By the end of the Yuan dynasty, which ran from AD 1279 to 1368, the law prescribed it mainly for theft of high-value livestock, or for repeated offences involving the theft of less valuable animals.

The practice is sometimes associated with punishment during the Yuan dynasty. Wang suspects she was buried isolated from her family or community, possibly face down to hide her disfigurement.

It is now legal to buy and use plug-in solar panels in Great Britain, but safety concerns surrounding them haven’t yet been addressed by the UK government. With plug-in solar panels, you simply buy a kit, place it in a sunny spot and plug it into a wall socket. There’s no installation cost, no certification and no planning permission. The devices are popular in many European countries and the UK government legalised them on 27 August to boost renewable energy generation and cut down on household bills.

Prior to this legalisation, Mark Coles, the head of technical regulations at the UK Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET), told New Scientist about several potential issues. One surrounded residual current devices (RCDs), the safety devices found in fuse boxes that sense when current is leaking to ground – a sign of electrocution or a short circuit – and almost instantaneously cut power. Most RCDs used in the UK aren’t suitable for current flowing in both directions and so could malfunction if used with plug-in solar panels.

Advertisement

Another of the IET’s concerns is what happens if there are multiple kits in use in an area and a power cut occurs. In theory, the plug-in kits should also shut down in order to prevent “islanding”, when one home’s power stays live. But if they are still generating power, then they could deceive each other into thinking the grid is live and keep running. The problem then is that power can jump past the fuse box and electrocute maintenance workers in the area fixing the outage.

The IET made these concerns clear to the UK government both before and during the consultation by the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) that ended on 30 June. But Coles says the issues weren’t addressed and now present a risk.

“It was a done deal before it went out, I’m sure,” says Coles. “It’s been rushed. There needed to be time to develop a proper standard for these things, because we feel under certain circumstances that there’s an increased risk to life.”

Plug-in solar is coming – how dangerous is it and is it worth it?

Coles says the risks emerge only when there’s a perfect storm of problems, but that this will inevitably lead to an injury or a death over time if plug-in solar panels are widely adopted.

Extensive scientific studies have been carried out to determine how quickly damage is done within the human body from electric shock. Based on that research, UK RCDs are required to trip and cut off current within 40 milliseconds. But there are no similar standards for plug-in solar panels, which Coles suggests could – if things go wrong, and in very limited circumstances – take longer to shut down.

“You could be exposed to the electric current for longer than you should have been,” says Coles. “You’re in the danger zone.”

The IET’s advice is to get an electrical inspection prior to committing to plug-in solar in order to minimise risk.

Free newsletter

A DESNZ spokesperson told New Scientist that “we have funded an independent contractor to fully test the electrical safety of plug-in solar devices on UK electrical house wiring practice, which found these products to be safe”.

The department added that it had looked at testing with older household electrical safety devices and found no evidence that their ability to provide protection was affected when used with the type of plug-in solar systems sold in Europe.

Coles agrees that tests were carried out, but says that they focused on plug-in solar kits sourced outside the UK, because none was legal here at the time, and with brand new RCDs. That has two problems: legal RCDs in the real world can be much older, and of older design, and there was no clear definition or regulation for plug-in panels that were tested, meaning that ones now for sale may act differently.

“They spent this money on getting these units tested, but these units were non-standard units,” says Coles. “So it’s not like I’m testing something that’s been made to a product standard and I’m seeing how it conforms to this product standard. So I don’t see the point of spending the money. From our point of view, it’s being rushed.”

We may have finally spotted a dark matter particle – but figuring out exactly what kind of particle it was is a daunting task. Even as researchers race to confirm they really did detect an unknown particle, physicists around the world have already started working out what sort of dark matter particle it might have been.

The potential particle in question was found at the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) detector in South Dakota and announced on 1 September. The detector uses a huge tank of liquid xenon to look for signatures of dark matter particles smashing into the nuclei of xenon atoms, which are expected to produce a burst of light in response to any collision that would then be picked up by the arrays of cameras surrounding the tank.

The LZ group recorded only a single burst of light, and there is about a 1-in-200 chance that the signal was a fluke event rather than evidence that dark matter was there – but nevertheless it is tantalising.

Advertisement

What makes the signal even more intriguing is that it was at a higher energy than would be expected if the particle were a standard weakly interacting massive particle, or WIMP, the simplest proposed type of dark matter. “It’s an anomalous event,” says Henning Flaecher at the University of Bristol in the UK, part of the LZ group. “It’s not what you would expect from the most general dark matter models.” The fact that this high-energy event was spotted, with no accompanying lower-energy collisions, makes it exceedingly unlikely that this particle, if it exists, is a “vanilla” WIMP, he says.

In the weeks since the announcement, theorists have released scores of papers digging into the data, searching for answers. “The large number of papers is less a statement that theorists believe the event is a [true] dark matter discovery and more a reflection of the fact that, if it persists, its energy already tells us quite a lot about types of physical processes that could produce it,” says Juri Smirnov at the University of Liverpool in the UK.

Many of those papers debate the possibility that the particle could be what is called a higgsino, a type of non-“vanilla” WIMP. It arises from a theoretical framework called supersymmetry, in which every known particle is proposed to have a “superpartner”, with some similar properties but different spin. In supersymmetry, the higgsino would be the superpartner of the Higgs boson.

Subscriber-only newsletter

A higgsino is the simplest WIMP explanation still available to explain the LZ signal, according to JiJi Fan at Brown University in Rhode Island. “It gives rise to a wealth of signals that could be searched for at different experimental frontiers.” Plus, a higgsino detection event is predicted to be unaccompanied by a host of lower-energy collisions, matching the signal detected by the LZ group.

However, the higgsino has its problems. The most basic model of that sort of particle that could explain the LZ detection seems to be ruled out by constraints from other experiments. This doesn’t mean the particle couldn’t have been a higgsino, but it does suggest the higgsino in question would need to have had a much higher mass than expected.

Many other models have been proposed to explain the detection, though. Among them are several models of dark matter particles originating in extra dimensions. While this may seem an unnecessarily complicated line of enquiry, these models were already being studied to solve other problems in particle physics, says Lisa Randall at Harvard University, a co-author of one such paper. “In some sense, the data looks like it’s calling out for something like this: it avoids the pre-existing constraints and fits quite naturally.”

An extra-dimensional dark matter candidate could both fit the LZ detection and explain why the fundamental particles have the masses they do, a long-standing puzzle, she says. Other models propose a whole dark matter sector, with multiple types of dark particles.

Right now, there is no way to tell which, if any, of these models might be correct. “I don’t think the data currently justify saying one of these is ‘the’ explanation,” says Smirnov. Some of them do come with additional predictions, though, which will be particularly useful when trying to pick through so many ideas, he says.

Are there new territories/questions in theory or experiments we should cover? No matter whether the LZ event is confirmed, some of these topics would lead to long-term research.”

Armed with this knowledge, the team was able to grow functional human hindbrain motor neurons in a dish for the first time by starting with the correct type of progenitor cell.

The hindbrain coordinates fundamental life-sustaining processes, such as breathing, sleeping, eating and the beating of the heart, whereas the forebrain is the centre of higher-level thought. Conditions like amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), the most common type of motor neuron disease, and spinal muscular atrophy cause speech and swallowing difficulties because they affect the hindbrain. Recently, scientists also discovered that GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy suppress appetite in mice by acting on the hindbrain.

Now that it is easier to grow human hindbrain neurons in a dish, it should assist ALS and spinal muscular atrophy research, and allow us to investigate the precise mechanisms of how GLP-1 drugs work in people, says Loh.

When does your brain reach adulthood? We’re now understanding the many ways the organ continues to mature decades after society first deems you an adult

The researchers also studied early-stage embryos of chickens, zebrafish and acorn worms, and found their nervous systems are similarly derived from two different types of progenitor cells. This suggests our shared two-origin brain system arose at least 550 million years ago.

But jellyfish, which we diverged from around 600 to 700 million years ago, have two separate nervous systems. These may have joined up in our distant ancestors because it improved their overall processing power, says Loh. “You get more efficient communication when things are closer together,” he says.

Having our brains develop along two separate pathways might also have facilitated the evolution of complex thought, says Loh. While the hindbrain was taking care of all the basic functions for keeping us alive, “evolution could play around with the forebrain, and make mistakes and give rise to all the fancy things like memory and creativity”, he says.

Nature Neuroscience DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02433-7

The Michelin Guide team has crowned 28 New Zealand hotels as among the world’s best.

That includes 10 two-key hotels - the equivalent of two stars for restaurants.

Wallingford Homestead, an East Coast food destination stay, is the newest two-key restaurant, while Waiheke Island’s Delamore Lodge and Queenstown’s Rosewood Matakauri have moved up from one-key to two-key this year.

Seven famous Kiwi hotels held onto their two-key status from last year, which was the first year New Zealand was included in the ratings guide.

They included: Blanket Bay (Glenorchy Otago), Huka Lodge (Taupo), Otahuna Lodge (Christchurch), Rosewood Cape Kidnappers (Hawke’s Bay), Rosewood Kauri Cliffs (Northland), The Lindis (Omarama), and Wharekauhau Country Estate (Featherston).

Another 18 hotels either became new one-key hotels or retained their one-key status from last year.

New Zealand’s 10 highly rated hotels compare strongly against Australia, which had nine hotels score a two-key status and three achieve three keys.

Globally, 155 hotels achieved three-key status - including a new addition in Rwanda that sets guests up to trek to see gorillas.

Another 657 were rated two-key and 2020 as one-key hotels.

New Zealand’s best hotels sit in stunning locations across the country.

New entrant Wallingford Homestead sits in rolling farmlands with a focus on rustic furnishings and bringing local ingredients to guests’ plates, according to the Michelin Guide.

Promoted two-key Rosewood Matakauri sits by Lake Wakatipu.

It features “interiors that rival, in their sheer luxuriousness, the finest city hotels and the most exclusive resorts” and a Swiss chef among the best in the hemisphere, Michelin says.

Delamore Lodge is on an island with a “surprisingly successful blend of Mediterranean architecture and Maori décor”.

Returning two-key restaurant The Lindis sits in a stunning South Island valley where guests can watch stars arc over the Southern Alps - “reminiscent of the best Patagonian hotels”.

It is the second year New Zealand hotels have been listed in the Michelin keys global review, which is a new set of ratings from the Michelin team famous for the restaurants guide.

To be included on the list, hotels must have the highest standards of architecture, design, service, character, value, and contribution to the local community, and are awarded based on post-stay ratings from verified Michelin Guide guests.

A memorial service is planned this weekend, but neither Panettiere’s boyfriend Brian Hickerson, nor her mother Lesley Vogel, were expected to attend, TMZ reported.

Act faithful line up for selfies as Paul Henry roadshow rolls through New Plymouth

New Zealand Herald September 18, 2026

Paul Henry’s Act roadshow drew more than 250 people in New Plymouth. Photo / Sylvie Whinray

By Robin Martin of RNZ

Paul Henry brought showbiz razzle-dazzle to the campaign trail last night as his Unlocked roadshow rolled through New Plymouth.

The former journalist and television presenter mixed politics and banter with a few anecdotes from his long career in front of a friendly crowd of more than 250 people at a packed Devon Hotel conference centre.

There was no sign of the type of interjection that led to a security guard removing a podcaster from a similar event in Dunedin.

Dozens of party faithful lined up politely for selfies with the man of the hour at the end of the show.

Nicky Howarth was one of those who posed for a picture.

“I just decided why not, he’s a bit of a celebrity, isn’t he. So, I can actually share that on Facebook, which is what I was thinking of doing, you know, just sharing on Facebook to say that we’d been and to encourage people to vote.”

She liked Act’s plans to scrap the Waitangi Tribunal and Climate Change Commission, but wasn’t so sure about its support of data centres and genetic engineering technology.

A woman, who preferred not to give her name, had also got a snap with Henry, ranked number four on Act’s party list.

“Well, I’ve actually already had a photo with him. I’ve always loved him, always loved his shows and stuff.

“He’s awesome. I was always going to vote Act, but when Paul Henry’s standing I was like perfect, cherry on the top.”

She reckoned Act had strong values, and was not afraid to challenge the status quo.

Henry told the audience there had been some trepidation at Act headquarters about the roadshow’s name – Paul Henry Unlocked.

“One of the chiefs said it sounds like he’s been released from prison? And another chief said, ‘You haven’t been to prison, have you?’”

Cue a Henry anecdote about being jailed in Iraq while working as a foreign correspondent.

“I was beaten up quite badly with a group of other journalists and some other combatants and other annoyances to Saddam Hussein.

“All of us were locked up in the desert. It was horrible. I was the only one that got out. After about four days I was let out ... that is just how bloody annoying I can be.”

His audience chuckling, Henry then rolled through Act policy – cutting red tape, equality under the law, no new taxes, lowering of corporate tax, a tougher benefit regime for those out of work, targeted immigration settings and the general encouragement of excellence – before taking questions from the floor.

He was quizzed about cutting immigration when some New Zealanders didn’t want to work, the breaking up of the electricity gentailers, supposed handouts to iwi, the emergence of data centres and how to get young people into homes.

He reached into the Act policy grab-bag for responses which, for the most part, mollified his audience.

Henry finished the evening with another anecdote about meeting Queen Elizabeth II while working as a royal correspondent. It involved a swan-shaped hors d’oeuvre, paté and a mistimed expletive ... and then it was time to queue for selfies.

Those choosing to head home were mostly happy with what they’d heard.

Glen Stevens was in property development.

“I’ve liked him for a while, he’s got some guts and stands up for what he believes in and doesn’t sit on the fence, which I like.”

Stevens was attracted to Act’s promise to cut red tape.

Denise Wood enjoyed what she’d heard.

“I thought it was fantastic. I’ve changed my views on politics. What Paul said made sense and he answered [questions] honestly.”

She supported Act’s policy to broaden assisted dying laws.

Mike Morrissey was not happy with Act’s strategy of targeting the party vote, arguing it could contribute to a parliamentary overhang.

“We need a smaller Parliament, so it doesn’t cost us so much money. It’s costing taxpayers a lot of money having extra people in Parliament because they have staff and everything else that comes with it.”

Mount Maunganui landslide: Adams Ave and Pilot Bay boat ramp open, but another business closes

New Zealand Herald September 18, 2026

Adams Ave has been closed periodically since January's landslide into Mount Maunganui Beachside Holiday Park. Photo / Kelly O'Hara

New fencing at the Pilot Bay boat ramp and impending warmer weather have improved the Mount’s future prospects, locals say.

This comes as Tauranga Mayor Mahe Drysdale announced at a community meeting on Thursday that some Mauao walking tracks should be open for summer.

However, the changes are coming too late for one long-standing business, which closed its doors last month.

Adams Ave and the Pilot Bay boat ramp have been closed periodically since six campers died in a landslide from Mauao into Mount Maunganui Beachside Holiday Park and Mount Hot Pools on January 22.

Businesses in the area have been impacted by restricted customer access.

Hot Spot Superette has closed after more than 20 years on Adams Ave, making it the second business on the street to shut since the landslide.

Saed Rajput, who owned the dairy for the past three years, closed its doors two weeks ago.

In August, Rajput told the Bay of Plenty Times that sales were down 90%, and he was paying business expenses out of his own pocket.

He declined to comment about the closure.

Rustica pizzeria on Adams Ave closed amid a road closure in August.

Owner Michele Delaini told the Bay of Plenty Times his business relied on foot traffic from people visiting Mauao.

He said the pizzeria was closed indefinitely.

Copenhagen Cones next door remained open.

Manager Shannon Hope said new Adams Ave fencing had cleared more outdoor seating for her customers.

The new fencing and warmer weather had made her optimistic for summer.

“I think those fences made people think that there was some kind of danger down here, like keep out. Whereas now it’s a lot more open and inviting.”

Hope said this summer would be different to previous summers.

“But we’ve just got to take it as it comes.

“If the sun’s shining, there are people out. It’s got to get better.”

Tauranga Business Chamber chief executive Matt Cowley said Mount Maunganui business confidence “has been stronger”.

However, future prospects were strong with summer approaching.

“Businesses are eager to get back to a new normal.

“While the camp is unlikely to reopen, they are looking forward to Mauao opening and visitors once again enjoying the experience that makes the Mount so special.”

Cowley said he was surprised so many businesses had remained open.

“It’s a credit to each of the business owners and locals who have supported them during winter.”

He said businesses had experienced significant financial and personal challenges.

The reopening of Adams Ave created “increased certainty” for businesses and would have an immediate impact.

Mount Maunganui Sports Fishing Club president Mark Hemingway said closures of the Pilot Bay boat ramp had been a “big inconvenience” for members.

“Most of our members are regular users there.”

However, member safety was a priority.

Hemingway said he knew one member who used the boat ramp most weekends when it was open.

Instead, he said members were using the Sulphur Point ramp, which was already at capacity on fine weekends.

Members had told Hemingway the boat ramp closures were a “pain”.

He said the club held tournaments throughout the year that used the Pilot Bay ramp.

“It’s an iconic boat ramp location, and locals have used it for many years.”

Adams Ave was last closed temporarily after renewed landslide movement at the campground in July.

Recovery manager Charlie Rahiri said new protective measures meant the area was now secured.

The existing shipping containers at Mount Maunganui Beachside Holiday Park had been ballasted with 900 bags, each weighing about a tonne.

Rahiri said the temporary fencing was removed once the ballasting was installed.

The existing fencing at the campground was also repaired, and a new fence was installed at the Pilot Bay boat ramp.

“It is anticipated that Adams Ave will no longer be subjected to periodic closures under the Trigger Action Response Plan (TARP).”

The TARP was developed by geotechnical engineers for monitoring land movement and rainfall on Mauao.

Rahiri said the boat ramp and car park were in an active landslide-risk zone and could close again if level three conditions of the TARP were met.

“Before launching, boat ramp users will need to understand that access may be restricted or closed at short notice for safety reasons.”

Bijou Johnson is a multimedia journalist based in Bay of Plenty. A passionate writer and reader, she grew up in Tauranga and developed a love for journalism while exploring various disciplines at university. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies from Massey University.

By Katie Todd of RNZ

Some Wānaka residents are appalled an off-licence has been granted for a new bottle store next door to a Plunket clinic, which has also been used as an Alcoholics Anonymous meeting space for 30 years.

The proposed Super Liquor drew 117 public objections but the Queenstown Lakes District Licensing Committee approved the licence, finding there was not enough evidence the store would increase alcohol-related harm or create more than minor effects on the neighbourhood’s amenity and good order.

The licence is approved for a 12-month trial period on the basis the licensee, The Gate Limited, does not advertise its products outside the store. It also has to put up and maintain a 1.8m-high hedge along the boundary with Plunket.

The Plunket clinic on Ardmore St is already two doors down from a bar with a Liquorland, and Betty’s Liquor store 90m away.

Nine off-licences were within half a kilometre of the clinic, the committee heard.

Wānaka resident Ben Tutty said as a father-of-two and frequent visitor to Plunket, he was appalled to learn about the application and compelled to submit an objection.

He believed the store risked normalising alcohol for young families.

“To me it feels like an instinctual - that’s just wrong ... putting it next to a Plunket feels crazy. There’s a children’s playground out front of Plunket where children and babies and young families are all the time,” Tutty said.

Other objectors told the District Licensing Committee they believed the store posed a risk to recovering Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) members, who met twice a week at the site.

Expert witness Paul Watson, clinical lead for Whānau Āwhina Plunket, presented evidence heavy or problem drinkers were particularly responsive to alcohol advertising, imagery and physical proximity.

The committee said the premises previously operated as a Woolworths Metro with an off-licence, without any history of community objections or evidence it degraded the amenity for Plunket users.

No expert medical evidence was presented to show a nearby bottle store could trigger a relapse for AA members or maintain alcohol dependence, it said.

The licensing inspector also noted AA had chosen not to comment on or object to the application, despite being contacted about it, and had continued to hold its meetings at the site despite a steady increase in nearby on-licences and off-licences.

Liz Gordon, a lawyer for some of the objectors at the hearing, said she felt that was not a fair counter-argument.

AA publicly states it has no opinion on outside issues and refuses to be drawn into public controversy, she said.

“I felt that was a really unfortunate comment by the committee, because everybody knows AA isn’t going to say anything. So other people took the opportunity to speak for AA at that hearing in terms of the concerns about alcohol harm in the area,” she said.

Tutty said he felt the increasing number of alcohol outlets in the area was a problem.

“In the hearing I cited a bunch of studies that said when there’s more density of alcohol outlets, alcohol-related harm increases,” he said.

Neither New Zealand Police nor the Alcohol Licensing Inspector opposed the application.

Police data submitted as part of the hearing showed a 40% decrease in alcohol-harm related incidents within 1km of the site over the previous three years.

The Gate Limited told the committee the store would be a modern bottle store with clear sightlines, low shelving, CCTV coverage, monitored point-of-sale areas and a layout that supported supervision and compliance.

It would be locally owned and operated by a team with more than 35 years’ hospitality experience and deep regional connections, it said.

Tutty said opponents were hoping to appeal the decision.

The Gate Limited has been contacted for comment.

Colleen Burrows murder: Siblings fight for justice four decades after tragedy

New Zealand Herald September 18, 2026

Colleen Burrows was murdered in Napier in 1987. She was 16.

It’s been four decades since the murder of Napier teenager Colleen Burrows.

But her sister and brother say their fight for justice and closure is not over, despite exhausting all avenues in a complicated legal battle to be granted compensation from her convicted murderer Sam Te Hei.

Te Hei got $17,664 in compensation for maltreatment and abuse by Corrections Department officers during his 30 years in jail, of which 12 years were for the attempted murder of a fellow inmate. Te Hei’s settlement was from a Crown offer of more than $820,000 to settle the claims of 51 men subjected to prison practices breaching their human rights.

Tracey Peka, now 52, and Christopher Hawkins, 36, say their fight for their own compensation from him in return was never about money, and none has been paid to them.

They still hope to see out the wish of Colleen’s mum Ida Hawkins, who died in 2024, hoping the claim would help other families who become victims of violent crime.

Tracey says that if the claim was successful – it was initially upheld by the Victims’ Special Claims Tribunal but then turned down by the courts on appeal – the proceeds would have gone to the victims’ rights movement that supported them.

“It never was about the money,” Tracey says. “It was to set a precedent for victims facing loss and grievance, and the issues are about what support there is for victims.”

“We definitely feel that justice hasn’t been served, and it’s a very disappointing decision,” she says. “The New Zealand justice system needs a big makeover.”

“It took a huge toll on my mother, on her health, mentally and physically. Our mother was broken-hearted, yet she stayed strong and courageous.”

“It had a huge impact on our whānau, and it still does to this day,” says Tracey, who left Hawke’s Bay 23 years ago, struggling amid the daily reminders, and the anxiety attacks she suffers as a result.

Aged 13 at the time of the killing, she shared the “special bond” of a young teenager growing up with an older teenaged sister.

She could talk with Colleen about things she couldn’t with anyone else.

“I hardly go back to Hawke’s Bay any more, and I stay no more than three or four days,” she says.

“Even 39 years later I have days where I sit and wonder what it would be like, I still find myself grieving, and I break down and cry and wish that she was still here.”

She thinks of her own children and grandchildren, and how her sister never got to enjoy those experiences, because it was “taken away” by the killers.

Her brother Christopher, who also no longer lives in Hawke’s Bay, wasn’t born when Colleen’s life was taken, but came to know the recurring nightmare his mum and the family went through whenever the subject came up.

They had a brother, Joseph, who died in a car crash in 2003, and their mother helped raise numerous other children.

He says he never saw his mother heal or have closure.

“It was a case of trying to find a sense of closure,” he says.

“It was pretty disappointing to see the court take the side of the prisoner again.”

They believe it’s been beaten on a point of law, and legal experts have suggested to Hawke’s Bay Today it will now take changes in the law to enable victims in the situation their mother was in to be able to sue.

In a decision based on a hearing in March and released on September 4, the Supreme Court bench of five of New Zealand’s most senior judges determined on legal grounds it could not award compensation or damages to a person who was not a direct witness to the killing.

It happened on the night of June 17-18, 1987.

Sixteen-year-old Colleen Burrows was raped, beaten, and run over by a vehicle and left for dead beside a track on the banks of the Tūtaekurī River, near Brookfields Bridge.

She was found in the morning, about the time six-year-old Teresa Cormack was being abducted in an unrelated event in the streets of Maraenui, which led to Napier having two major homicide inquiries running simultaneously.

Te Hei and another man were convicted of her murder and sentenced to life imprisonment, Te Hei eventually serving 30 years in jail.

He was released on parole in 2018, and in 2020 the Crown agreed to pay him $17,644 as compensation for breaches under the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, arising from mistreatment while incarcerated.

Ida Hawkins, who Tracey says never recovered from the trauma and stress arising from the killing of her daughter, then lodged a claim under the Prisoners’ and Victims Claims Act for emotional harm and exemplary damages compensation from Te Hei.

The Victims’ Special Claims Tribunal upheld the claim of emotional harm and awarded her $15,000, although because of the complicated legal argument that followed, it would never be paid.

It also turned down the claim for exemplary damages.

In 2022, the High Court allowed Te Hei’s appeal against the decision and quashed the Tribunal award and also dismissed a cross-appeal by Ida Hawkins in relation to the exemplary damages claim.

The court held that the Tribunal had “failed to identify a cause of action” on which Ida Hawkins could sue under the general law.

In February last year, by which time Ida Hawkins had died, the Court of Appeal allowed an appeal on behalf of Ida Hawkins’ estate.

It referred it back to the Tribunal on the basis that she may have had a claim against Te Hei on grounds not previously considered by the High Court or the Tribunal, “namely, a common law claim for psychiatric harm”.

The estate, represented by Tracey Peka, pursued the matter, and the Supreme Court’s latest decision dismissed a further appeal and allowed a cross-appeal, setting aside the direction to return the matter to the Tribunal.

Citing precedent, it said a previous Court of Appeal left open the question of whether a secondary victim had to be a direct witness to the event.

It declined to overrule a precedent decision, saying a claim for mental injury was not necessarily excluded, but if there was to be change it needed to be by legislation.

Doug Laing is a Hawke’s Bay Today reporter with 39 consecutive years in Napier, covering news events and issues throughout Hawke’s Bay.

Rise in firearm-related convictions in Hawke’s Bay

New Zealand Herald September 18, 2026

Guns seized by police during an operation in Hawke's Bay last year. Photo / NZ Police

There has been a rise in firearm-related convictions across Hawke’s Bay, according to new data.

Ministry of Justice figures show the number of people being dealt with through the courts for firearm offences, including those being convicted, has reached its highest level for at least a decade in Hawke’s Bay.

Local police say there is zero tolerance for anyone causing harm in the community, and offenders will be held to account “who choose to cause fear or harm with firearms”.

For the 12 months to June 2026, a total of 96 people were convicted for firearm-related charges across all Hawke’s Bay courts (Napier, Hastings, Waipukurau and Wairoa courts).

About 18% of those convictions led to imprisonment.

That was up from 87 people convicted in 2024-25, 69 in 2023-24, 86 in 2022-23, 61 in 2021-22, 77 in 2020-21 and 58 in 2019-20.

The figures do not include a breakdown of each offence.

However, nationally, the most common firearm-related offence dealt with through the courts - by far - was unlawfully obtaining or possessing regulated weapons or explosives.

Despite a rise in Hawke’s Bay, there was actually a slight dip in the number of people convicted for firearm-related offences nationally, when comparing 2025-26 to 2024-25.

Eastern District Police acting district commander Inspector Danny Kirk said police had “zero tolerance” for offending in the community that caused harm.

He said police were committed to help ensure safety.

“This includes disrupting illegal firearms activity, therefore reducing the harm it causes our people.

“When we come across those who choose to cause fear or harm with firearms, our officers will not hesitate to hold those individuals to account.

“This can, and does, include removing illegal firearms from circulation when we are able.

“We encourage members of the public with concerns or details about illegal use of firearms to please contact us as soon as possible and with as much detail as you can safely provide.”

Meanwhile, 139 people had firearm-related charges finalised in court in Hawke’s Bay during the year to June, which included people convicted and not convicted. That figure was also a high for the last decade.

In New Zealand, you need a firearms licence to legally own and possess most guns and ammunition (that aren’t prohibited).

You can possess an airgun if you are aged over 18 without a licence, as long as it’s not a high-powered airgun.

Each year, police seize a large number of firearms over breaches.

In 2025, 6760 firearms were seized throughout New Zealand, up from 6153 in 2024 and 5926 in 2023.

Earlier this month, a sawn-off shotgun and a pump-action shotgun were seized by police during a raid in Hastings, with one man charged with firearms offences.

In May, police uncovered and seized 17 firearms and hundreds of rounds of ammunition during an operation across Hawke’s Bay, charging multiple people with firearms offences.

Shooting incidents were also reported in Wairoa earlier this year, including around Easter, which led to an arrest and charges.

The definition of a firearm is anything from which any shot, bullet, missile or other projectile can be discharged by force of explosive.

People should call 111 if a firearm incident is unfolding, or report information about illegal firearms to 105.

You can also report information about illegal firearms anonymously to Crime Stoppers through 0800 555 111 or the Crime Stoppers website.

How this team of experts guides 80-metre turbine blades down our roads with just millimetres to spare

Sydney Morning Herald September 19, 2026

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

These massive blades are the largest objects moved through our streets. This is how it’s done.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

It is just after midnight on a winter morning when we gather at the Port of Newcastle.

In the background coal ships slink by, in the foreground an almost inconceivably vast wind turbine blade lies along the spine of a truck bed like some sort of alien life form strapped to a gurney in a sci-fi film.

It’s so big that it’s hard to fit it all into the frame of your eye from any reasonable perspective. At its tip it tapers to the length of schoolkid’s ruler. Towards that tapered end it has a jagged edge like a cartoon dragon’s teeth, a shape designed to reduce noise as it slices through the air. Peering up at its midsection, you could be looking at a warship’s prow from the ocean’s surface.

A team of transport specialists are making last-minute preparations to move this beast through the sleeping streets of suburban Newcastle and the coal villages of the Hunter Valley, along the Golden Highway to a hillside outside Wellington on the NSW Central Slopes, where it is to be raised upon a tower as part of a Squadron Energy wind farm that will soon be generating enough electricity for about 220,000 homes.

It seems absurd that this thing can be moved at all, let alone along busy roads, but the man in charge of this circus, Steve Spiller, seems impossibly calm. Jovial, even.

Wind turbine blades, explains engineer Dr Rosemary Barnes, are the largest single-component objects that humans regularly either build or seek to move. Artefacts of the modern world tend to shrink as technology advances, but wind turbines, shaped by both economic and physical forces, keep growing.

Longer turbine blades scoop up more wind and generate more electricity with each rotation, says Barnes, who has spent a career designing, building and repairing turbines and blades around the world and now runs a renewable energy consultancy. A dozen huge turbines need fewer gearboxes, less cable and wiring, less maintenance, less concrete and steel to generate as much electricity as dozens of small ones.

As the turbines grow in length, so do the forces exerted upon them. In extreme conditions, a large blade might bend 10 to 15 metres from a straight line. Imagine, says Barnes, a diving board wilting under the weight of a herd of elephants.

“They have to survive that transfer of force hundreds of millions of times over a life of about 30 years. Every time the blade is in the three o’clock position, gravity is bending it one way, and then when it goes into the nine o’clock position, it’s bending the exact opposite way, and it keeps repeating like that as it spins. It’s just like if you bend a paperclip back and forth repeatedly, you know that small load is not going to break it, but you do it enough times, and you get fatigue loading, it is going to break.”

All this means that not only must a blade be handmade from tough, light composite materials, they are stronger when they are crafted in a single piece, rather than disassembled for transport, which brings us back to Spiller and his crew in Newcastle.

The monster they are about to move is 82 metres long and weighs just over 20 tonnes.

The crew is doing last-minute checks on vehicles and equipment. Craig Carpenter is inspecting the Kenworth truck and the purpose-built trailer he is about to drive. The trailer has a long spine that can be extended to suit its load, and six sets of axles at the rear.

Tonight Carpenter’s load from front grille to blade tip will be 92 metres long. Carpenter picked up the nickname Blade Runner One for his smooth driving while moving blades in Western Australia last year, but just as crucial is Freddie Scheepers, who is “steerer” and will pursue Carpenter in a van close behind the truck.

Scheepers must not only keep his own vehicle on the road, but when necessary will use a remote control to steer the rear axles of the trailer. He keeps in constant contact with Carpenter so at any given moment the two know exactly where the blade tip is in relation to the road and the rest of the rig.

When the front of the rig moves upwards and is forcing the tip towards the ground, Scheepers will also be able to raise and lower the blade itself, the last metres of which rest in a hydraulic jack that sits over the axle sets.

“Those two are very, very close, and they’ve got a really good bond,” says Spiller, watching Carpenter and Scheepers make final preparations. “They know what the other bloke is going to do before he does it.”

The convoy pulls out at about 1am. There are two police cars, as required by law when moving a load of this size in NSW. There are four pilot vehicles which help manage traffic around the truck and trailer. Scheepers’ steering van hunts along behind the blade like a sheepdog, and we follow in a four-wheel drive with Spiller, the project manager.

Also in tow is a Transport NSW vehicle with a couple of observers, there to see if anything can be learnt or improved for future runs. After this, there are still another 195 blades to go, let alone the turbine hubs, tower sections and generators.

“When you pull back the curtain, this is what building a wind farm looks like – thousands of individual movements, decisions and people are needed to get every component to site,” Squadron Energy’s chief executive Rob Wheals later observes.

“At 80 metres long and shaped like a banana, each blade is one of the most challenging pieces of infrastructure to ever move.”

From Spiller’s radio we can hear occasional chatter from the pilot vehicles, but he leaves the “Bladerunners” to their own quiet comms channel so they can concentrate. Before we’ve even left the port precinct the blade tip sweeps out over a cyclone fence, clearing it by what seems like centimetres.

Spiller doesn’t flinch. Every move is rehearsed, every distance measured.

At a McDonald’s on a roundabout on Industrial Drive in the neighbouring suburb of Mayfield, the cop cars and pilot vehicles splay out to halt traffic coming from three directions, and Scheepers climbs out of his van to flick a switch on the rig to remote control. He adjusts the height of the suspension, and then he steers the rear of the rig around the turn.

Speed picks up, at least until the caravan reaches the Hunter Expressway. To make it onto that section, the pilots block traffic on the expressway in both directions while the Bladerunners navigate the rig 80 metres down an off-ramp into what would otherwise be oncoming traffic, then drive a kilometre down the wrong side of the road before crossing back. Spiller seems pleased by how smoothly this dance of traffic and truck is performed.

As we head northwest towards the Golden Highway, Spiller relaxes enough to tell his story. He became an expert in moving big stuff almost by accident. At 19, he took a job with a logistics firm and began moving shipping containers. Half a decade later he was moving wind turbine parts, and the work took him around the world with the global giant GE. He has moved bits and pieces of wind farms by sea and land and even air, at one point chartering the world’s biggest aircraft, an Antonov, to move a wind turbine hub and six generators from Leipzig to Adelaide.

In Germany, near the Polish border, he recalls coaxing blades through tiny villages on a truck that could raise them to near vertical from the base to navigate tight spaces.

In Australia, it’s easier because we have so much space. “I moved 300 blades through Toowoomba without complaint,” he boasts. Today he works for the Ares Group, which was contracted by GE, who built the blade at a factory in China, to shepherd it safely off the ship in Newcastle and on to the Squadron Energy site outside Wellington.

Despite the late hour you can tell the convoy is having an impact along the way. In one hamlet we pass within metres of the old coal miners’ cottages. A man in a dressing gown watches on in the pre-dawn from his veranda. His expression is impossible to read in the revolving lights.

From the sections of widened road you can see along the way the years of preparation that went into this operation. EnergyCo, the NSW government authority responsible for delivering the state’s five renewable energy zones, has spent $130 million preparing this route.

There are rules about moving oversized loads in the dark on the Golden Highway, so the convoy pulls over before dawn. A quiet pall descends across the still convoy, except for cheerful noises from Carpenter’s cabin. He hums and sings to himself and taps out a rhythm before drifting into silence.

In bright early light, against the country homes in Denman, the enormity of the blade begins to become clearer. It is longer than whole blocks of the little town. Along the Golden Highway, the convoy at times creeps up to something approaching normal traffic speed, and time passes quickly until we reach the site of the wind farm, headquartered on a sheep and cattle operation on rolling green hills east of Wellington.

As the truck prepares to tackle the narrow dirt roads built for the project we are taken into a sprawling site office for a safety induction. Whiteboards on the walls show the progress in the construction of each of the 69 turbines that will soon be operational here. There are posters boosting the “core values” of Squadron Energy, which is owned by Tattarang, the investment company that is in turn owned by Andrew Forrest and Nicola Forrest. The values include “Humility” and “Frugality”.

It is midafternoon on a hilltop I had last seen two years earlier when Energy Minister Chris Bowen and Forrest attended a sod-turning ceremony. Bladerunner One finally steps out of his cabin and offers up a great two-armed stretch to the sky. By now Spiller has left the site on his way back to his head office in Melbourne. Workers on-site scramble over the blade, breaking it free of its harnesses and lowering it into a cradle by a half-built tower. By the time it is operational it will stand 148 metres from base to blade tip.

There’s no getting around the impact the project is having on a beautiful landscape. Construction pads are scraped into the ground by each tower and the new roads hum with the sort of traffic flow you’d expect in a prosperous town.

Later I ask farmer John Holland, owner of Uungula, for which the wind farm is named, what he makes of it all. He speaks with a careful, precise manner, aware of the controversy that wind projects attract. Squadron, he says, will clean up after the construction is complete, leaving him with new roads, giving even better access to the property’s ridge lines.

He says he has no fear about the impact of the turbines on his stock. Visiting other wind farms, he has seen sheep “camping” under the towers for shade. He reckons the turbines look majestic, but admits that when he saw renders of what they would look like spread across the land he loves he found it “a little confronting.”

He thinks renewable energy is a part of the solution for Australia’s growing energy demand, but not the only one. Like many farmers, he opposes grid-scale solar plants taking up agricultural land. But he has practical considerations too. The rent Squadron will pay for each turbine will let the family retire a fair chunk of debt, though he won’t say how much. Nor will he say how many turbines his farm will host. “That’s a bit like asking how much money I’ve got in the bank. It’s a bit rude.”

But he is happy to say the income has helped settle the questions of succession that can cause such grief to farming families, and to update equipment and improve fences and dams.

“It’s the confidence to be able to run the property the way it should be run.”

I ask him what Uungula means.

“It’s an Aboriginal word,” he says. “It means wind in the hills.”
