What the cameras missed after Lloyd Meek copped a spray from his coach

Sydney Morning Herald September 19, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Sam Mitchell charged into Hawthorn’s change rooms at half-time of his team’s round seven clash with Gold Coast, ruckman Lloyd Meek firmly in his sights.

An errant backwards handball by Meek in the dying stages of the second quarter had led to a crucial turnover, allowing the Suns to score a goal with four seconds left on the clock.

Mitchell, fuming, delivered an animated spray – which amateur lip-readers discerned contained a lot of f---s – that quickly went viral on social media, largely due to the wide-eyed expressions of Meek’s shocked teammates.

“I know that when he’s aggressive and he’s fired up, it’s because of how much he cares, and I’m the same,” Meek told this masthead.

“I’m exactly the same. So like, we’re all competitive people. We wouldn’t be here if we weren’t. We all want to win. And sometimes those conversations are just what it takes to get the message across.

“At the time, obviously no one likes being yelled out. But I was still so stoked with how we were able to respond and come out of that.”

Hawthorn went on to win the game by 49 points, holding Gold Coast goalless in the final term.

Meek points out there’s a lot the broadcast cameras don’t see or show. The ruckman said Mitchell checked in with him before running out for the third quarter, and again after the game, to check he was OK.

“He came up to me and said ‘well done, you responded really well’, and we had a good chat, no one sees that,” Meek said.

“You just see one 30-second snippet and think ‘geez, he’s copped a spray’. But it’s like no, we’ve actually had conversations all day.”

Growing up in Mininera in regional Victoria – Meek hails from a prestigious rowing family, with his dad and his siblings all winning Head of the Lake titles. He was selected by Fremantle with pick 69 in the 2017 draft, but did not debut in the AFL until his fourth season at the Dockers. He later moved to Hawthorn during the 2022 trade period to seek more opportunities in the ruck.

As an example of Mitchell’s close connection to his players, Meek revealed the coach delivered handwritten letters to each of them before their qualifying final win, on the road, against Fremantle.

“[In the letter] he mentioned that he was glad that I picked Hawthorn and had faith in me, and how we’ve both, I guess, grown over that four-year period,” Meek said.

Meek said he found it difficult to fully articulate what Mitchell meant to the playing group, heralding the head coach as someone who “makes every single person feels valuable”.

“He [Mitchell] is Hawthorn,” he said.

“He’s so pivotal and so important to what we’ve built … not discrediting the[other] people; the board and the football club and the other coaches and staff, but he has built so much of the environment that we get to come in and enjoy every day, and that’s probably been something that I have valued and appreciated since coming to Hawthorn. ”

“Everything he spoke about and his vision for us and the club was so aligned with what I wanted in my career.”

Meek has endless praise for Mitchell’s coaching abilities, but has some doubts about the coach’s prowess at chess. Mitchell and a few other Hawthorn players regularly play chess online, with the head coach known to have a solid winning streak.

“I don’t know if I’ve ever played [against] him, but I reckon I’d be able to beat him,” Meek joked.

“I think he likes to play on chess. com, so I think he’s pretty handy. He probably uses AI to cheat.”

Hawthorn’s preliminary final clash with Brisbane on Saturday comes six weeks after the back-to-back reigning premiers took them to the cleaners in round 22, the Lions storming to a 67-point win at the Gabba.

After the thumping loss Mitchell remarked, “we’re better than that, and we’re going to have to prove it”.

When he spoke to this masthead this week, Meek was yet to watch footage of the Lions’ semi-final victory over Adelaide because the game clashed with his 10-year-high school reunion in Ballarat; an event the 28-year-old attended alongside his childhood sweetheart, now wife, Elonie, who he met in Year Nine.

Ahead of the prelim, Meek intended to keep things simple.

“I am very big on my rituals. I like having my routine. Yeah, I like to think I’m not too superstitious, but I do find comfort in doing similar things,” he said.

“In big games, the tendency is you want to think about it more, but you can’t really change what you do out there until you get out there.”

Inside a grubby political blackmail plot that backfired spectacularly

Sydney Morning Herald September 19, 2026

A nasty campaign against a political rival is a reminder that democracy in Sydney is still at risk of being bought, sold, and weaponised.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

On January 8, 2022, four newly elected councillors gathered at the Crossways Hotel in Strathfield to divide the spoils of political war. Little did they know the meeting would trigger one of the grubbiest feuds in NSW politics, and feature in a major corruption inquiry four years later.

Over lunch and drinks that Saturday, real estate agent Matthew Blackmore, kidney transplant recipient Karen Pensabene, migration agent Sandy Reddy and lawyer-cum-development executive Sharangan Maheswaran struck a handshake deal over who would become the mayor of Strathfield Council following elections the month prior.

The agreement was for Blackmore, an independent, to take the job for at least one year and then hand it over to Pensabene, a Labor councillor. Everyone seemed happy. The only problem was that Blackmore ended up liking the job a little too much. With a big mortgage and rising interest rates, he also liked the $46,010 allowance that topped up his meagre annual councillor fee of $21,000. When the time came to hand over the mayoral chains, Blackmore wavered, and all hell broke loose.

At the Artisaint cafe in Burwood in early 2023, Blackmore told Pensabene and Maheswaran that he wanted to stay on. Anticipating he might say that, the Labor duo helpfully produced a resignation letter written in Blackmore’s name, and told him to sign it.

Maheswaran allegedly told the mayor: “I’ve got a reputation in the party that if I don’t like someone, they don’t get away with crossing me. It would take me about six weeks to take you down.” Blackmore told Maheswaran to “get f---ed”.

Within days, the campaign to assassinate Blackmore politically was in full swing. He fielded sudden media inquiries about his relationship with the council’s controversial former mayor, Antoine Doueihi. He also received a text message from Pensabene in which she said Maheswaran was preparing to print 20,000 scurrilous flyers. “I tried to stop him but he is angry!” Pensabene wrote.

Two days later, the highly stressed Blackmore found several yellow and white flyers stuck under the windscreen wipers of his car in Homebush. The document was a good old-fashioned political “shit sheet” full of potentially damaging information about Blackmore, including his past legal difficulties. “And this isn’t even the worst of it – more to come,” the flyer promised. That same weekend, Maheswaran messaged Blackmore with a warning: “If I can’t convince you, I can’t convince you. I only thought to reach out before things got more serious.”

Blackmore fought back tears when recounting the incident to the Independent Commission Against Corruption this week. He also broke down when discussing a meeting in the council chambers at 5.15pm on the same day he found the shit sheet. At that meeting, mayoral aspirant Pensabene and her enthusiastic backer Maheswaran again told Blackmore he had to honour his agreement to quit as soon as possible.

Maheswaran then made a bombshell revelation: he’d had “operatives” following the mayor the past five months. “I’ve got recordings of you and transcripts,” he said. He read out at least one transcript of a private conversation that Blackmore instantly recognised.

The mayor was told that his enemies knew he and his wife had bought a new home outside the local government area, which could be a bad look with constituents. Maheswaran also said he knew that the mayoral Toyota RAV4 had been used to drive Blackmore’s family to the NSW South Coast town of Gerringong for a holiday. “All of this will go away when you resign from the mayoralty. It’ll all stop,” Maheswaran allegedly said.

Blackmore relented and agreed to step down on March 7, which he scribbled on a piece of paper. Pensabene took over. Remarkably, Blackmore voted for her to become mayor despite everything that had gone down. Why? Because he had sought and received a guarantee that she would get Maheswaran to back off.

The alleged blackmail plot illustrates how the ICAC’s Operation Rosny probe, which is nearing its conclusion after eight weeks of explosive public hearings, is much more than an investigation into dodgy donations or breaches of electoral laws. It is a reminder that democracy in NSW is still at risk of being bought, sold, and weaponised.

Under the laws pledged by the then-premier Dominic Perrottet, all third-party and in-house lobbyists would be required to register with a new lobbying regulator and all MPs – not just ministers – would need to disclose their diaries each month. Senior political advisers would also be precluded from engaging in any lobbying relating to any matter that they had official dealings with in their last 12 months in a government office.

The laws were never introduced by the Coalition or Minns Labor government. The Herald has been told the government is monitoring Operation Rosny closely and will consider a package of reforms likely to come next year once commissioner Fabian Gleeson, SC, hands down his report.

In some ways, the Strathfield saga shows that the public accountability system in NSW can work well. It turns out that Blackmore lodged a complaint with the ICAC over the affair in early 2023; so too did the council’s general manager, Michael Mamo, who had been briefed on the ugly political tussle. The tip-offs immediately attracted the watchdog’s attention, and a senior officer wrote back seeking more information. The chain of events ensured the incident was investigated as part of Operation Rosny.

The ICAC is investigating Maheswaran for dishonestly or partially exercising his official functions, as well as potential blackmail offences and breaches of the Surveillance Devices Act. An aggravated form of blackmail can include threatening to make an accusation that the victim has committed a serious indictable offence – something the flyers left on Blackmore’s car potentially did.

But what unfolded in Strathfield is probably not an isolated incident in the world of local government, which is being overrun by ambitious or compliant party operatives instead of genuine community representatives. Some senior political figures such as John Howard believe political parties should not field candidates for councils. The former prime minister has called the involvement of the Liberal Party in council chambers “crazy”, and a distraction from the main game of the state and federal arenas.

The push to build 800,000 new homes in Sydney over the next 20 years also heightens the risk of undue influence being applied to councils dealing with rezoning and development applications.

The ICAC has for more than five years argued for lobbying regulations to apply to local government, but neither the Coalition nor Labor have made it happen.

At the same time he was orchestrating various political plots at Strathfield Council, Maheswaran was also a senior executive for the Toplace development firm run by fugitive Sydney developer Jean Nassif. The ICAC has heard evidence that he was one of the top henchmen for Nassif, who fled to Lebanon in 2022 and whose company collapsed in 2023 owing $2 billion to home owners, small business operators and others.

Toplace paid Maheswaran nearly $850,000 over just two years.

Exactly why he and his lackey Pensabene went to such lengths to get Blackmore out of the mayoral seat at Strathfield Council remains unclear. He clearly angered them by not honouring a deal to stand aside, and is no angel himself.

In taking the mayoralty for himself in 2022, Blackmore double-crossed a group of independent councillors he had signed an agreement with over which of them would share the top job. He admits to signing the document without any intention of honouring it. And when he was being pressured to quit, Blackmore engaged in threats of his own by telling Maheswaran that he had a photograph of his Subaru Forester parked in the same street as a Croydon brothel, noting “it wouldn’t be good if that photo came out”.

None of this made for harmonious relations. But the ICAC appears to be probing other potential motivations behind Maheswaran’s actions.

In his lengthy written complaint to the ICAC, Blackmore noted that Maheswaran was particularly interested in making sure the council, rather than the state government, led a 30-year plan for the rezoning and redevelopment of Parramatta Road – a potential boon for developers (the strategy was eventually run by the government and promises to deliver 27,000 new homes). This topic also came up in questioning at the ICAC this week.

Curiously, when Blackmore threatened to resign from council entirely over the alleged blackmail plot, Maheswaran apparently urged him to stay – possibly because he needed his vote in the future. “I am concerned that if Sharangan Maheswaran wants to ensure a proposed motion is passed at a council meeting he will continually threaten to publish the information he has obtained about me if I do not vote the way he wants me to vote,” Blackmore wrote in his complaint to the ICAC.

While Strathfield Council was imploding, across the harbour a group of Liberal Party operatives were busy practising their own subversion of democracy. As has now been well ventilated, Charles and Jean-Claude Perrottet, two brothers of the former premier Dominic Perrottet, as well as Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood, allegedly took illegal donations from prohibited donors – including Nassif – in exchange for pursuing political outcomes in Macquarie Street and Sydney’s north-west.

Maheswaran played a starring role as a middleman for Nassif and the conservative Christian Liberal figures. For example, when Charles Perrottet messaged Nassif asking if he could pick up “assistance for the upcoming preselections”, it was Maheswaran who arranged a cheque for $148,500 and gave it to him at the Longueville Hotel.

The ICAC has previously heard Maheswaran also organised private investigator Shane De Kauwe to surveil Toplace critic-in-chief David Elliott in an attempt to dig up damaging information on the then-police minister. De Kauwe has previously told the Herald he “plays with a straight bat” and said allegations about his conduct were untrue.

De Kauwe, a former AFP detective, was also part of the operation to tail Blackmore, the Strathfield mayor. “It’s changed my view about people and safety,” Blackmore says of him and his family being followed. “I can’t go to sleep without checking my house is locked.”

The ICAC says Maheswaran deployed the same playbook in Strathfield as he did in north-west Sydney: damaging and discrediting those who stood in his way. Australian Border Force officials seized his phone and laptop at Sydney Airport in 2023 just days after police raids on Nassif’s home and office.

Maheswaran – a lawyer since 2016, who now works at a firm founded by former senator Nick Xenophon – has been stalking the ICAC proceedings for the past two months, regularly drifting in and out of the hearing room as witnesses provided evidence. He’s even been posting on social media platform X about the proceedings.

Maheswaran will be asked for his version of events, including the serious allegations made about his conduct, at the ICAC next week. Pensabene has also been named by the agency as a key person of interest, but has been released from her summons due to a medical condition.

Maheswaran is no longer on Strathfield Council, but Pensabene is. Both have been suspended from the Labor Party.

If Matthew Blackmore had hoped his troubles would be over after relinquishing the Strathfield mayoralty, he was sadly mistaken.

In the months that followed, Maheswaran lodged his own complaint to the ICAC, accusing Blackmore of having, among other things, inappropriate dealings with Antoine Doueihi and Charbel Demian – two developers who have had various encounters with regulators over the years.

By this time Blackmore had also attracted a new enemy: Mohammad Abedin, a controversial one-time real estate agent who has been convicted of embezzlement and once received a good behaviour bond after screaming homophobic abuse at a Homebush barista who accidentally sprayed cleaning liquid on him.

Abedin ran the Innerwest Property real estate agency and Blackmore worked with him there, bringing in some valuable business. But a dispute over money soured the relationship. Abedin swiftly turned against him and embraced Maheswaran.

When ICAC investigators emailed Abedin’s office asking for any CCTV footage showing the “shit sheet” flyers being placed on the mayor’s car earlier that year, Abedin forwarded the email to his new friend Maheswaran, tipping him off that the ICAC was looking into him.

“You were trying to help him, weren’t you?” counsel assisting the commission Juliet Curtin asked Abedin. He replied: “It wasn’t help. It was just saying what I received.” Curtin didn’t buy that, or many of the other things Abedin told the ICAC this week.

In his complaint to the ICAC following the alleged blackmail plot, Blackmore said the whole experience had altered his life. “I still am in shock that what happened to me could happen in a local council.”

‘I never want to be that sick again’: Judith Lucy on what happened at a healing retreat in Peru

Sydney Morning Herald September 19, 2026

The comedian on burnout, feeling unfulfilled, middle-class guilt – and what has (and hasn’t) worked in tackling it all.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Judith Lucy is a workaholic. A stand-up comic since her 20s – she’s now 58 – and a regular TV and radio performer, Lucy has mined her personal travails including disastrous relationships, too much drinking and the indignities of ageing in her famous sardonic drawl. Life was work, until it wasn’t. In 2023, she had a “burnout”, and she’s turned her discoveries into a book about that deep exhaustion.

In 2023, you had what you call a burnout. What happened? I now look back and the burnout part started when I had COVID in lockdown in Adelaide, and the thought of doing stand-up ever again just made me want to cry and repeatedly punch myself in the face. And then, as luck would have it, I was offered the role of Winnie in the MTC’s [Melbourne Theatre Company] production of Happy Days, which I still can’t quite believe. It wasn’t great timing because I was at a point where I just needed a break, but of course, there is no business like showbusiness, so off I went. When I finished the play, I went to Perth. I thought, “I’m finally going to have a holiday.” I got really sick. Up until that point, I simply didn’t believe in burnout. If I’m really honest about it, I thought, “Oh yeah, sure, people are a bit lazy and weak,” with no judgment whatsoever.

What did it feel like for you? Exhaustion that I had never experienced before. Like I couldn’t get out of bed, was so tired, but also just a kind of grab bag of symptoms. I’m anxious anyway, but that just went through the roof. My digestion’s always been a problem and that went off the charts. Nausea, lack of appetite, freezing cold feet, inflammation went nuts. I was not exactly walking on sunshine. I came back to Melbourne, and my first alarm bell was that I didn’t want to come back to Melbourne, and that was crazy because I love Melbourne. I was meant to have a meeting with my management, which sounds like I’m a great deal more famous than I am. I couldn’t sleep at all the night before, and at some point during that evening, I just went, “Oh my god, I think I have to accept that this is what burnout feels like” because the idea of having any plans, just the thought of it made me want to cry. I went in the next day and said I need six months off, and that was the start of me going, “Holy hell, what now?”

There are a lot of laugh-out-loud jokes in your new book, Well, Well, Well. But it’s quite a serious book, too, isn’t it? I’m very deep, Gay.

You are. It’s taking this experience and thinking, “What is this?” I’ve got to my mid-50s and I just don’t feel happy. I don’t feel fulfilled. I thought work was going to fulfil me, but it doesn’t any more. How can I try to work out how to feel better, or how to feel less shit?

What does work in this era for a middle-aged person who – and a lot of us are like this – just doesn’t feel happy or fulfilled despite outward success? ”Wellness” is such an enormous umbrella. I got into yoga in my early 30s. I’ve always been interested in it for material because some of it is so ludicrous. But I think we all know that half the stuff about wellness, like meditation, like breath work, is great. And then there’s stuff like drinking your own urine.

We all know about midlife crises and mine really seemed to start about 15 years ago, and I don’t know that it’s ever going to end. But a lot of us reach that point in our life where we go, “Hang on a minute, I’ve done all the stuff.” In my case, I obviously didn’t have a family, but I did throw myself into work and worked hard and achieved a certain amount of success, and there were many aspects of my life that I certainly was happy with. But then I just sort of looked around and went, “I’ve never actually asked myself what I wanted my life to look like,” and I couldn’t believe that it had taken me up into my mid-50s to ask myself that.

You mention in the book a few times that wellness can be seen as middle-class or self-indulgent compared to people who haven’t got enough to eat. What did you mean? At the risk of making myself throw up here, I think, no matter who you are, you’ve got to work that stuff out, and once you have your basic needs met – and I am lucky that I am certainly a person who’s had those needs met – everyone needs love and joy and purpose, and I had lost sight of all of that. But yes, I still feel like a wanker. A privileged wanker.

What helped you feel better in the end? I was trying to live differently in terms of the things that we all know that are good for us, like being out in nature, like connection, like purpose. I was also making myself go outside a lot more, making myself take swimming lessons, for example. I was trying to find out what actually brought me joy.

Some things have stuck with you, like yoga and meditation. Can you talk about what they mean to you? Yoga is something I will do forever. I have very bad shoulder issues, and when that happened, I did get into Pilates. I’m a middle-class, middle-aged white woman so of course I do Pilates. One of the big lessons I learnt is to listen to your f---ing body, and that’s why I would recommend yoga if it’s your thing. Meditation came and went a lot more, but since the burnout happened, I’ve really doubled down on the meditation. The more I learnt about my brain, the more I wanted to meditate.

When I read your book, I related to it. It was “Oh, I’ve read that book you quoted,” and “I’ve tried internal family systems” and “I’ve been in a float tank.” Why are women more drawn to try to make themselves feel better, or do men just do it in different ways? Women tend to be more open to trying different things. Maybe it’s still not seen as very masculine by some people, some men, which is a shame because there are some great things out there, and I’ve thought on many an occasion that if straight men knew what going to a yoga class was like: it’s fish in a barrel, guys. You’re like one man with 30 women. We’re all wearing virtually nothing and going into some very interesting postures. Unfortunately, because of the patriarchy and the way of the world, there is a level of stress that women deal with, and I’m not saying that men aren’t dealing with stress, of course they are … but women live with sexism every single day. We’re not allowed to age. We’re not allowed to be overweight. Of course, we’re looking for things to fix us and women are constantly going, “Oh my god, if I have this juice, that could make me look younger,” and “Maybe I’ll lose some weight,” and “Quick, where’s my five minutes of gratitude?”

One of the things you did was a 12-day trip to the Amazon. That’s a much bigger thing to do than float in a tank for an hour. What interested you about that? Tell us about the experience. It may have been one of the worst things I’ve ever done. I was reading Gabor Maté’s book, The Myth of Normal, where he talks about how society is basically making us all sick, which I completely agree with. And then, just out of nowhere, there was a chapter about his experience of going to a place called the Temple of the Way of Light [a shamanic healing centre in the Peruvian Amazon]. I had heard of ayahuasca [a traditional plant medicine] years ago.

What is it? It’s illegal in Australia, I think [ayahuasca is a schedule 9 prohibited substance]. It’s been used by Indigenous peoples for a very long time, and particularly in the Amazon, the Shipibo people, so I was aware of it. I’ve always been interested in mind-altering substances – I mean, to relax, because I’m way too uptight – but also because I am just interested. I thought that if I’m going to do it, damn it, I want to go to the Amazon rainforest.

It’s six ceremonies, using ayahuasca, and all the information you get about it is that this is going to change your life. It is set up in all the literature as a hero’s journey. It’s a plant that has been used for thousands of years and this is going to help clear you of your negative energies. It can help you mentally, physically, spiritually, dealing with addiction, dealing with abuse, all sorts of things.

There were 21 of us from all over the world. We took a bus and a boat, and then there was a trek through this incredible muddy jungle. And then we arrived at the temple, which was incredible. Just very simple huts with fly-wire, just basically a bed, a desk, a hammock, a toilet. Thank Christ, the most enormous pile of toilet paper I’ve ever seen in my life.

So what happened? You do an hour-and-a-half of gentle yoga before (the ceremony). After that, we would wait for the healers to arrive. It was actually a tea that was made from several plants. We would all take it in turn, going up, getting our tea. The first one, we all got just the tiniest amount so they could work out what everyone’s tolerance level was.

The second ceremony was when I really had my head blown off. It’s unlike anything I have ever done, it’s like a tidal wave. I don’t know if anything can quite prepare you for it, but it just feels like it’s crashing over you. Ayahuasca is known for making people vomit or have diarrhoea. I really leant towards the diarrhoea side of things, but that second ceremony I felt pretty great. Even though I was experiencing pain and nausea, (there was also) incredible euphoria. Then it was just this incredible feeling of kind of “Oh my god, everything’s perfect, everything’s inevitable.” I remember the next day just feeling amazing, thinking, “Oh my god! By the end of this, I’m going to start my own cult.”

And then things took a turn. I just got physically really unwell. The diarrhoea was no longer just happening as part of the ceremony. The diarrhoea was all the time. I was exhausted, and the ceremonies were awful. I was in chronic pain, the worst headaches I’ve ever had. It felt like someone had gotten a machete in either hand and was stabbing me in my lower and upper abdomen.

I got back to Melbourne and I kept waiting to feel better. I went to my poor GP – I say my poor GP because I’ve given that woman so many stool samples over the years. She sent me off to a gastroenterologist, and at the point of the gastroenterologist telling me that I needed to take a worming tablet, I thought this feels a long way from enlightenment. After doing some tests, she said, “You picked up two viruses while you were over there, and you’ll never know how much that impacted you.”

Two years after this trip, oh my goodness! It’s like I started with shit, and I’ve ended with it. What happened is, she said, “these viruses have completely stripped your digestive system, and you need to go on the FODMAP diet,” which I have done in the past. I thought, screw that. I know the diet pretty well, so I thought, “I’m just going to eat sensibly, be really healthy, and I’m sure I’ll be able to sort myself out.” But while the other burnout symptoms started to improve, the digestive stuff never ever got better. And finally, a faecal transplant was suggested.

I’ve never heard of it. Had you? Oh yes I had, because I’ve had gut issues for years. It’s basically someone else’s faeces. If your gut microbiome is a mess, you basically want to get someone else’s good gut bacteria.

Good material. Oh boy, it sure is. What a shit show!

How are you now? You’ve moved back to Melbourne. You’ve got digestive issues that are ongoing. Have you got a different approach to work now? We’ll see, won’t we? That is the challenge. I came back to Melbourne because Melbourne is home. I am in a much better place than I was before I went to Perth. The only thing that was really bad was the digestive stuff, and I’m only a few weeks out from that, and they say to you, it takes at least four to six weeks to for it to all calm down, and I am better this week than I have been. I am optimistic that once this calms down, I will actually feel pretty great.

I’ve introduced a lot of new habits into my life, from gardening to cooking to playing the guitar. I’ve got plans to do a show and a podcast, and we’ll just have to see if I can balance it. But I never want to be that sick again, and I never want to not work again. So my belief is that if I keep listening to my body, I can’t go wrong.

The heartbreaking question Mick Fanning asked his mum after losing three brothers

Sydney Morning Herald September 19, 2026

After three world titles, a shark attack, and the deaths of his three big brothers, the universe has been both generous and unforgiving to the champion surfer.

You really couldn’t script a more perfect moment for meeting Mick Fanning. A blazing sun rises from the watery horizon to the east, throwing golden light onto sandy Coolangatta, while a breezy, briny combo of spray and spit kicks up off the Pacific Ocean sky and into our eyes. A strange hippie woman is dancing and bellowing and smacking clap sticks together on the beach – she’s a regular here, apparently – while fishermen cast for bream off the big black basalt rocks on the headland. Oh, and there’s an old dude nearby smoking a very fat spliff.

This place – Snapper Rocks, at the quiet southern edge of the Gold Coast – is already putting on a show for us when a brush turkey struts through a clearing, an eagle arcs on the wind, and a rainbow – no, wait, a pair of rainbows? – beams down on Rainbow Bay ­(seriously), where fearless, frothing grommets carve lacerating turns into the famous point break.

Fanning, meanwhile, stands barefoot in jeans and T-shirt, blond stubble over anvil jaw – a study in coiled power – posing for a picture. And that’s when it ­happens – the ludicrous exclamation mark on this preposterously pretty scene. As his blue steel eyes lock in on the lens for the money shot, an enormous humpback whale breaches – right behind him – before smashing back down into the blue and sending a surge of foam skyward.

Fanning, now 45 and with smile lines betraying his years, offers a knowing yet grateful grin. “We’re so lucky. People travel all the way around the world for this,” he says. “But to me, it’s the place where I grew up, the place where I learnt my skills. It’s home. It’s a place to reconnect with Mother Nature, but also with yourself. A place where you just switch off.”

Mick Fanning: 'There's no right or wrong way to deal with grief'

Three-time world surfing champion Mick Fanning on how the loss of loved ones has shaped him and his success.

If anyone has earned the right to just switch off, it’s Michael Eugene Fanning. Don’t know his life story? Allow me to share the cinematic crib notes.

Once a bleach-blond quicksilver teenage surfer, he becomes a three-time world champion (in 2007, 2009 and 2013). Then in 2015, he punches a great white shark off the coast of South Africa. As you do. He ­becomes a meme – “Unless someone defeats ISIS with a boomerang,” went one tweet, “then Mick Fanning definitely wins Australian of the Year, right?” – but he also experiences recurring night terrors and triggering moments in the water.

Far more pivotal to his life story, however, is his family, much of which is taken cruelly from him. Fanning once had three big brothers – Sean, Peter and Ed – but all died early, after (respectively) a car accident, a heart condition and a badly infected wound. His dad, John, sipped his last Guinness earlier this year before slipping away, too. His sister Rachel lives overseas, but his doting mum, Liz, lives just down the road (thankfully).

Fanning’s been married and divorced – now remarried with two kids – and I’m wondering what an ­average day looks like after he cooks brekkie for the family, kisses wife Bree at the door, does the school run for son Xander, 6, and daughter Lyla, 2, then later ferries them between soccer practice and dance lessons. What does his middle-aged dream life look like?

“Being a fat old retired surfer!” says Fanning, laughing. “I guess I just want to show my kids the world that I had – seeing all the beautiful places, the beautiful cultures – and exposing them to how incredible life is.” But he also wants them to understand the importance of the values that helped him survive and thrive through tragedy and triumph. Namely kindness, and resilience. And heart. “You never want to be scared to take that unknown step,” he says. “You’ve only got one shot at life – you might as well give it all you’ve got.”

Everything starts with Sean. Ask anyone. Three years older, Sean was his closest brother both in age and temperament – his best mate and ­biggest supporter, too. “Don’t get a big head,” he used to tell little Mick. “Otherwise, I’ll come and bash it in.”

Liz points to a photo of them on the wall of her ocean-view apartment, arm-in-arm as kids, and then to framed images of her eldest sons, too. When Ed, 48, died in 2024, having cut himself on coral in Madagascar (then failing to recover from the infected wound), she remembers how Mick offered up a vulnerable and plaintive question: “Mum, is this going to happen to me? Am I not going to be here, too?” When Pete, 43, died in his sleep from a heart condition in 2015, she adds, Mick was again tender and beautiful – “Mum, let me make you a cup of coffee” – but he was also bereft.

Sean’s death was different. That particular grief was an ocean. Vast. Powerful. Bottomless.

Mick had grown up as the youngest sibling, the ­protected one – an affectionate, happy, athletic boy – and maybe even a bit of a sook. “He probably slept with me until he was 12 years old,” Liz says. “He just wanted to be with me.” Sean was his boyish ballast and source of confidence. “They were like two little peas in a pod. Very close, always,” she murmurs. “When Sean passed away, Mick spent one week in his room. He wouldn’t come out, he was so grief-stricken. Because they were always going to do it all together.”

Fanning opens up about Sean to Good Weekend on the lookout atop Kirra Hill, which looms over the town, but before he can dive into the memory, he sketches out their shared world below. There’s Point Danger to the east, and there – “See it?” – the apartment block with the blue roof where they grew up. He traces a line down the beach to where every Australian surf season began with what’s now called the Gold Coast Pro. “If you looked out on a competition day, that was just thousands of people lined up and celebrating. It was nuts,” he says, wistfully. “Then everyone would spill into the surf club and get raging drunk.”

Next comes Greenmount, Coolangatta, and down the cliff from where we’re standing, Kirra – “arguably in the top five waves in the world when it’s on” – then Bilinga, Currumbin, Burleigh, Nobbys, Broadbeach and finally, to the far north-west, “Gotham City”, meaning Surfers Paradise. And the biography behind the geography?

“Oh mate,” he says, shaking his head, “there’s a lot of ghosts in this town. Too many.”

Fanning gestures to the main street of Cooly: stay on this side of the road and you were safe, but cross after dark and things’d get gnarly. “Dingo” lived that way, he points, across the road from the old Pizza Hut, and “Parko” a few blocks away. And that road running ­perpendicular to the beach, one block inland? That’s where Sean died at 20, when Fanning was just 17. Later he points out the median strip where the car hit a tree, but right now, his eyes turn forward to a little memorial up here on the hill. Sean’s ashes are buried here, next to a stone surfboard and a native frangipani, flowering with little clusters of white and yellow petals.

“When it first happened, I would run up here every morning in the dark and water the trees,” Fanning says. “This has all changed, though.”

This was the place where “the Cooly kids” would party. If anyone in the crew won an event they’d put on a keg for the others, and the whole town would converge. In Fanning’s new memoir, he describes a New Year’s Eve up here only a year after Sean passed – passing a bottle of Bundy while watching the reflection of the fireworks on the seaboard. It’s well after sunset on the last night of the ­millennium, he writes, and it feels like we’re on the brink of something momentous.

When you meet him in person, a thing that stands out about Mick Fanning is just how little he stands out. Maybe it’s the black hoodie or the way he’s hiding under the bill of a green corduroy cap. He almost makes his five foot 10 (178 centimetres), 75-kilogram stature look like a conscious decision – an understated touch ­designed to disarm.

The frame fits the personality, too. He’s quieter and more gentle than you might ­expect. When summoning his old black mutt, Harper, he makes kissing sounds in the air, and she comes waddling to his side before drifting into sighing slumber at his feet. Good girl.

We sit at a cafe watching golden-haired grannies buzz up and down the footpath on electric gophers, and barefoot boys with soaked rashies amble past on the way to the board store. Fanning was once one of them, though perhaps not so carefree.

“Mick was just turbo-thrust into adulthood with the passing of Sean. That changed the dynamic of his existence,” says Ronnie Blakey, his manager, who was writing for Tracks magazine when Fanning came up. “He went from being a kid who was living his best life to someone who was suddenly burdened by this ­incredible grief.”

But it also grew inside him curiosity and empathy. He was the good listener on tour – the wise kid who found solace in the surf. “There’s a saying: ‘Only a surfer knows the feeling,’” says his longtime coach, Phil McNamara. “You have to understand the therapeutic nature of being in the ocean, often on your own, and the feeling you get when you’re struggling, just from making it to the end of the wave.”

He didn’t have long to dwell. Fanning joined the tour at 18 and found himself carrying boards down cobbled streets in Portugal, drinking caipirinhas in Ipanema and flipping out over the boardwalk freak show in Venice Beach, California. He started winning, too.

“It’s the best shit ever. Your heroes are ringing you up to go have a beer, and no one’s telling you you can’t,” he says. “It’s like going on school camp with no teachers. There were no rules.”

He did well to resist the worst of it, largely with help from McNamara, who preached a new type of professionalism by breaking the sport down into its quantifiable components. Focusing on wave selection and error elimination, McNamara kept tabs on the number of forehands and backhands he was surfing, and they would go hunting those conditions to equalise his practice count – basically hunting reps. Many were leery of the calculated approach – almost suspicious that trying too hard would ruin the instinctive magic of the act.

“Read that as this: there was an underlying drug culture and social malaise in surfing and Coolangatta that Mick and I were desperate to avoid,” says McNamara, who was often openly abused by other surfers on the beach for being a kind of sober “sellout”, as if he was spoiling the sport itself. “I wasn’t in that lifestyle – I didn’t drink – so I was a good foil for him, standing in as the bad cop: ‘The coach says I can’t go out tonight.’ ”

Fanning also found a new work ethic through injury after his hamstring was torn off the bone in Sumatra in 2004, necessitating a gory operation where they sliced his buttock cheek open, peeled it back and screwed a metal hook into his hipbone. The gruelling rehabilitation that followed demanded everything from core strength work to yoga. “It opened up this whole level I’d never been able to get to, because I never thought I needed that work,” Fanning says. “I finally figured out that this is what training looks like, this is what a diet looks like, and this is how it feels when you get up and surf after doing all of that.”

He’s had a few nicknames over the years. White Lightning for his bright blond teenage locks. Eugene – his middle name – for the excitable mayhem merchant he becomes after a few too many. The crew came up with another nickname for his newly robotic mindset. They called him Cyborg.

His mum, a “Ten-pound Pom” who had worked long hours as a nurse before climbing into senior administrative hospital roles, took over his finances at his request. Joining him on tour, she also reminded him that brands weren’t just buying performance but association, encouraging him to consider what it means to be marketable. Yes, Mark Occhilupo was a world champion – but also a loveable comeback story. Sure, Rob Machado was one of the most stylish surfers ever – but his charisma extended beyond the water. She told him everything he needed to hear. “Don’t mess with her,” Fanning cautions. “She’s a powerful woman. We call her The Lioness.”

Finally, he had help from leading sports psychologist Dr Michael Gervais, the Californian author of Finding Mastery, who he began seeing in 2009. They practised breathing exercises and visualisation techniques – conjuring the sight of an approaching swell, the sound of a wave, the feel of water on skin. They also talked about Sean.

“I wasn’t there to have a cry, but I walked in and he just kept probing,” says Fanning, who realised he’d become adept at telling people the quick version – never loosening the knot enough to share his whole story. “I didn’t realise I was holding on to so much pain and grief,” he says. “I thought about the kind of things people tell boys, like ‘Be strong’, and I think now, to tell a 17-year-old kid who’s lost his brother to be strong, what the f--- does that even mean?”

Surfing is a sport that lends itself to psychedelic hyperbole. It’s all monstrous closeouts and grinding slabs – thick lip pitches and bright blue drainers. Once in a while, man, you even fang it into a collapsing freefall – a cataclysmic detonation of wash. Yet none of that elicits the resonant fear of a single black fin.

When Fanning came face-to-face with a great white shark in Jeffreys Bay, South Africa, in 2015, it ­appeared to him as a dark shadow, then a splash. Next came a violent lurch and full-body panic.

Mick Fanning attacked by shark

The three-time world champion was competing in the final of an event at Jeffreys Bay in South Africa when a huge shark launched at him.

In the viral video from that day, it’s hard to tell exactly what is happening but essentially, a three-metre predator bites into his leg rope and knocks him off his board, at which point Fanning begins flailing blindly. He’s hidden behind a wave in much of that competition footage, and this is the precise moment when ­reality really bites, when, underwater, he starts to yell and scream, punch and kick. The next thing you know he’s being ferried to shore on a jet ski. He looks ­composed, too, but that ride is one of maniacal laughter and nervous giggles, his pupils dilated into empty black holes.

He was, he says now, “shitfaced” on adrenaline and relief. On shore, people began hugging him and weeping, which is when the gravity of the moment – the cold horror of what almost happened – kicked in. He did interviews right away, because it was the quickest way to let ­family and friends know he was safe, and so the story went global. His phone began pulsing like a strobe light, practically melting down, and in the ensuing days he found himself hounded by crews from Europe and the US, the Middle East and Asia.

“He only did media to feed them something, so the story would die, but the attack of the media was almost worse than the attack of the shark,” says Blakey, who tried to manage the press. “They were insatiable. People camping in front of his house. The attention was so confronting.”

Then the dreams began – vivid nightmares back on the water, his legs dangling in damp darkness. Fanning woke regularly to the sound of his own screams, and the feeling of his heartbeat and cold sweats. He had PTSD.

“But I feel like I’ve done enough work to give myself the tools to deal with that emotion,” he says. “When someone else is attacked, it just reaffirms how lucky I actually was, and how lucky I am to have 10 fingers and 10 toes. But I don’t go out of my way to talk about it and make it my identity. I don’t want to be that guy.”

He made a few changes, the most public being to the colour underneath his boards, which used to be a specific fluorescent hue – “yum yum yellow” – which marine experts speculated might attract ­curious sharks. The biggest change, though, he says, was becoming statistically driven. “It happened, but what was the chance of that, what’s the chance of it happening again, and how does it compare to the chance of crossing the road and being hit by a car? I had to look at it that way. And after the initial shock, that was enough.”

Mick Fanning first surfed big waves – truly big ones – in Oahu, Hawaii. The water there is raw, with ocean storms generating giant swells that break with immense power over deathly shallow volcanic reefs. He has no shame in admitting that when he first saw such conditions, he freaked out. Completely.]

Hale’iwa is raging, he writes. A giant, surging, ­triple-overhead rip bowl that’ll just as quickly suck you out to sea as it will hold you on the inside and unload set after set directly onto your head in a never-ending ­impact-zone washing machine.

His coping method? “Get out into it,” he says. “Get the mind, body and equipment right, and a feeling that you belong. Then you have to paddle out, and it’s terrifying. There are people who just freeze. I didn’t.”

He says that probably comes back to his first game of footy as a five-year-old, when young Mick came up against a kid that looms in childhood memory as every inch of a six-foot-four giant. His brother Peter was adamant – “You’ve gotta go tackle him” – which young Mick promptly did, because the fear of his brothers ragging on him later was worse than a ­couple of stitches.

In time, he developed another method for psyching himself up ahead of such pulverising conditions. He’d get angry. Hot-headed. “I’d just start swearing at myself,” he says. “My Gemini kicks in and there’s one guy whispering, ‘Hold on,’ and one guy whispering, ‘Go you weak c---, go!’, and you’re to-ing and fro-ing between the scared one and the crazy one. You go into fight-or-flight, and I’d always choose fight.”

That wasn’t so simple, however, at the Pipe Masters event in Oahu in December 2015, chasing his fourth world title. It had already been a tough year, starting with separation from his wife, Karissa. The book goes into their split in some detail, not with prurience or bitterness but an open and elegant explanation for how busy people often drift apart.

“It was hard for me to switch off,” explains Fanning. “Even if we went on holidays, it was hard for me to enjoy drinking good wine or eating good food and, definitely, being away from the ocean. But there was no malice,” he notes. “If there’s a lesson, it’s that when you’re in the room, you’ve gotta be in the room. It would be the same thing for busy ­lawyers or FIFO workers.”

After the marriage breakdown came the shark ­attack; then, on the eve of the event in Hawaii, those psychotic North Shore waves maimed a trio of his mates in quick succession. Bede Durbige was thrown onto coral and suffered a broken pelvis and ­internal bleeding. Owen Wright was wiped out, too, the full force of the waves that hit him causing a traumatic brain injury. Young Floridian surfer Evan Geiselman was demolished, then rescued from the water by Fanning and others, before being taken to hospital limp, his face blue and blank. Then the news broke. Fanning’s brother Peter had died at home after his ­enlarged heart – caused by a hyperthyroid problem – gave out in his sleep.

Just to summarise, then. In 12 months, Fanning’s marriage ended, he was attacked by a shark, his brother died, and three friends were sent to hospital by the very surf he was meant to ride, while defending his world title. He got in the water anyway. “I just had this feeling I knew Pete would keep me safe, and that nothing was going to happen,” he says. “Then I went into this other mode: I am going to f---ing send it.”

As soon as he dived into the waves, it was the most confident he’s ever been when faced with that familiar terror. He didn’t get the title, but everything was easy and free-flowing and fine. “You grit your teeth and grind through it,” he explains. “That’s life. It’s like a rollercoaster, up and down, and sometimes you do a few loops.”

If that sounds a little mystic, superstitious or hippie-dippy, I’m sorry, but if it wasn’t already abundantly clear, I’m here to tell you that Fanning is a sentimental and spiritual soul.

When he first started touring, for instance, he would head to Kirra Hill and pocket a leaf from Sean’s frangipani tree, put it in his wallet, then drop it in the water wherever he went in the world. He sees his brothers in flickering ceiling lights and slow sunrises. His mum’s voice trembles while telling me how, just before he won a world title in Brazil, a dolphin kept knocking up against his board: “When Mick came in from the win he said, ‘My brother was out there! I know it was my brother!’ ”

He’s seen a medium and sat with his eyes closed, imagining a ball of white energy shooting through the top of his head, where it turns into a fountain of raindrops. Every now and then he’ll be driving down the road and get sucker-punched by a brotherly memory, and other days he’ll summon those spirits himself, asking them for courage or a decent wave. He feels their energy every time. A crazy, cheeky life force from Sean. Calm confidence from Peter. Ed shows up to mess with his baby daughter, he thinks, keeping her awake. “Look, I’m not burning incense – not ­totally woo-woo – but I’ve always had this belief that energy stays. Always,” he says. “There’s no right or wrong way to heal.”

He thinks travel has a way of healing the soul, too. Makes sense. We wander the world for a sense of harmony and perspective, less to lose ourselves than to find ourselves – not to fall in love with places but with the version of ourselves those places make possible. Near the end of his career, an ­episodic search for the perfect wave (filmed by Rip Curl) ­became a critical form of self-soothing.

Once a control freak, Fanning was now a ­passenger on the most magical ride. He surfed choppy waves off the Cliffs of Moher in Ireland, icy slush ripples in Alaska (created by gargantuan blocks of glacier plunging into the sea), and at the dark mouth of a fjord in Norway, lit only by the twisting purple and neon green ripples of the aurora borealis.

Naturally, it grew harder to imagine resuming a life of press conferences and corporate keynotes. He had won three world titles, but the next competitor for him to chase and catch was the inimitable Kelly Slater, sitting on 11 titles, too far away. Still, giving up was tricky.

He would swear he was done and then every season would start right back at Snapper Rocks (his home break) before moving to Bells Beach (the site of his first major victory), creating an annual temptation to go again. And again. No one in his circle wanted him to quit, either. “Even I would semi-discourage him from retiring,” says Blakey. ” ‘Why don’t you take a few friends on the road with you? Why don’t you pick and choose your events?’ But he wasn’t built that way.”

He also began to realise the weight of all the barbecues and celebrations he had piked on or ducked out of early to train and compete. The cumulative personal cost was too great, because here’s another thing about Fanning: he’s a creature of community.

I spend two days with him and witness more than a dozen authentic interactions with people he knows and people he doesn’t. He’s polite and dutiful to a fault. A publicist fights with an umbrella and Fanning pipes up: “Need a hand?” A photographer struggles shifting a trolley full of gear and Fanning is there: “Need a hand?” A wet bench needs to be dried with paper towel, and you better believe Fanning is on the spot: “Need a hand?” (He never waits for an answer, either – just gets to work.)

He took that to the nth degree in 2022, when flooding swallowed the nearby Northern Rivers town of Murwillumbah – an entire landscape reduced to a brown, churning lagoon. Fanning and his mates spent a week on their jet skis, ferrying people to safety, helping a chemist deliver medications and bringing generator fuel to a local hospital, while their partners were on boat ramps preparing lunches and gathering donations. “It was this whole community of people putting themselves second,” he says. “Even though it was really tragic for a lot of people who lost everything, there was a lot of beauty in how strong community can be.”

He turned that effort into an annual golf day to raise funds for affected families, because if there’s something else Fanning knows well, outside of ­surfing, it’s money. He’s a multimillionaire, in fact, with investments in everything from a seaweed ­supplement for cattle (Sea Forest) to a sustainable dog food (Scratch). “The phone never stops ringing,” he says. “But I can be in as much as I want or out as much as I want.”

His earliest success was a pair of personally branded Reef sandals with a bottle opener built into the sole. He gets a small cut of every pair sold, thanks to his mum’s insistence. “I think they’ve sold about 7 million pairs,” he says. “That was a giant fluke.”

Then there was the craft beer Balter, an idea conceived in 2014 with a few mates, because … free beer for life sounded good? He did everything from mopping spillage between kegs to coming up with the name, along with a governing philosophy: no one is bigger than the brand. “Whether you’re a founder or first day on the job,” he says, “everyone gets treated the same.”

Balter was sold in 2019 to Carlton & United Breweries for about $200 million, leaving a question in the air for Fanning about whether to drift from business into sleepy, well-heeled retirement. “Do I want to be in an office every day, do I want to travel every day, do I want to do a podcast?” he asks. “I dibbled and dabbled.”

Dibbled and dabbled? Fanning has further ­interests in a protein powder and his own eco surfboards, not to mention diverse real estate holdings – plus sponsorships and ambassadorships into retirement. He quit surfing in 2018 and, one year later, Rip Curl signed him to a new 10-year deal, his appeal – and acumen – seemingly unmatched. “He knows when a good idea is under his nose,” says Blakey. “I don’t say no to anything on his behalf, even if I don’t like it at all.”

When we speak, he’s just finished a week filming a new American Express campaign, and the Land Rover Defender we’re driving through town – with his son’s shin guards in the front – is a loaner from a promotional day spent four-wheel driving around Stradbroke Island. If his wealth has a purpose, it’s creating experiences for his kids. “I don’t want them to be spoilt brats, but I want to give them core memories,” he says. “That’s the biggest driving force at the moment.”

He does that with his American wife Breeana, of course, who he met in 2016 on a trip to Las Vegas. They went back and forth a little online, and stole time between travels, and then she settled here. “It was one of those secret knowings,” Bree says now. “We both knew, but it was a slow burn.”

Theirs is an easy pairing. Her empathy and ­patience. His honesty and authenticity. Conversations flow ­effortlessly, whether surface-level or deep. Even their division of labour is harmonious. “I make sure the kitchen is clean every night, so we don’t wake up with a menacing pile of mess,” laughs Fanning. “But I ruin too many of her clothes, so I stay away from the washing and drying.”

Bree wrote the foreword to his book, too, noting that grief, grit and grace are the hallmarks of his life so far. “The loss of his brothers was his grief, but that gave him the grit to persevere, and now he channels it all through fatherhood and family to lead a graceful life,” she says. “He’s still learning what his mission will be, and I think he’s OK with that. Magic happens when the next chapter isn’t written yet.”

Magic for Fanning right now is taking the kids surfing. We sit high on the hill above Cooly now, watching the waves roll in at Duranbah Beach – D-Bah to locals – and he shows me a video on his phone of him and Xander cruising into shore. His little lad looks like a cape hanging off Dad’s neck and shoulders. Then he shows me a video of Lyla in the same spot, held up in his arms, in front of a wave, flapping her wings, pretending to be a superfairy.

Surfing is his constant but also his joy. He hopes it will be theirs, too – that they’ll love the same things he does, from the idea that no two waves are ever the same to the unique sensation of “surf exhaustion” when you step back onto the sand. “It doesn’t matter how you go into the ocean, you always come out feeling better,” he says, nodding. “It’s like washing the world away.”

All Heart by Mick Fanning (Simon & Schuster Australia) is out September 29.

Wakefield reach Super League playoff semi-finals after eliminator win against Leigh

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 21:13:27 GMT

Wakefield 26-16 Leigh

Vagana and Faatili’s second-half tries seal victory

Wakefield Trinity survived the sending off of Emre Guler to progress to the semi-finals of the Super League playoffs for the first time after proving to be far too strong for Leigh Leopards.

Trinity, so long one of Super League’s perennial strugglers, have been revitalised under the ownership of Matt Ellis and the head coach Daryl Powell. In just three years, they have taken the club from the Championship to within 80 minutes of a first appearance in the Super League Grand Final.

Even the dismissal of Guler with 20 minutes remaining couldn’t derail Wakefield’s push as they had far too much quality for a Leigh side who simply couldn’t live with the skill and physicality of a Trinity team who look well equipped to go again next week. They will face either Wigan Warriors or Leeds Rhinos for a place at Old Trafford on the line.

Wakefield, roared on by a full house in West Yorkshire, began with the greater intent and purpose. They took a deserved lead from the boot of Max Jowitt after Joe Ofahengaue’s late hit on Mason Lino, the least their early dominance deserved. It was clear even from such an early stage that the Leopards were struggling with the pace of the game, which was being dictated by the hosts.

They were then unpicked as the midway point of the half approached with a piece of brilliance from Trinity’s star hooker, Tyson Smoothy. It was the Australian’s 40-20 which put Wakefield on the front foot again and with their next meaningful attacking opportunity they scored the first try of the night, as Smoothy dummied over from close range to make it 8-0.

The game was already threatening to spiral away from Leigh, and that was emphasised further on the half-hour mark. Smoothy was again influential, his pass opening up the space for Trinity to execute a pinpoint set move, giving Tom Johnstone just enough room to touch down in the corner despite pressure from Umyla Hanley.

Jowitt couldn’t convert that second Wakefield try but 12-0 seemed like a scoreline which felt huge given the prize at stake, as well as underlining Trinity’s dominance to that point. One more score before the break may well have swung the tie emphatically their favour but as half-time struck it was Leigh who delivered their own decisive moment.

Lachlan Lam’s imperious work close to the ruck afforded the space for a rare Leopards break downfield and from it David Armstrong was set free and had the pace to beat the chasing Wakefield defenders. Adam Cook converted and suddenly, a game that felt like it was only heading one way was back in the balance, with Wakefield ahead by just six.

The first score was crucial. And just like in the first half, Wakefield not only started the stronger of the two sides, but they were the side to claim the next points. First a superb carry from Caleb Hamlin-Uele gave Smoothy the chance to gain a quick play-the-ball and from it Trinity exploited Leigh’s right edge and Isaiah Vagana forced his way over the line under pressure.

That restored their 12-point advantage and four minutes later another of Trinity’s interchange forwards, Caius Faatili, burst through after more good work from Smoothy to make it 24-6. The tie felt as good as done but as the hour mark struck Guler produced a moment of madness, striking out at Owen Trout in the tackle and being sent off. From nowhere Leigh had chance in a game that felt as though had already passed them by.

It briefly looked as though a grandstand finale was on the cards when Lam scored to narrow the arrears. But Trinity dug deep and withstood further Leigh pressure, with a penalty from Jowitt heading into the final ten minutes giving them valuable breathing space.

Innes Senior scored a late consolation for Leigh, but their season is over. Wakefield’s, however, rolls on .

Brentford blitz Chelsea as Fábio Carvalho caps stunning second-half display

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 21:12:38 GMT

Those early-season thoughts that Chelsea might be the team best-placed to challenge Arsenal are beginning to look extremely over-optimistic. The two chaotic wins with which they began were always difficult to read: they might have been useful points picked up on the way to a more solid structure, or they might have represented evidence of significant problems. After three games without a win, and 12 goals conceded in five games this season, it’s beginning to look like the latter.

At the final whistle, Keith Andrews tipped his head back and roared at the sky, celebrating Brentford’s first home win over Chelsea since 1938. They remain unbeaten, third in the table, coherent and disciplined. The comparison is impossible not to draw: as one side flails in an orgy of structured spending, their far less wealthy neighbours thrive with a clear plan and sense of direction. “It was a performance I felt was bubbling,” said Andrews. “I could see it in the players’ eyes over the last two days. They were very focused, very determined.”

Such is the state of perpetual flux at Chelsea that the usual homilies about the benefits of stability always seem a little redundant when applied to them. With 11 new signings this summer maintaining the sense of the club as a trading hub, learning the names of everybody in the dressing room has probably been a greater priority than worrying too much about boardroom wrangling. But, still, their first game since Todd Boehly and Mark Walter agreed to sell their 12.8% stake in the club to the major shareholder Clearlake Capital felt significant. At the very least, a more harmonious boardroom should be beneficial.

Boehly, the great disruptor, who arrived blithely telling English football it was doing everything wrong, has departed having achieved very little other than splurging £300m on players who didn’t fit and giving Raheem Sterling a £325,000-a-week contract in his shambolic spell as de facto sporting director. Four years on, after 60 arrivals, do Chelsea look any more like title challengers than they did then? It was, in truth, very hard to say what this looked like, other than a team that is every much still under construction. Jordan Henderson made his full Chelsea debut at his former club, while Danny Welbeck, Pep Chavarría and Valentín Barco made their first league starts.

Barco, whose overenthusiastic celebrations after Argentina’s winner against England at the World Cup earned him a post-match slap from Jude Bellingham, was booed with impressive consistency from the home fans. The lesson was clear: if you’re going to be a major irritant while in possession of a distinctive shock of hair the colour of burnished copper, there will be consequences. Emí Martínez was jeered as well for the crime of being Argentinian. Henderson, by contrast, was treated relatively gently, his booing as a returnee more sporadic and muted, tending to the perfunctory.

The pattern for Chelsea was a familiar one: a fast start, fading to something a little scratchier. The opening, for the second successive game, did not produce an early goal, although Pedro Neto would have given them a ninth-minute lead had it not been for a sharp save from Caoimhín Kelleher.

“We have dropped out consistency our competitive mentality in the second half,” said Xabi Alonso. “We have not been able to keep our level. When you lose shape you are out of control. To be able to understand and know what it takes to be competing to the end, it’s a process and it takes time.”

The longer the game went on, the less assured Chelsea looked and a Brentford opener arrived just after the hour. Perhaps inevitably, it came from a dead ball; the stats had suggested that Brentford this season had been creating significantly more chances from set plays than they had converted. As modern corner routines go it seemed very straightforward, Jannik Schuster climbing above the diminutive Barco to head Mikkel Damsgaard’s corner back across goal where Jaidon Anthony nodded in from close range, his first goal since his summer move from Burnley.

Chelsea belatedly applied some pressure, but although the final minutes were played largely in the Brentford half, they created little beyond corners, as Brentford maintained their composure and structure. The second arrived seven minutes from time. Damsgaard, perhaps the tidiest player in the league, led the break, laying in Kevin Schade. Martínez saved his side-footed effort but Igor Thiago guided an awkwardly bouncing ball inside the post for his first goal of the season. Fábio Carvalho made it 3-0 in injury-time, slamming in a cross from Schade, who had been left inexplicably unmarked on the left after a long throw was half-cleared.

As Brentford begin to consider that European qualification is a real possibility, Chelsea remain what they have been since the takeover: a work in progress – and, particularly at the back, it feels that progress has a long way to run.

Women’s Super League: Lauren Hemp hits double as Manchester City see off lively Liverpool

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 20:10:59 GMT

Manchester City continued their winning start to the new Women’s Super League season but the defending champions needed a 90th-minute own goal from Grace Fisk to help them edge past an ever-improving Liverpool side after an entertaining game in which Lauren Hemp scored twice.

Fisk inadvertently turned Grace Clinton’s dangerous cross into her own net to put City 3-2 up and then – with Liverpool searching for an equaliser and committing players forward deep in stoppage time – Hemp added another on the counterattack to make it 4-2 and widen the margin of victory, but that slightly masked how well the visitors had played.

Gareth Taylor – against his former side – will have taken significant encouragement from his Liverpool team’s performance, on a night when they made the league leaders dig deep.

“Playing that way, we believe we’ll win a lot of games this season,” Taylor told Sky Sports, as he praised his team’s effort. “What you saw was a more improved version of what we were towards the end of last season.”

That certainly seemed the case. Nevertheless, the result ensured that City, who had already been the only WSL side who held a 100% winning record after the opening two rounds of games and now will certainly stay top of the table for at least another week, have still not dropped any points in home league fixtures since Andrée Jeglertz took charge in the summer of 2025.

It had looked as though Jeglertz’s City were set for a routine evening when Hemp met Carlotta Wamser’s incisive inside ball and sent a controlled, low finish into the far bottom corner. It was Hemp’s first goal since scoring for England in a victory over Spain in April, her first club goal since scoring in the FA Cup in February and her first WSL goal since last November’s Manchester derby.

Moments after Hemp’s opening goal, with 13 minutes on the clock, the entire crowd rose to applaud the late Matt Beard, the former Liverpool manager, in reference to the year 2013, when he won the first of two consecutive WSL titles with Liverpool.

Supporters of clubs across the WSL and WSL2 have been invited to applaud at the same time in games across this weekend, to mark a year since Beard’s death on 20 September 2025. He was a much-loved character and hugely successful coach at Liverpool, whose performance – particularly in the remainder of the first half – would have done him proud.

The away side deservedly struck back and found themselves 2-1 up before the half-hour mark, as their pressing gave the defending champions a headache. First a misunderstanding between Wamser and Alex Greenwood allowed Vivien Endemann to set up Alice Bergström for the equaliser, which she calmly tucked past Ayaka Yamashita.

Soon afterwards, after City failed to clear a cross, Endemann – who had opened her Liverpool account with a debut goal at Charlton on the opening weekend – fired in a shot that Yamashita got a hand to but could only help into the net.

Khadija Shaw struck a post from a difficult angle after rounding Khiara Keating, but Shaw eventually did equalise after a goalkeeping error shortly before half-time. Keating – returning to face her former club after her summer move to Liverpool – did well to block Hemp’s strike but was unable to prevent the ball trickling into the path of the onrushing Shaw, who gratefully poked home.

Keating impressed in the second half with a fine reaction save, keeping out a Shaw effort that had looked destined for the top corner at her near post. But the hosts began to build pressure and the introduction of the lively Clinton inside the final 15 minutes boosted their attacking threat.

Her near-post cross proved too difficult for Fisk to clear and – just as they did on countless occasions last term – City lived up to Jeglertz’s mantra of “we will find a way to win”, a message that has been imprinted on the walls of their training base.

Jeglertz hinted at that again as he told Sky Sports: “I’m very pleased with the mentality of the group. They never stop believing, they keep on going and – in the end – we are winners.”

Trump bans CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 19:36:16 GMT

US president has overseen an unprecedented restriction of access for major traditional news media since start of second term

US politics live – latest updates

In his latest attack on the US constitution’s first amendment and the press, Donald Trump abruptly announced that he is banning outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House over their coverage.

In a post on his Truth Social platform on Friday, the US president said he was expelling the news outlets “effective immediately” over what he called their “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and threatened that bans for others outlets could follow.

He went on: “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”

Trump defended the ban at an Oval Office event to promote his administration’s healthcare policies.

“I don’t get fair press. I get it from Breitbart. I get it from a little bit from Fox,” Trump told reporters, referring to friendly media outlets. “But what I do ask is just a semblance of truth.”

Reminded by one reporter that every president takes an oath to uphold the constitution, including the first amendment right to free speech, Trump said: “You get so tired of reading and seeing fake news.

“I don’t think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day,” Trump added. “I think that somebody has a right to keep them away if they’re going to write false stories all the time.”

Near the end of a chaotic news conference, when a reporter asked Trump to explain how his ban on the three outlets would work, the president expressed some confusion. “When you say ‘the ban,’ which ban? Do you know how many bans I’m involved in?” Trump asked, seeming genuinely confused.

After another correspondent rephrased the question, asking, “What do you envision the bans would look like on the media outlets?” Trump said: “Oh, the ban on the free press, right?”

On Friday, the Washington Post reported that more American service members have died in the war on Iran than the Pentagon has publicly disclosed; CNN revealed that an “entirely false” intelligence report about a Chinese ship in the Middle East generated with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) had “almost started a war”; while a Politico report uncovered a Hill investigation after sensitive F-35 fighter jet technology unexpectedly made its way to Hong Kong, possibly giving China access to them.

Trump said his decision to ban the three outlets was unrelated to the stories. “It’s really just cumulative stories over the last few years,” he said, before threatening more media prohibitions could follow.

“There may be others to join them,” Trump said.

In a statement, a spokesperson for CNN said the network “stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting”.

“We have a right under the US constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally protected right,” the spokesperson said.

MSNOW and Politico did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The move drew swift condemnation from Democrats and free speech groups. hris Coons, a Democratic senator, wrote on social media, “Trump is once again trying to use the power of the presidency to punish a free press, now banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House. That is the behavior of an authoritarian, and we must defend the press’ right to hold those in power accountable.”

The White House press pool is a “public forum” under the first amendment, so the president cannot expel journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints, said Jameel Jaffer, executive director at Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University. To do so, would be “doubly unconstitutional”.

“The first amendment prohibits the president from punishing journalists because he doesn’t like their coverage, just as it prohibits him from punishing universities because he doesn’t like the courses they offer, or from punishing law firms because he doesn’t like the clients they represent,” said Jaffer. “With so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you’d think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now.”

Similarly, Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, said: “It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the first amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the People’s House for criticizing the government. It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move.

“The historically unpopular president has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn’t helped him. The press keeps exposing his corruption and his failures. These outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public.”

Joining Trump in the Oval Office for an announcement on Friday, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the governor of Arkansas who served as Trump’s second press secretary during his first term, defended the president’s attacks on news outlets.

Asked about the newly announced press bans, Huckabee Sanders told the reporter: “I think its hard for you to argue against a free press when you’re literally standing in the Oval Office asking questions.” She said Trump was “more accessible and easier to talk to than any president in history”.

Since returning to office, Trump has overseen an unprecedented restriction of access for major traditional news media at the White House, including the Associated Press, which was banned from press pool events in the Oval Office and on Air Force One after it continued to use Gulf of Mexico instead of Gulf of America in its coverage. The AP sued and that case remains in litigation.

Trump’s White House also seized control over the organization of the presidential press pool, a rotation that determines which news organizations and reporters are allowed to follow – and question – the president in places such as the Oval Office and aboard Air Force One. The White House Correspondents’ Association, an independent association made up of members of the media, traditionally coordinated rotating pool coverage of more than a dozen journalists allowed access to the president in smaller settings.

The Pentagon also attempted to introduce a new press policy to restrict the ability of journalists to gather and report on sensitive information, which culminated in a mass walkout of news media outlets who refused to sign the pledge. A federal judge later ruled the policy was unconstitutional.

The president has also launched high-profile legal battles with major outlets including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, CNN, ABC News and the BBC.
