Letter to Brezhnev review – terrific return for Merseysiders’ romance with Russian sailors

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 19:00:25 GMT

Royal Court, LiverpoolEllie Clayton and Angela Simms are superb in a funny, tender adaptation that hugs close to the 1985 film

By some quirk of marketing, Letter to Brezhnev is always associated with Margi Clarke. In the 1985 movie, she was the actor who played Teresa, the sharp-talking chicken-factory worker out for a good time in post-industrial Liverpool. The film, though, rightly belongs to Alexandra Pigg as Elaine, Teresa’s best friend, who trades a dead-end life of unemployment for a fantasy fling with a Russian sailor.

A few years before the collapse of the Soviet Union – and a year before Willy Russell’s similarly themed Shirley Valentine – Elaine dared to believe in escape and in border-defying love. On stage, she is played just as winningly by Ellie Clayton and with much the same combination of wit and wonder. She is the Kirkby girl who has a night on the town with a wallet of stolen cash and finds the world unexpectedly opening up to her. Elaine can be naive, petulant and cynical, but she never lets you stop rooting for her.

As Teresa, Angela Simms is the necessary corrective to Elaine’s dreamy romanticism: she lives for the moment and gives as good as she gets. Only in her quieter moments will she admit her rebelliousness is skin deep. They make a terrific pair.

Frank Clarke’s if-it-ain’t-broke adaptation hugs closely to his original screenplay, adding the odd joke but sticking to the same sequence of taxi rides, club nights and ferry crossings. You might expect that to constrain the director – but no, Nicole Behan injects her production with tremendous energy, exchanging the movie’s subtle charm for ribald theatrical flair, drawing out the humour and the passion without diminishing the tender emotional heart.

The show takes shape around a multi-level set by Mark Walters, inventively lit by Ian Scott, with gangplanks, bedrooms and barbed wire neatly emerging from a towering frontage of wooden cupboards. In lesser hands it could dwarf the performers, but it is too cleverly conceived for that: something also true of Rob Green’s musical direction. At choice moments, he elevates the soundtrack of 70s and 80s hits by mixing in live vocals, whether it’s You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real) or Lips Like Sugar, showcasing an excellent ensemble.

Say what you like about movie adaptations, but with cast members from the film in the first-night audience, this one is joyfully at home on the stage.

At Royal Court theatre, Liverpool, until 17 October

Why Europe has been absent from the great AI safety debate

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 18:37:36 GMT

Though Europe has measures that address how consumers might encounter AI, technology will impact them if the worst scenarios bear

Europe’s dilemma over AI was rendered in stark terms this week. The head of the continent’s central bank, Christine Lagarde, said Europeans have two options: shun the technology and lose out on growth; or embrace it and become dependent on tools developed by the US and China.

The great debate over AI safety that has erupted in recent days threatens to make the choice moot. If the worst scenarios come to bear – and experts have differing views on this – then the technology will impact the continent regardless.

Europe has largely been absent from the highest levels of that debate, a result of the continent’s longstanding inability to produce a Silicon Valley-scale titan like Apple, Google or newcomer OpenAI. While it is a powerhouse in regulation, much to the White House’s chagrin, its lack of an Anthropic or Nvidia-sized frontrunner in the AI race has diminished its voice in the safety debate.

Ursula von der Leyen, a powerful political figure on the continent as president of the European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, addressed the issue this week by saying she will “invite the main frontier labs for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier”.

Her remarks gained nowhere as much traction as Donald Trump and China’s dismissal of a slowdown. Without the support of Washington or Beijing, any sort of pacing is impossible – with our without Europe’s input.

Lagarde’s speech on Monday underlined the continent’s relative weakness. She asserted that Europe must develop its own AI technology and build more datacentres in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China.

If Europe invests in its own AI tech, said Lagarde, “the threat of being cut off loses its force.” Self-sufficiency would also give Europe a chance to develop its own answer to the AI safety crisis.

Margrethe Vestager, who clashed with the US tech industry as the EU’s former competition commissioner, co-authored a report this week – A Transformative AI Strategy for Europe – that echoed Lagarde’s warning. AI threatens to accelerate a development already affecting Europe, where citizens “are already bearing the economic and social consequences of decisions taken elsewhere”, she says.

Solutions to this, according to the report, include building more datacentres – the central nervous systems of AI – and also to ensure the continent is resilient enough to withstand “AI crises” like a powerful model slipping out of control.

Vestager said that Europe does have a voice in the safety debate through its EU AI Act, the rare piece of AI legislation that sets out requirements for developers of “high-risk” AI systems to report safety incidents and address risks like a cutting-edge model evading control.

But she adds: “Europe must … build its own AI to strengthen the ecosystem, retain talent, and inspire innovation.”

Vestager acknowledges that if there is an existential threat, it requires a global solution; one that does not hand power to the US and China. And that requires a different kind of supranational body.

“As for existential threats to humanity, we must first assess the actual level of threat – then act with urgency. The UN general assembly is an opportunity to address this. It is vital to move beyond the US-China rivalry narrative. There must be space for humanity between the egos of leaders like President Xi and President Trump.”

Frederike Kaltheuner, an adviser to the AI Now Institute, a research body, says that Europe is dependent on US technology in ways that will be hard to undo, from search engines to chips to datacentres. But the narrative that Europe is grievously behind in the race depends on a particular view of artificial intelligence aggressively promoted by American tech bosses.

Because of their doomsday warnings, “we are exclusively talking about AI in a very narrow, specific kind of way – namely, the idea that there is such a thing as the AI frontier, which is getting better and better, and that access to the frontier is the most important thing that Europe needs for its security and economy.”

The reality of the market points at something else, she says: many companies are not adopting so-called “frontier models” – like ChatGPT and Anthropic – because of high costs and fears over what might happen to their data.

If this trend continues, Europe may not be so terribly positioned: the EU AI Act has a number of pragmatic measures which address how consumers might encounter AI on a day-to-day basis, legislating over matters such as labelling AI content, and the use of AI in medicine and hiring.

“Europe has a competitiveness problem, that’s true,” says Itxaso Dominguez de Olazabal, a policy adviser at EDRI, a European digital rights organisation. But US tech boosters are “blaming it on laws and protections, and have promised that deregulation will make European companies more competitive … in a race to the bottom to see if we can catch big tech”.

Nonetheless, the EU AI act is not viewed as model legislation for other countries or a vehicle for a global slowdown. Georgina Kon, a partner at law firm Linklaters, says the act is unlikely to be adopted as a global benchmark for several reasons, including criticisms of the heavy compliance burden, which has led to delays in parts of the act becoming active, and a narrow territorial focus on Europe. Those criticisms have also meant that lawmakers elsewhere have looked to differentiate their approach to AI legislation from the EU’s. “The EU AI Act is not something that everybody else in the world feels constrained by, although many tech companies will of course want to sell to the EU,” she says.

Big tech still has a vast customer base in Europe. Kaltheuner worries that the doomsday narratives will push Europe towards dependency, encouraging it to adopt US AI models across the economy out of ill-defined fears over being left behind.

“There’s a vision of the future where Europe’s economy, its public sector, its education system runs on models and on infrastructure that is controlled by a very small number of companies that happen to be also in the US. This would be a sovereignty problem.”

Earl Spencer doubles down on claims about ‘monstrous’ call with Charles after Diana’s death

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 17:40:49 GMT

Buckingham Palace has rebutted claim by Charles Spencer, Diana’s brother, that then prince told him ‘we’ll forget her soon enough’

Earl Spencer has doubled down on his bombshell claim that King Charles said of Diana, Princess of Wales, “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough” days after her death, saying he is telling the truth.

The alleged comments, revealed in Charles Spencer’s memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, which is being serialised in the Daily Mail, prompted Buckingham Palace to issue an extraordinary statement suggesting Diana’s brother had misremembered events, saying “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise”.

In an interview with the BBC, Spencer stood firm in his recollection, telling Laura Kuenssberg: “I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said.”

Responding to the palace’s statement, Spencer said: “Well, is he furious? Is he furious, or is he embarrassed?” When asked about the inference that his memory was coloured, Spencer said: “They’ve sort of smudged that one, haven’t they? They’ve said that recollections may vary.”

Spencer said the call was one of two he had with Charles in his lifetime and said he told his friends and family members at the time about the comment “because it was so monstrous”.

The alleged comment was revealed on Wednesday in an extract from the memoir published in the Daily Mail. The comment by the then prince was allegedly made during a heated argument over funeral arrangements. Spencer says it reflected Charles’s “pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death”, the Daily Mail reported.

Among other claims in the book are that Diana told a friend on the eve of her wedding to Charles that he said he was happy to marry her, but was not actually in love with her.

On Friday, the second extract from the memoir was published. Spencer writes Charles was “polite and formal” on the day of Diana’s funeral and says Prince Philip told him to look ahead while walking in unison alongside his nephews and former brother-in-law.

“It was hellish, entering that tunnel of grief, particularly because we were unable to put a face to it by looking at the individuals in the crowd,” said Spencer of the procession.

In the extract released on Wednesday, Spencer says he insisted to Charles that Diana would not have wanted her sons, Prince William, then 15, and Prince Harry, then 12, to walk in her funeral procession. In the end, her sons walked behind her coffin, which William later called “one of the hardest things I’ve ever done”.

Spencer wrote that when one of Queen Elizabeth’s most senior aides told him in the days before the funeral that William and Harry would take part in the procession, he responded: “That’s not going to happen.”

But minutes later he received a phone call from Charles, who insisted it should. It was during the ensuing argument between the two men that Charles allegedly made the comment, with Spencer writing: “‘Rest assured,’” he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough!’”

Spencer wrote that he was stunned and took a few seconds to reply, writing: “‘I can’t believe you just said that,’ I said flatly, before hanging up.”

Spencer also claimed that Diana “never would have wanted” her sons to walk behind her coffin, to which Charles allegedly replied: “That’s the problem with your family. They’ve got no bloody sense of duty.”

Swan Song is due to be published globally next Tuesday – in the UK by Penguin Michael Joseph, a division of Penguin Random House.

Diana, who died aged 36 after a car crash in Paris in 1997, would have turned 65 on 1 July this year.

Uefa and Concacaf ask Gianni Infantino to give Fifa’s billions to its member associations

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 17:33:40 GMT

Leaders want plan to be considered by Fifa Council

The presidents of Uefa and Concacaf have written to Gianni Infantino requesting that Fifa release money from its $6bn (£4.5bn) reserves to its member associations, stating that the plan to fund them via the doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme was unnecessary given the cash pile it is sitting on.

Aleksander Ceferin and Victor Montagliani proposed a payout of at least $10m to each of Fifa’s 211 member associations (MAs), initially as a one-off during the 2027-2030 commercial cycle. They called for an independent review of Fifa’s financial position and said their own study “raises an important question as to whether the proposed transaction was necessary to deliver greater resources to the MAs”.

The proposed $10m would be handed out on top of money committed by Fifa’s existing Fifa Forward programme, which paid each MA about $8m over the previous four-year cycle. In a separate letter to the presidents of the Asian Football Confederation, the Confederation of African Football, Conmebol (the South American federation) and Oceania, Ceferin and Montagliani asked their counterparts to support the motion. Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, the AFC president, is expected to send an endorsement of their plan.

The leaders intend their proposal to be considered at the next Fifa Council meeting on 15 October, where Infantino is due to face Fifa’s nominal decision-making body for the first time since scandal engulfed his reign.

The letter to Infantino states: “Our analysis indicates that Fifa should make at least $10million available to each of its 211 MAs over the 2027-30 cycle for investment in infrastructure and football development – an aggregate of approximately $2.1billion. This would be a one-off release of reserves, over and above the approved Fifa Forward Programme, which would continue in full as already committed.”

It points out Fifa’s reserves would not dip below $1.5bn even after that scale of distribution, and says a larger handout could be possible “once a clearer picture of Fifa’s financial position at year-end is available”.

Ceferin and Montagliani said Fifa “already has the capacity to deliver substantially more to its MAs from its own balance sheet – without any sale of interests in its competitions, and without asking anything of the MAs in return”.

They proceeded to point out that releasing part of Fifa’s reserves would “demonstrate that MAs should not have to choose between development and good governance; between investment and integrity; or between financial support and the ability to consider proposals on their merits. Development is an institutional responsibility of Fifa – not a matter of individual discretion.”

While Fifa Forward Enterprise had promised member associations about $40m, half of that sum was an optional $20m payment for those signing up to his plan.

Survivors recount panic and struggle to breathe in Nigerian prison cell where 37 died

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 17:27:39 GMT

Police fire teargas as protests break out in city of Minna after deaths of suspected illegal goldminers, many of whom were children

Survivors from a prison cell in Nigeria where 37 suspected illegal goldminers died while in the custody of a paramilitary group this week have recounted their panic and struggle for breath, as police on Friday fired teargas at people protesting against the deaths and imposed an overnight curfew in the city of Minna.

The victims – many of whom were children – were found dead on Thursday in the cells of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), which had raided suspected illegal gold mines and ⁠locked up dozens of miners in the city, the state capital of the mineral-rich state of Niger.

NSCDC – a paramilitary group that works with police – initially blamed the deaths on a disease outbreak. However, an intelligence report seen by Agence France-Presse (AFP) said preliminary information suggested that overcrowding and inadequate ventilation were responsible.

The state governor, Umar Bago, said many of the dead were children, aged 14 to 18, who had been working in the mines instead of going to school. “There are issues of illegal mining and it is taking a toll on our children,” he said.

Dauda Shehu, a survivor from the cell, told journalists at a hospital on Friday: “We were jam-packed in the cell, no ventilation for us to breathe well. All of a sudden we realised that we could not breathe and we were all scampering for where to get fresh air, we even appealed to them several times, banged the cell door, but they refused to answer us.”

A video shared online showed the bodies of dozens of young men clad only in shorts, most of whom appeared to be teenagers, sprawled on the ground out in the open. Volunteers wearing gloves can be seen standing over the dead, while veiled women try to identify the bodies of their relatives. Voices shouting curses on those responsible can be heard in the background.

AFP reported that another survivor, who asked not to be named, said he had made it out alive because he was near the cell’s entrance, where he could breathe better. “We were screaming for help,” he said, with detainees telling the guards that “people are dying one after the other. They did not believe us.”

President Bola Ahmed Tinubu ordered an investigation into the deaths after his government earlier suspended some senior officials.

But protests over the deaths broke out on Thursday evening in Minna. On Friday dozens of young people, including miners and their relatives, gathered near the NSCDC’s office in the city. Police cordoned off the area and attempted to disperse the protesters by firing teargas.

A Reuters witness saw security forces fire live rounds as protesters – ​some armed with sticks, machetes and traditional hunting rifles – called ‌for justice. Some protesters tried ‌to set fire to government buildings in the Tunga neighbourhood. “We are not thieves – we are simply seeking a way to make ‌a living by mining,” Yusuf Auwal, a miner who joined the protesters, told Reuters. At least one body lay on the streets. Soldiers and police officers patrolled Minna to try to restore order.

As ⁠curfew began at 6pm local time on Friday, security forces appeared to have at least temporarily restored order to the streets of the city.

The NSCDC said the detainees had been held in raids on suspected illegal mines on 15 and 16 September in the Wushishi-Lukoto area west of Minna. Nigeria’s interior minister, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, ordered the immediate suspension of Niger state’s NSCDC commandant, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, pending the outcome of an investigation.

Niger state, which is Nigeria’s largest and is more than twice the size of Belgium, is rich in minerals and attracts thousands of artisanal miners, most lured by gold.

Police and the NSCDC did not initially provide a precise number of deaths but the state governor, Mohammed Umaru Bago, later confirmed 37 people had died.

“It’s so sad, it’s so tragic,” he said, adding an inquiry into the deaths had already started work. He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections due in January. The men were buried on Thursday, according to Islamic tradition, without any forensic investigations.

The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state is fuelling violence by criminal gangs, according to officials and experts. The gangs tax the miners and demand a cut from the extracted ore as a levy to allow them access to the pits.

Most of the illegally mined gold is smuggled to the United Arab Emirates, where it is laundered into the global supply chain in Europe, the US, Asia and South Africa, according to a 2024 Swissaid report.

Apart from gold, the state of Niger sits on deposits of other minerals including tantalite, copper and lithium, which are in strong demand for use in electric vehicles and clean energy technology.

This Israeli election could be the country’s last – this week I saw that for myself

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 17:20:45 GMT

Spend time on the ground and you see how high the stakes are for next month’s contest – for Israelis and Palestinians alike

Candidates always say it, but this time it’s true. When Israel goes to the polls on 27 October, it really will be the most important election in the country’s history – and not just for Israelis. I saw that for myself this last week, in a visit that served as a sharp reminder of both what is at stake – and the role of those watching from afar.

More than one voter I spoke to voiced the fear that, if the coalition headed by Benjamin Netanyahu is returned to power next month, 27 October will not merely be Israel’s most important election: it will be its last. They were not referring to the absence of democracy in the occupied territory of the West Bank – which we’ll come to – but rather to Israel’s internationally recognised, pre-1967 borders: what you might call Israel-proper. There, the last four years have seen a sustained assault on the machinery of liberal democracy by the most rightwing government since Israel’s establishment in 1948 – a committed, focused attempt to remove the checks and restraints on its own power, installing instead a kind of elective dictatorship.

Democratic norms are breaking down all the time. While I was there, Netanyahu joined calls to strip two Israeli film-makers of their citizenship, as a livid mob surrounded the home of the parents of one of the two directors. The film in question is NAZA, produced by the Guardian, which features interviews with two dozen Israeli military insiders, their identities disguised, and which is named for the acronym euphemistically used by the Israeli military when calculating the number of civilians it expects to die in an airstrike. Unlike everyone protesting against it, I have actually seen the film: I have some misgivings about specific choices it makes, but that is irrelevant. A country true to its self-designation as the only democracy in the Middle East would not threaten with expulsion or violence those who say what its rulers do not want to hear.

But such egregious behaviour is becoming commonplace. Last month, Netanyahu’s wife, Sara, implied, without evidence, that Yair Golan, leader of the left-leaning Democrats party, had inside knowledge of the 7 October 2023 attacks that saw the massacre of 1,200 Israelis and the abduction of 251 hostages – the trauma of which still touches every aspect of Israeli life and looms over this election campaign. It’s part of a baseless conspiracy theory pushed by Netanyahu and his “poison machine” of acolytes and media allies to shift the blame for the PM’s own 7 October failures, but it’s especially despicable when directed against Golan. A former general, he leapt into his car on 7 October, drove south and personally rescued six of those who had come under fire. He is a hero of that dark day – and has threatened to sue Sara Netanyahu. As it happens, soon after her intervention, it was reported that someone high up in Israel had indeed been explicitly warned before 7 October that a devastating Hamas attack was on the way. That someone was Benjamin Netanyahu and the warning came from the president of the United Arab Emirates. Netanyahu vehemently denied the allegation.

It is a dirty campaign, filled with disinformation and lies, utterly in keeping with the degraded state of Israeli politics in the age of late-stage Netanyahu. Thanks to Israel’s unwritten constitution, there now remains only one serious obstacle in his way: the courts. He has had the judiciary in his sights since he returned to office nearly four years ago, not least because he wants to halt the ongoing corruption trial that could send him to jail. He tried to gut the supreme court once already, in early 2023, and, if he wins next month, most observers are clear: the court will be gone.

That matters for Israelis, who will find themselves in a Turkey- or Russia-style autocracy poorly disguised as a democracy. But it also matters for Palestinians. Yehuda Shaul, an Israeli anti-occupation activist fully aware of the court’s inadequate record as a defender of Palestinian rights, told me that Israel has been on the wrong road for a long time: “But so long as the courts and basic democratic institutions are standing, we can still turn back. If they’re gone, we’re heading off a cliff.”

I was with Shaul driving around the West Bank, seeing the changing reality there up close. I stood in the burnt-out and broken mosque of what had been the small Bedouin village of Mu’arrajat, its population chased out by settler terrorists – to use the formulation favoured, remarkably, by the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee. Through harassment and violence, they made the lives of the inhabitants there so unbearable that the villagers could hold on no longer. It was the same story in Ras ‘Ein al ‘Auja, where I stood among similar ruins, including a small, abandoned school, and where a herd of settler-owned goats now grazes. Shaul points out the vast swathe of land, more than 100 sq miles, in the east of the West Bank, close enough to see Jordan, where now next to no Palestinians live. Small wonder that former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert speaks of ethnic cleansing, or that UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband does the same.

I saw, too, in what the settlers call northern Samaria, the four settlements that Ariel Sharon dismantled in 2005, now returned and rebuilt along with 14 others either built or approved for construction. Their arrival sees roadside buildings demolished and olive trees uprooted, in the name of safety for settlers as they travel. And dotted, seemingly on every ridge and hilltop, the distinct, bright white caravans that mark a new officially “unauthorised” outpost, popping up with such frequency that Shaul can barely name them all – he estimates 250 new settlements and outposts have gone up since 2023 – and which are steadily encircling the major Palestinian cities, reducing them to isolated enclaves, thereby preventing the territorial contiguity that would be essential for a viable Palestinian state.

Netanyahu’s coalition, with radical settler Bezalel Smotrich in de facto charge of the West Bank, has directed this settlement expansion and turned a blind eye to the pogroms staged by the movement’s most aggressive wing. The best chance to stop it going farther and further comes on 27 October.

Those outside the country appalled by what they see in Gaza or the West Bank sometimes struggle to know what they can do to help. The temptation is to rally around, say, the rapper Macklemore, calling out “Free Palestine” from Ed Sheeran’s stage – but that temptation fades a little when you see that the same Macklemore once performed dressed up as what looked unmistakably like an antisemitic caricature of a Jew, complete with a false, giant nose. He later apologised, saying a “Jewish stereotype” had never crossed his mind.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Or you might want to get fully behind Miliband’s sanctions package, which at long last signals that the settlement enterprise will not be allowed to continue with impunity – until you hear from those involved who say that the immediate impact will fall not on settlers but on Palestinians. That’s because the Netanyahu government’s predictable and predicted response – which included the closure of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem – has robbed Britain of its main mechanism to aid Palestinians through delivering development programmes and the like.

The truth is that, for those desperate to see change, the best hope is the ejection from office of what has been a vile, cruel, bigoted and lethally dangerous government. Be under no illusion: even if Netanyahu is toppled, he will not be replaced by a peacenik who will instantly lead the country in the opposite direction. It doesn’t work like that. But there is a bloc, unofficially led by former general Gadi Eisenkot, which is defined by its opposition to the man who has ruled Israel on and off for much of the last 30 years and there are campaigners and activists, such as Shaul, who are fighting every hour of every day to avert further disaster. They are branded as traitors at home and shunned simply for being Israeli by too many supposed progressives abroad. They need allies and friends, because right now they are all that stands between this moment and the abyss.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Brazil’s Lula announces higher welfare payments and free weight-loss jabs ahead of election

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 17:10:37 GMT

Critics say moves from leftwing incumbent president are electorally motivated two weeks before Brazil’s elections

Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced a 15% increase in the country’s main cash-transfer programme for poor families, as well as free weight-loss jabs, prompting criticism from opponents who say the moves are electorally motivated just two weeks before the presidential election.

On 4 October, the leftwing incumbent will face the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who has been gaining ground in recent weeks.

The rise in the monthly payment, from about £98 to £113, that he announced on Thursday is due to take effect on 19 October, just before the likely runoff vote on 25 October.

The increase is expected to benefit between 15% and 20% of voters in what promises to be one of the closest ever presidential races in Latin America’s largest country.

Lula said it was not really an increase, but an adjustment in line with inflation to “protect the purchasing power of the most vulnerable families”, but his opponents have criticised its timing so close to the election.

Flávio Bolsonaro called it an “act of desperation” after polls showed him gaining ground – although the most recent survey, released on Thursday night, still showed Lula numerically ahead despite the technical tie. The senator added that Lula was trying to “buy the votes of the poor”.

Created in 2003 during his first term as president, the programme, called Bolsa Família, was a flagship cash-transfer policy that helped lift millions of families out of poverty during his first two terms.

Currently, families with an income of up to £32 per person are eligible, covering about 50 million people, or roughly 27 million of voting age.

The programme has long been fiercely criticised by rightwing politicians, including by Jair Bolsonaro, although he kept it in place during his presidency.

On the eve of the 2022 election, Bolsonaro announced a 50% increase in the monthly payment, prompting Lula’s campaign to file a case with the electoral court alleging abuse of political power and electoral use of the state machinery.

The similarities have sparked a debate between those who say Lula is doing the same thing Bolsonaro did four years ago, and others who argue that the two cases are different.

The journalist Miriam Leitão wrote for O Globo that although both Bolsonaro and Lula made the adjustments “out of electoral interest”, the current incumbent’s increase is in fact limited to inflation over the past four years, during which there had been no adjustment.

She also noted that Bolsonaro’s increase had an expiry date – precisely at the end of the electoral period – while Lula’s is permanent.

Victor Escobar, a researcher at the Laboratory of Parties, Elections and Comparative Politics, agreed. He said that although Lula, like his predecessor, is also being criticised for unveiling a package of benefits on the eve of the election – including a promise to distribute weight-loss jabs free of charge through the public health system – Bolsonaro’s measures were “even more irresponsible from a budgetary point of view”.

In addition to increasing benefits for poor families, Bolsonaro introduced temporary monthly payments of up to £727 for two groups that broadly formed part of his support base, taxi drivers and truck drivers, along with a series of other social benefits whose projected impact on the budget was so large that critics dubbed them the “kamikaze” package.

Escobar acknowledged that Lula’s intention was also electoral, but said that, as long as the measures comply with the law, “it’s something entirely expected when we’re talking about an incumbent running for re-election, who will try to use the legal mechanisms available to improve their voting numbers”.

Some electoral law experts have said that an inflation adjustment is not, in principle, prohibited, but another far-right candidate, the influencer Renan Santos, filed a case with the electoral court seeking to suspend the increase until the president-elect takes office. Although critical of the measure, Flávio Bolsonaro has not done the same, reportedly because of concern about the impact such a move could have among voters who benefit from the programme.

‘In almost every French game, there’s theatre’: Dean Richards on bringing joie de vivre back to English rugby

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 17:00:23 GMT

Doncaster Knights’ new director of rugby is passionate about the Champ, who Steve Borthwick should pick from overseas and getting players to have a bit of fun

Turn up at Castle Park in Doncaster this week and, bang on cue, a pony and trap is being driven in stately fashion down the nearby main road. There is, some might argue, a similarly retro feel about the Knights’ latest choice of director of rugby. It is now 40 years since Dean Richards barged his way into the public consciousness with two tries on his Test debut against Ireland at Twickenham but, at 63, he is still very much up for a challenge.

As with vinyl records and fine wine, old-school rugby nous never goes entirely out of vogue. That, at least, is the rationale behind Richards’ return to the upper rungs of the English club ladder, commencing with a 740-mile round trip to Cornish Pirates on the opening weekend of the 2026-27 Champ season. “If it’s ingrained in you and you love the sport, then there’s no reason why you shouldn’t continue in some capacity,” he says softly, gazing out of the window at his latest field of dreams.

After an illustrious 22-year association with Leicester, the Bloodgate era at Harlequins, a decade at Newcastle Falcons and briefer spells at Grenoble and, most recently, Wymondham in Norfolk, his latest rugby reincarnation in South Yorkshire certainly lends extra intrigue to this year’s Champ as the league seeks to frame itself as an attractive standalone alternative to the Prem after years of slashed Rugby Football Union funding.

Because Richards has seen it all in his time and has plenty of interesting views on the English game. For starters, he thinks the RFU has been guilty of underestimating the Champ’s potential value as a breeding ground for aspiring players, coaches and referees alike. In his opinion, the standard is improving and a glance at his Knights squad underlines the increasing depth in the second tier since the Prem was reduced to 10 teams. Semesa Rokoduguni, Telusa Veainu and Logovi’i Mulipola are all former standout Prem performers while Newcastle’s erstwhile head coach Alan Dickens is now on the coaching staff and the legendary Sir Ian McGeechan, now 79, is also on board as a consultant.

The caveat is that Doncaster’s playing budget is believed to have shrunk by around 45% compared with last season, when they finished eighth. Richards, however, has long argued that rugby success “is not all about money”, having secured second-tier titles with Quins and Newcastle. During both those campaigns his players were actively encouraged to buy their opposite numbers a post-match drink. This time he is thinking about organising a post-match eating contest, involving the club’s renowned “cow pie”, after the Knights’ opening home game against Hartpury on 27 September. “With Quins we set our stall out to have fun and I did the same at Newcastle. You ask a lot of the boys and it was probably one of the most enjoyable seasons they had. Preparation wasn’t key to everything. It was about having a bit of unity and fun. And it still is.”

Richards, warming to his theme, also believes English rugby in general would benefit from lightening up a bit. He is not sure if the Red Bull era at Newcastle would have been his bag: “The way they’ve done it probably wouldn’t suit me … it’s become very corporate, as I understand it, rather than personal”, but remains a fervent admirer of France’s vibrant Top 14. “I went to the Nou Camp in Barcelona [in 2016] when they held the Top 14 final there and it was an unbelievable occasion. You go to Twickenham to watch our Prem final and … it’s all right. But it doesn’t get anywhere near that.

“The French have got some things right. Their clubs’ style of play is absolutely fantastic. In almost every French game, there’s theatre. And I love that. Here we’re inherently conservative. We don’t want to make a fuss.” Similarly he queries the value of excessively earnest preparation, at English club and international level. “I do think we are typically Anglo-Saxon. We put our noses to the grindstone every day. And I don’t think you need to do that.”

In short, Richards would love to see English rugby display more imagination and vision on and off the field, not least in picking overseas-based players such as the Willis brothers. “If I was in Steve Borthwick’s shoes I’d be pushing to pick those boys.” At some stage he also reckons the Northampton duo of Phil Dowson and Sam Vesty would be a breath of managerial fresh air. “They’ve got a good handle on creating an environment where people want to come to work rather than have to come to work.

“Dows is a real maverick and, for what it’s worth, I think Sam is as well. And I think with that goes the ability to manage people really well. If you’re looking at somebody in the future to be an England coach, I’d certainly look at those two boys. I also like Dave Walder. He is equally as capable but very different to Sam.”

He also wonders aloud whether today’s young full-time pros need to get out more. “They’re far more like athletes than we probably ever were.

“Having said that, I think there’s something missing in their lives. And it’s that balance between work and life. Years ago the life experiences you had prepared you to cope with setbacks. Because many of the guys don’t have life experiences these days, it’s harder for them to accept the adversity and the knocks.”

Resilience was never a problem for Richards. During his days as a police constable, for example, he once attended a traffic accident on the M1 hours before playing for Leicester in a big East Midlands derby. A vehicle was stranded on the hard shoulder and its two occupants were Northampton fans travelling to the game. After racing back to fetch his kitbag and drop off his police car, Richards ended up giving them a lift to the game, which the Tigers duly lost. “Things like that, you wouldn’t think twice about,” he murmurs now.

Richards, however, is not one to wallow indefinitely in the past. After copping a three-year ban in the wake of the messy Bloodgate saga, he used his spare time to become a more skilful trout fisherman; now he is hoping to catch a few more opponents unawares and propel Yorkshire rugby back to the top table. “I’d love for Doncaster to get promoted. I think Cornish Pirates had us down the other day [on social media] as finishing 11th [out of 14]. [But] you look at what’s in place stadium-wise here and at Worcester. You’d want those clubs in the Premier league.” Whatever happens, Deano wants his hard-running Knights to enjoy the ride.

Sensitive UK police data vulnerable to ‘compromise’ by US government and foreign actors

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 17:00:23 GMT

Exclusive: Official UK security assessment found Microsoft cloud platform storing files was at potential risk from hostile hackers

Vast troves of highly sensitive police data are lying on Microsoft cloud platforms which an oﬃcial UK security assessment deemed to be vulnerable to “compromise” by foreign actors and the US government, a Guardian investigation can reveal.

The files include criminal records, victim statements, internal emails and sensitive information held by more than 40 police forces across the UK.

Some files exceed “oﬃcial” classification, according to a police document seen by the Guardian, raising the possibility the information could be classed as “secret” or “top secret”.

The cloud platform is Microsoft Azure, one of the main commercial offerings of the US tech company. It is used by businesses and governments globally and rests on a web of IT infrastructure – datacentres, networking gear, fibre optic cables – that spans more than 100 countries.

In recent years, doubts have surfaced about how cloud platforms store data and whether they are truly secure.

British police decided to put some of their most sensitive data on the Microsoft platform in a 2017 meeting, a record of which was examined by the Guardian.

In doing so, officers accepted that “US government insiders” would be able to see the data, and that it could be “transmitted worldwide”, with “the extent of this … unknown”.

According to five specialists who reviewed the Guardian’s findings, the risks identified in that document persist today. Almost every UK police force now depends on Microsoft Azure, and the UK government spends at least £1.9bn on Microsoft software each year.

“There’s no evidence that this has been properly understood,” said one source who has held senior roles in UK policing. The data is “some of the most sensitive that exists”, he added. “You’re talking about information that, if it gets into the wrong hands, or if the information is incorrect, [means] people can get hurt or may die.”

When the Guardian approached the police about the possibility that sensitive information was not secure, they appeared to wave aside these risks, saying Britain’s contracts with Microsoft meant US authorities could not view data without express permission and that the data it stored on Microsoft remained in the UK.

These statements appeared to contradict public admissions by Microsoft, which said in a disclosure to Police Scotland in 2023 that data “can go outside the UK” and that it “cannot guarantee data sovereignty”.

Microsoft said it “does not provide any government with direct or unfettered access to customer data”, and that it had not provided UK data in response to a US government request. It added that, like all US-based tech companies, it responded to US government requests made through valid legal processes.

In 2017, a senior police oﬃcer, Ian Dyson, chaired a meeting in which stakeholders considered 15 risks the UK would face if police forces decided to transfer their data to Microsoft’s global cloud.

That meeting considered both the police’s use of Microsoft’s software, such as Office 365, and the reliance on the cloud that underpins these services, Azure. Those risks, and the resulting police decisions, were set out in a summary document seen by the Guardian and signed off by Dyson.

This was four years after the advent of a policy called “cloud first”. Introduced by the Cabinet Office in 2013, it became a government-wide effort to push almost all departments to migrate their data on to the “public cloud” – commercial offerings by tech companies, often based in the US. Departments that did not want to do this had to jump through burdensome administrative hoops.

Dyson was the police commissioner of the City of London at the time, but he held another title: senior information risk owner for all of Britain, or the SIRO. It was his job to set the norms for how British police could safely handle their data.

In their assessment, officers came to startling conclusions about what would happen if they put police data on Azure. Firstly, they considered it would be vulnerable to hackers: Microsoft’s software “carries vulnerabilities which will be exploited by cybercriminals and other threat actors in due course”.

Separately, it added: “Police forces cannot be certain where their data will be processed or stored.

“The hyper-scale and global nature of the Microsoft cloud means that police data, and metadata relating to police data could be transmitted and stored worldwide by Microsoft, and the extent of this will be unknown.”

The document specifically identified the potential risk from what it described as “US government insiders”. It said: “There is a risk of compromise of sensitive data shared by, or taken from, Microsoft by the US government being released by US government insider attackers.”

The document explained that the data intended for migration was sensitive. In fact, “a significant volume” of it exceeded the classification “oﬃcial”. In the UK, this suggests it was either “oﬃcial sensitive”, “secret”, or “top secret”.

The assessment also suggested Microsoft’s platform was unable to guarantee this data would be secure. “This places sensitive data, inadequately protected in an environment which then becomes a significantly more attractive target for attackers,” it said.

As well as risks, the report also listed mitigations. On the problem of cyber-attacks, it mandated that police servers should be repaired promptly, kept up to date and have antivirus software.

To address the risk of “US government insiders” and the concern that Microsoft might store UK policing data “worldwide” it suggested “applying Microsoft’s ‘out-of-the-box’ native encryption” and leaving the final decision about using Microsoft up to individual police chiefs.

Several experts interviewed by the Guardian, including cloud computing specialists and engineers working for Microsoft, suggested these mitigations were inadequate. Microsoft’s internal encryption does not prevent its employees accessing UK police data; nor would it stop the US government obtaining British policing files.

The National Police Chief’s Council (NPCC) said access to data stored on the cloud is limited to those with a genuine need to access it and that this is subject to strict controls. Despite that claim, a Microsoft engineer who reviewed the Guardian’s findings said the information “could be viewed by hundreds of people around the world, some of them not vetted, many of them not directly employed by Microsoft”.

Despite the risks identified by the assessment, every police force in the UK put its data, wholly or in part, on Microsoft’s cloud. Some began migrating their information in 2017. A few forces, such as Police Scotland, are still finalising their adoption of the technology.

The files cover the “full gamut of data: intelligence, body-worn video, digital evidence and case files, as well as the non-law enforcement data any organisation has”, said the source who held senior roles in UK policing.

The UK government spends billions each year on services oﬀered by three US tech companies: Amazon, Google and Microsoft.

Up to 60% of its IT infrastructure is hosted on cloud platforms. Britain’s intelligence data is hosted on Amazon’s cloud services, as is its customs data. The Ministry of Defence uses Azure. There is “a deep dependency on US hyperscalers”, said Dave Michels, a researcher with the Cloud Legal Project, at Queen Mary University of London.

This is the result of 13 years of decisions like Dyson’s. It is unclear if the potential consequences are broadly understood.

When the Guardian approached the NPCC over the document signed by Dyson, it said: “UK policing as standard requires the use of UK-only datacentres,” but added that “on occasion” Microsoft employees could access the data “to provide support”.

Asked whether the US government could access the data, a police spokesperson said they could not comment on the phrase “US government insiders”, because “terminology … changes continuously” and the document was “outdated”.

“In line with the contract signed with Microsoft, we do not expect any sharing with the US government without the express permission of the UK government,” they added.

Microsoft said: “The suggestion that use of Microsoft cloud services means customer data is inherently insecure or automatically exposed to foreign governments is inaccurate.” It said it had “never provided UK government data in response to any US or global authority request”.

Two legal experts, as well as several Microsoft engineers who spoke anonymously to the Guardian, suggested these assertions did not give an accurate picture of the potential risks.

By default, Microsoft’s cloud was “a global network of datacentres”, said Michels. It had facilities on every continent and this meant, generally, that data stored on it was stored everywhere: pieces of a single file could be held across multiple countries, from Sweden to Ethiopia.

In recent years, Michels said, Microsoft had begun to offer clients in Europe greater assurances about where their data was stored, including assuring some customers that their data would remain within EU borders. But “the focus on data location is a bit of a red herring”, he said.

This was because thousands of engineers from more than 100 countries maintained Microsoft’s systems. Some were directly employed by Microsoft, others worked for subcontractors in countries potentially hostile to the UK, from Israel to Egypt, China and Kazakhstan. “You’ve seen the list of their sub-processors of people who have access to customer data,” said Michels. “It’s a long list.”

Some of the engineers could access data, such as UK police data, directly as part of customer support. Many more could see key features of what the data included.

Microsoft said it had “strong guardrails” around data access by engineers.

Douwe Korff, a professor of international law at London Metropolitan University, said the police statement that “we do not expect any sharing [of our data] with the US government” was “typical lawyers’ wriggling”.

“The risk is obvious, even though the providers of the cloud and the government both have an interest in talking it down,” he said.

Michels said: “As a cloud customer, if you’re relying on a contractual commitment from a cloud provider not to hand over data when forced to under foreign law, that is not worth much more than the piece of paper it’s written on.”

US law, including the Cloud Act, allows US authorities to access any data held by US cloud companies, including data held abroad. US authorities do not need a warrant to do this, and they can require US companies to not disclose such access to cloud customers.

Microsoft, Amazon and Google have insisted they would fight such requests, said Korff. But there is “nothing that is legally binding” that would prevent them from sharing other governments’ data if US authorities demanded it.

In response to a query from the Guardian, Microsoft said it “has never provided UK government data in response to any US or global authority request”. It added in a follow-up that it was bound by its “contractual commitments”.

“If UK law prohibits us from turning over data to another government, that is a binding law that would govern our response to any hypothetical demand,” it said.

The Guardian spoke to six people who have closely followed the country’s data storage arrangements over the past decade. Several of them said that senior leaders did not view dependence on US tech companies as a concern, and trusted them not to give data to US authorities.

“Government security departments are painfully aware of all the risks,” said Mark Butcher, a cloud expert who acts as a strategic adviser across government. “But the way that most senior leaders talk about it is: ‘Well, we’ve been reassured by Microsoft that it would never happen.’”

But the source who has held senior policing roles said: “All the security guys I worked with when this policy came in expected a big breach by now, and we know it will take that to change the police’s position.

“The truth is, however, the level of logging and information in the cloud systems would not necessarily tell us if there was a problem. We really don’t know if the data has been breached or not.”

We wanted to let Max Dowman bloom in the shadows but he has become hard to ignore

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:59:40 GMT

This most modern and well-honed of footballers will not be able to escape the spotlight in an age of constant scrutiny but looks equipped to handle it

The poet Jorge Luis Borges wrote a famous short story about a society that had become so good at making maps, so obsessed with capturing every detail, that its rulers decided the only way to do the job right was to make a lifesize map of its entire empire, which could then be laid out across the actual land from coast to coast. Imagine a map of Britain the exact same size as Britain, showing every branch of Greggs, every nail bar, every vape shop in perfect detail. Only then can we really see what Britain looks like, by standing on a fake Britain laid over the top of actual Britain.

Borges was writing in the 1940s, at a time when people were fascinated by the mechanised future, with its new forms of measuring out the world: the wireless, the 30mph motorcar, the rise of Big Tape Measure. And to be fair, the mega-map is a pretty accurate vision of our own fully networked present, a place where you can snoop around a village in Mozambique from your laptop in Egham, where no one ever stops committing acts of minute self-surveillance, even if they think they’re just searching “What is beetroot?” on the internet.

Borges also hated football. “Soccer is popular because stupidity is popular,” he wrote, which probably seemed a bold statement at the time. But then Borges also didn’t live to see an episode of Wow Sports Premier League Breakfast at Breakfast with Roger McRoger and a puzzled Lee Trundle. After which, perhaps less of a surprise. But the process he describes is also a good description of what football is doing to itself. Endless data, endless analysis, no spaces or free air, matches that are just schematised movement. At times it can feel like football is out there laying a lifesize real-time map on top of itself.

In Borges’s story, the land soon begins to decay beneath the massive map – which is reassessed by later generations as insane, pointless and stupid – and left to rot in the desert. We haven’t reached this point. Nobody is de-mapping football. But it does perhaps explain why everyone gets so excited when a talent emerges that seems to be playful and human, to exist outside the grid. And also why it has felt wrong to gush too soon about Max Dowman, to fear placing the hex on him. We know how this works. Here is a fluffy new thing. Let us break him. Let us heap pressure on his shoulders. Don’t talk about Max Dowman. Let Max Dowman exist, breathe, bloom in the shadows.

So, Max Dowman then. It has become quite hard to ignore him. He was brilliant against Ipswich in midweek, and brilliant in a way that seems solid and real and comfortable with itself. Most obviously there were the two goals, both a perfect snapshot of why Dowman seems equipped to survive, more state‑of‑the‑art than some other young players we’ve burdened with expectation.

The second goal is particularly good, five perfect little actions packed into six seconds of football. Arsenal have the ball on the edge of the Ipswich box. Dowman shows for a pass, sees it’s going elsewhere, changes his mind, and makes a three-yard sprint to create space. Finally he has the physical capacity to control a bouncing ball in that sliver of space, to move his feet so much quicker than the nearest defender it looks like a glitch in the machine, and to finish in a way that involves sifting the options and timing the shot, all without breaking stride.

The first goal is on his other side, and involves a more classical piece of one-on-one deception. This is the same defender: Cédric Kipré, 29 years old, came through Paris Saint-Germain’s youth system. Dowman walks through him with a micro-feint and a switch of feet, then reels off another hilariously understated finish, doing it all while a second defender is still gathering himself to lunge, like a man operating in a different time signature to everyone around him.

This is the key point of difference, the ability to make everything stop, the fly-vision that means he sees what’s about to happen while everyone else is whirling about trying to read the charts, in the same way Lionel Messi (yes, sorry, sorry) always seems to have time to pass the ball into the net, like this is all a kickabout in a pair of sliders.

Our way of understanding young creative players has often seemed to lag behind where the game actually is, to be driven by nostalgia for what this thing used to look like. I remember the excitement over the 18-year-old Jack Rodwell’s physicality at the exact moment physicality was no longer going to be a thing, like proudly unveiling the latest horse‑drawn train just as the Ford Model T rolls off the production line.

Michael Owen was brilliant at 17, but he was mainly brilliant at running very fast in a straight line and smashing the ball into the net. Plus of course there was Wayne Rooney, who emerged a pale, unformed teenager composed entirely from energy drinks and white bread, out there making the game up on the fly, as though some urban foundling had come barrelling over the advert boards with a string of sausages still dangling from his mouth.

The narrative around Rooney is that he lost this vital native quality. But Rooney adapted and survived, and clearly understood what he had to be a lot better than those of us watching. And even now creative players have to exist against this. Cole Palmer is exciting because he does surprising things that seem to be striking a blow for freedom, beauty and older people who struggle to make their email work. But his real challenge is to retain just enough of this while fitting the world around him.

Dowman is a bit different. The things that make him stand out seem to speak very easily to how football is now. Being a modern creative footballer is not jinking runs, rasping drives or dribbling across a cabbage field in a pair of cowboy boots. It’s targeted energy, high-intensity semi-freedom. Lamine Yamal and Désiré Doué have the same fast-twitch foot and brain speed, the ability to operate in micro-moments, to see patterns just ahead of time. Dowman is 6ft tall and getting stronger. He won’t be kicked to pieces. He can repeat this without taking bites out of himself.

There is still the issue of his youth. But maybe this doesn’t matter so much either. The world has changed. In the age of Rooney and Owen there was no care, no data, no softness. This is where the structures of modern football are an advantage. Dowman will be GPS’d to the last decimal point. Endless physical scientists will have a say on his output and stress levels.

The money is too big. The talent is too valuable. It also comes ready to plug and play. You don’t get to this level unless you can ingest systems and briefings. You’ve already been pressure-cooked and stress-tested. What you’re being asked to do in the orderly spaces of professional football is the same thing you were asked to do in the orderly spaces of academy football, just five levels up and with more people watching.

Borges was anti-football because he saw it as inauthentic, the players no longer sports people but “actors in jerseys before the TV cameras”. And this is also fine, further evidence that boomer-dad nostalgia is one of the key archetypes of human behaviour.

Life is also different now; not harder or easier, but more instant, a series of moments, the creation of rapid-fire energy. Dowman has grown up inside this. He can parcel his time out, disappear for a bit, maybe make a show of things in the spring.

And yes, this is another way of fitting him to a model, laying a lifesize map of future Max Dowman across the present. But I strongly suspect he will be fine, and that unlike so many other things out there he’s pretty well adapted to whatever the future is supposed to look like.

It’s not just ‘spermageddon’ that’s stopping us having children

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:54:36 GMT

Aubrey Foard and Nina Plummer respond to Zoe Williams’s interview with Camilla Cavendish about the reasons behind plummeting birthrates worldwide

I appreciate Zoe Williams’s excellent interview with Camilla Cavendish (Spermageddon, ‘greedy jobs’ and abject fear: why birthrates are plummeting – and why it matters, 17 September), but I have to take issue with one of her statements: “Of course, the climate crisis is playing a big part in that, but it still doesn’t wholly stack up – in the 80s, there was the wraparound threat of nuclear annihilation and it didn’t seem to dent anyone’s joie de vivre.”

Yes, the buildup of nuclear arms and the terror surrounding it reached its peak in the 20th century, but it was kept in check by policies of Mutually Assured Destruction: a singular launch of a nuclear arsenal would have instantly ended humanity.

As an older, childless millennial, climate change figures profoundly in my desire to not have children: the cause of climate change has been known for 50 years, it’s happening before our eyes, and there is not enough being done about it.

While it’s true that we may overcome rising emission rates with renewable energy, the current and near-future effects of the climate crisis mean we are in for a very difficult road ahead as a society – and that’s if we succeed. If I’m going to go through the financial, physical, emotional and psychological burden of raising a child, I don’t want to also have to explain to them that there’s a very good chance that they’re doomed, because billionaire, capitalist greed couldn’t figure out how to stop itself from ruining the world for human civilisation. Aubrey FoardBaltimore, Maryland, US

Camilla Cavendish notes that the falling birthrate is fundamentally “a story about pessimism”. I would like to offer an additional perspective we can begin to hold alongside (not in lieu of) this bleak view.

The link between women’s education and empowerment and the falling birthrate is well established. It is only two generations since contraception became widely available in western countries. It is therefore only a split second since human beings have collectively been given the opportunity to consider what other forms of joy, meaning and fulfilment are available to us as a species. While children are an enormous source of joy and meaning for many, we are now also discovering other ways to build beautiful, meaningful, fulfilling lives that include loving communities of non-biological kin, as well as deep affinity for our home and the other beings that inhabit it.

Beyond pessimism, choosing not to have children or to have fewer children might be the exact investment of hope in the future that Cavendish is struggling to see. It is not just an act of “giving up”, but an investment in the belief that the decisions we make today can create a better future. By acting now to reduce the strain on the planet while simultaneously reducing competition for future generations; by becoming more mindful of our individual limitations as potential parents as well as the systemic limitations of our circumstances; by considering deeply and ethically whether here and now is the best time to bring more people into the world; by learning to savour deep connections alongside our biological relatives; and by finding a story of hope, meaning and fulfilment beyond the cycle of biological reproduction alone, people, and women in particular, might be making hope out of the freedom that has been offered through being able to control our own fertility.

For some, choosing not to have children, or choosing to have fewer children, in order to dedicate ourselves more fully to helping, as well as savouring, the world already here, might be as much an act of hope as deciding to have (more) children is for others. Nina PlummerEdinburgh

On assisted dying, MPs grappled with a difficult bill

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:53:26 GMT

Readers respond to the bill’s narrow defeat in the Commons earlier this month

For many, the failure of the assisted dying bill (MPs vote against legalising assisted dying in England and Wales, 11 September) has brought relief that a manifestly unsafe law will not be entering the statute book. But it should also prompt reflection about how it got this far.

Two hundred and seventy MPs voted for the bill despite multiple warnings from the medical royal colleges and other professional groups responsible for implementing it that it was unsafe and unworkable. Supportive MPs appeared to be voting on an abstract principle rather than engaging with the concerns raised.

But an MP’s role is not that of a campaigner. If MPs believe there is a case for assisting some people to end their lives, their role is to consider whether and how that could be achieved safely. Instead, parliament was presented with the latest iteration of a proposal first drafted in the 1930s by medical eugenicist Killick Millard, who held disturbing views about “a last service to society by relieving it of a useless burden”. His proposal has returned to parliament repeatedly over the past century, vigorously promoted by the organisation he founded, now calling itself Dignity in Dying. Only its justification, not its content, has been updated as social values have changed.

If parliament returns to this issue, it should approach it afresh and honestly grapple with the complex ethical and practical trade-offs. I, and many others with relevant expertise, would welcome the opportunity to help. Lucy ThomasPalliative care and public health doctor

Andy Burnham talked at length about the importance of leadership in his recent campaigns. His decision to abstain in the assisted dying bill gave a clear compass bearing to those Labour MPs keen to follow their leader. It led to the defeat of the bill and will literally cause untold suffering to innocent citizens. This is not leadership, and to hide behind the barricade of “we must improve social care and palliative care first” is disingenuous in the extreme. Gary NethercottWoodbridge, Suffolk

Sweden’s soul and worrying political shift

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:52:44 GMT

Alvin Engström and Jean Fridh respond to an article by Martin Gelin in which he argues that the country has entered a new era of cruelty

I am writing in response to Martin Gelin’s article (How Sweden lost its soul – and stopped being Sweden, 11 September). Gelin is right to lament how far Swedish politics has moved from the liberal internationalism of the Fredrik Reinfeldt era. Having grown up in Malmö, I have seen how border controls with Denmark affect an Öresund region whose everyday life has long depended on easy movement across the strait. Gelin is right to see this retreat from openness as consequential.

But to say that Sweden has therefore “lost its soul” goes too far. Its political shift is neither uniquely Swedish nor evidence that the country has somehow ceased to be itself. Reinfeldt’s “open your hearts” Sweden faded in much the same European political moment as Angela Merkel’s “Wir schaffen das” Germany. Across the European mainland, mainstream parties have adopted more restrictive positions on migration.

The cases involving British citizens that Gelin describes are troubling, but Britain’s departure from the EU is also part of the explanation for why Britons in Sweden now face immigration rules from which freedom of movement once spared them. Sweden has changed. So has Britain. Neither exists in a vacuum.

There is nothing wrong with romanticising an open, internationalist Sweden. As a young Swede studying at Cambridge, I am susceptible to that image myself. But defining one particular political settlement as Sweden’s “soul” risks turning nostalgia into national essentialism.

Perhaps Jantelagen – the Scandinavian suspicion of thinking oneself exceptional – offers a more Swedish conclusion. We should not imagine that our political upheavals make us uniquely fallen. Sweden has changed, considerably and sometimes regrettably. It has not stopped being Sweden. Alvin EngströmCambridge

Martin Gelin’s analysis of how Sweden is losing its soul rings true – unfortunately. After living in Sweden for 33 years, I have never felt more like a foreigner than I do now. I am British (of Scottish origin) and moved to Sweden in 1993, at the age of 37, to live with my Swedish husband and our two children. I remember being so impressed by the social benefits, the access to good and affordable childcare and the job opportunities for women – precisely the ideals Martin describes. Over the past 10. years, opposition to immigration has grown in the wake of the so-called refugee “flood” of 2015, when the door was wide open. Sadly, that door is now permanently closed, and locked.

In recent years, I have repeatedly been asked whether I consider myself Swedish (I have dual nationality). At first, I didn’t think much of it, but over time, I began to find the question very irritating. On one occasion, an older Swedish woman said it didn’t matter if I didn’t feel Swedish, because “we see you as one of us anyway”. I am ashamed to admit that I snapped at her over the word “us”; I know she meant well, but it made me realise just how divisive the question was. The mere fact that it was being asked by nice, ordinary, polite people was playing right into the hands of the far right.

Spot the conversation hogger – and do something about it

These conversational hoggers … don’t they know we were born with two ears and one mouth for a reason? Thank you, Anita Chaudhuri, for a fun, well observed and useful article (‘But enough about you …’ How to survive in a world of monologuists, interrupters and trauma dumpers, 13 September).

It is an interesting reflection to see which of the five hoggers more frequently turn up in our own lives. As a people pleaser and introvert, I have a track record of meeting many monologuists. I pretend to listen, but secretly resent them and their audacity. I just want them to ask about me.

I have learned that although interruption can feel violent, sometimes it is a courageous act. When the speaker has just lost connection with the audience and themselves, we have to bring them back. That is what I loved most about the article – it reminded us that we do have options. We can start noticing how we turn up. How am I listening and speaking? What is my responsibility here?

A great listener can help to transform the conversation – listening is not a passive act. And in talking, am I actually being interesting? Am I talking as if being listened to?

Life is always inviting us into a conversation … with ourselves and each other. Penelope MavorDirector, Earth Converse

The Guardian view on NAZA’s persecuted directors: journalism is not treason

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:46:30 GMT

Politicians who threaten filmmakers rather than investigate alleged military crimes expose not strength but a leadership frightened of the evidence

Across Israel, politicians, military leaders and much of the media are trying to discredit a documentary that almost none of them have seen. Produced by the Guardian, NAZA examines the AI-powered targeting systems used by the Israel Defense Forces to bombard Gaza after Hamas’s brutal 7 October 2023 attacks. Named after the Israeli military acronym euphemistically used for “collateral damage”, NAZA features interviews with 24 anonymous insiders who reflect on their role in the death-dealing. Israeli leaders have branded the film a “blood libel” and “fiction”. Its Oscar-winning directors, Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham, face being stripped of their citizenship for treason.

This is absurd. NAZA shows how bureaucratic distance and routine can turn extreme violence into ordinary work. More than 73,000 Palestinians, including more than 20,000 children, have been killed in the campaign by Israel’s military. A democracy that values life would at least investigate the film’s claims. Instead Israel’s government, which says it is committed to democratic accountability, is attacking journalists.

The allegations in NAZA come from military insiders. For many, it does not appear to be remorse that drives them to speak out. Some are proud of what they have done. One recalls the “insane fun” of planning airstrikes in Gaza. Crucially, Israeli soldiers describe the military accepting large numbers of Palestinian casualties as the price for killing a single Hamas operative. When civilian fatalities rise to as many as hundreds for one enemy combatant, proportionality looks less like a military assessment and more like a licence for mass death.

NAZA’s story is not only about death and destruction but also some of the people behind it: polite, educated members of Israel’s liberal middle class, much like the directors themselves. They built and operated a system that told them women and children would die in large numbers. Yet they told themselves that responsibility for the deaths of innocent Palestinians lay elsewhere. The acronym, NAZA, turns possible fatalities into a number per target. By the time an operator approves a strike, morality has disappeared up the chain of command.

An election campaign has seen Israeli politicians shamefully weaponise controversy to outflank each other on the right. If such leaders are saying that the conduct of the Israeli military is beyond independent review, that can hardly be consistent with the commitment to the rule of law. Israel’s government might invoke national security to defend its actions. But the film builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. Ominously, Israel’s domestic intelligence service may be involved in a leak investigation. By turning the army on the documentary’s directors, Israel is making an example of them. Far-right activists target their families by making threats. If the filmmakers were to return to Israel now, their lives might well be in danger.

The Committee to Protect Journalists and 10 other press-freedom groups have warned that Israel must protect its journalists and filmmakers – not brand them traitors and paint targets on their backs. Yet the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has seized on the controversy to threaten anyone who “defames” Israeli soldiers with loss of citizenship. Rather than investigate alleged crimes, he would punish those who expose them. Israel’s leaders ought to be protecting those who scrutinise power, not pointing a mob towards them.

The Guardian view on youth unemployment: too few jobs in too many places

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:45:29 GMT

Young people in Britain’s poorer towns have far fewer opportunities. Changing this will require targeted support – and industrial strategy

The ideas that Neets (young people not in education, employment or training) simply aren’t trying hard enough to find a job, or don’t want one, are “myths,” Alan Milburn wrote in his interim report on the subject earlier this year – “sometimes cruel ones”. Although 84% of Neets say they want to work, their prospects are unfairly limited by where they live. Rotherham has one suitable vacancy for every 22 young adults. The Cotswolds has one for every four. For too many young people, particularly those in deprived parts of Britain, there simply aren’t enough jobs.

This is the finding from an index published last week by the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), which ranked British towns according to the availability of jobs for young people. Like so many features of Britain’s Neet crisis, from poor mental health to school drop-out rates, the index is a map of disadvantage. At the top are affluent towns in southern England that account for nine in 10 of the areas with the highest numbers of vacancies. At the bottom are places such as Inverclyde and East Renfrewshire, where young people might once have followed their parents into manufacturing and industry. Deindustrialisation destroyed those jobs, and such places never recovered.

Given that half of the rise in Neets aged 18 to 24 since 2019 is due to changes in the labour market, jobs are a good place for the government to focus. In 2024, the Starmer government launched a “youth guarantee,” including a pilot jobs programme that provides six months’ paid work to 18 to 24-year-olds who have been receiving universal credit for 18 months. This was a positive step, but 18 months is far too long for young people to wait for support, and almost half of Neets don’t claim benefits, so aren’t eligible for this scheme.

The IPPR has called for the creation of a new “youth contract”, comprising short-term placements for all people at risk of becoming Neet in areas where jobs are scarce, more apprenticeships at the smaller firms that dominate Britain’s labour market, and more dedicated work coaches. These would all be improvements to the status quo. But if today’s young people are to find employment that will sustain them into adulthood, the government will need an industrial strategy capable of creating long-term opportunities in places where few exist.

The devolution of vocational training to local authorities, which are better placed to understand the demands of regional labour markets than Whitehall civil servants, is welcome. But ministers will need a dose of realism about where “good” jobs will come from. Andy Burnham’s talk of “reindustrialising” regions resembles a Westminster pipe dream. As manufacturing has developed, it has lost the ability to reliably create widespread employment. Even in the US and China, where governments have generously subsidised industry, manufacturing jobs continue to fall as a share of total employment.

As the economist Dani Rodrik recently observed in an essay collection about reindustrialisation, much of Britain’s future employment won’t be in manufacturing or high-productivity service sectors, but in industries such as retail, hospitality and care. If Mr Burnham wants to create “good growth in every postcode”, his government must transform the conditions of work in these industries so they provide gainful employment – and opportunities for today’s young people to build future careers.
