Polanski request to postpone Greens’ conference to focus on byelection refused by party

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:26:35 GMT

Exclusive: Leader understood to have wanted to concentrate on Holborn and St Pancras campaign in London but executive committee voted against plan

Zack Polanski requested that the Greens’ ruling executive committee postpone the party’s imminent annual conference so they could focus on the Holborn and St Pancras byelection but was refused.

While party officials say the formal request came from staffers worried about diluting resources by staging a conference a week before Polanski tries to win Keir Starmer’s former Commons seat, the Guardian understands the party leader wanted this to happen.

In the end, the executive committee of the Greens in England and Wales, which has about 25 voting members including Polanski, voted against the plan on Thursday.

The party expects about 3,000 people to attend what would be its biggest gathering, beginning in Brighton on 2 October.

Calling off the event at such short notice would have cost the party a significant sum given it has rented a conference venue, and risked annoying members who have taken time off work and booked travel and hotels.

The byelection, in which Polanski hopes to challenge for a traditionally safe Labour seat, takes place on 8 October, just four days after the conference finishes.

The end of a byelection campaign is traditionally marked by parties trying to canvass as many voters as possible. Having thousands of the Greens’ most active members gathered somewhere else for the final weekend greatly complicates their operation.

Some Greens have also speculated that Polanski would have preferred to fight the byelection before the party votes on a contentious policy motion at its conference, which sets out a motion on Zionism.

Polanski is under pressure to take a stance on the motion, which came top of a members’ vote of policy motions to be debated at the party conference, and is thus almost certain to feature.

The Greens make party policy by member votes at conferences. If passed, the motion would equate Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state in Palestine – with racism and would call for a single Palestinian state. Members who support Zionism would risk being disciplined for racism.

A number of Greens fear passing the motion could alienate Jewish supporters. Polanski, who is Jewish, has not given a public opinion on the issue, but is understood to support a pair of amendments that would tone down the motion.

A Green party spokesperson said: “The party was exploring different ways of allocating our resources effectively while fighting the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. One possible option was to postpone our conference.

“After discussion we remain committed to running an incredibly ambitious Holborn and St Pancras byelection campaign and holding what will be our biggest ever party conference.”

Fleetwood’s exit at plus three, while less dramatic, was another obvious blow to the tournament organisers at Wentworth. On a day of high-profile departures, injury forced Patrick Reed out of the event midway through his round. That scenario might have repercussions as Rory McIlroy seeks to prise the DP World Tour’s order of merit from the American’s grasp.

The LIV backdrop also cannot be ignored; Rahm is fully expected to depart the ailing circuit when the formalities of a voluntary bankruptcy filing are completed. This is, however, a situation now in the hands of the courts. It would be perfectly natural if Rahm finds himself unable to appropriately focus when inside the ropes. Two Wentworth rounds involved three birdies, 10 bogeys and two double bogeys.

Fleetwood needed a change of fortune, albeit not a significant one, after Thursday’s 73. The 15th has proved his nemesis this week, with a bogey five during the first round followed up by a double bogey on day two. Despite delivering three birdies, the 35-year-old slipped to a 74.

Reed – who looked a candidate to win after the first round – played his first nine holes in 44, nine over par. He grasped his left wrist after a pulled tee shot on the 10th, before his withdrawal was confirmed and he headed straight for medical treatment.

Elements of normality were provided by Adam Scott, who is seeking to become the oldest winner of this event. The 46-year-old Australian backed up a 67 with an identical score. Scott would place huge stock in a Wentworth win.

“Let’s put the majors aside for a minute,” he said. “I think there’s the Players Championship, Wentworth and the Australian Open for me at that level of importance. So it would mean a lot? Absolutely. I mean, it would be huge.

“I’m not heaping pressure on myself to go and win this tournament. I feel like at this point I just need to put my head into a place where I can enjoy the next couple of days. I have done this many times in the past, not so much lately, but I think hopefully that kind of instinct and memory comes back in this position. If I can enjoy myself the next couple of days, I think I’ll get the best out of myself.”

Kylian Mbappé has ended a 20-year association with Nike to sign a boot deal with the Swiss challenger company On.

On is a newcomer to football and this week unveiled its first boots, the Lightspray Prototype, which will be available for the mass market from next year before a move into training kit.

Mbappé’s departure, which came at the end of his contract after the World Cup, is a significant blow for Nike, which also lost the Barcelona and Spain star Lamine Yamal to Adidas two years ago. The 27-year-old has been the face of many of Nike’s advertising campaigns.

Nike and Adidas dominate the football market with their boots worn by more than 40% of players at this summer’s World Cup, according to data compiled by the retailer Fútbol Emotion, with Puma accounting for about 10%.

Lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy murder trial speaks out

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 15:48:33 GMT

Michael P Desronvil was sole juror to vote guilty, resulting in deadlocked jury and judge declaring a mistrial

Ron DeSantis offers ‘asylum’ to holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy trial

The lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial is speaking out, saying that he “didn’t have any doubts” during the jury’s deliberations of the case which ended in a mistrial.

“I didn’t have any doubts. As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence present,” the 48-year-old male juror, Michael P Desronvil, said in a statement to NewsNation on Thursday.

“Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she (Clancy) knew exactly what she was doing and planned,” he added.

Desronvil’s public statement follows widespread debate online over the controversial case about whether Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse who fatally strangled her three children in Massachusetts in 2023, should be held criminally responsible.

Clancy has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder charges by reason of insanity, with her defense team arguing that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time.

The trial, which brought nationwide attention to systemic gaps in maternal mental health care, lasted nearly six weeks and culminated in a mistrial after nearly 40 hours of deliberation over seven days.

Several members of the 11-1 deadlocked jury, which comprised nine women and three men, have since publicly commented on the case.

Speaking to NBC10 earlier this month, Roni Carlson, the jury’s foreperson, said the single holdout juror “admitted he had reasonable doubt, and I started filling out the forms, I was so excited”.

“There were three forms I had to fill out and I started filling them out, I wrote my signature on each one, and then he said, ‘But I’m still not going to say that she’s not guilty by reason of insanity,’” she added.

Another juror, Kellie Farina, said: “He had the hardest time getting off the fact that Lindsay viciously killed her children … Every one of us in the hours of our frustration would get up and walk the room because you just couldn’t sit anymore.”

Meanwhile, juror Paula Devlin said: “He was very arrogant,” adding: “He really did not take anything that anybody said.”

Flight chaos for hundreds of thousands was caused in ‘millisecond’ by software error

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 15:45:18 GMT

Error first occurred at 10am but major incident was not declared until 12.30pm, says report

A software defect in part of the UK’s air traffic control system corrupted flight data “in the space of a millisecond”, leading to a six-hour outage and mass airline cancellations and delays across the UK last week, National Air Traffic Services has said.

But ministers said the Nats report into the incident still left questions unanswered, saying they needed “to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos”.

According to the report, the error first occurred at 10am and was notified to engineers who investigated – but the system appeared to be working again, until 12.30pm when a repeat occurred and a major incident was declared.

The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) industry regulator would now “check their findings” and investigate Nats more widely.

Hundreds of thousands of passengers had their travel disrupted after the Nats failure on Tuesday 8 September, which ended up delaying and cancelling flights across the UK and beyond late into the next day.

Airlines have called for compensation and a “credible plan”, with Ryanair demanding the dismissal of the Nats chief executive officer, Martin Rolfe, after the third major air traffic control failure in the UK since summer 2023.

A government source said the CAA review would be “a chance to fundamentally investigate” if Nats was fit for purpose.

Rolfe said the incident was unrelated to the previous failures. He said he could “confirm that it was a software issue and not caused by any incorrect actions by either military or civil operators”.

The preliminary report said the failure was a “legacy and previously unknown software defect and a combination of very specific events occurring simultaneously” in part of the National Airspace System (NAS), which allocates codes to individual aircraft to identify flights on radar.

Nats said the software error occurred at 10am, with engineers first notified at 10.02am that the link between the NAS and London area control system had dropped. The engineers reported at 10.06am that the system had apparently recovered with no operational impact, but continued to investigate.

The report said the fault presented when a manual request for an aircraft code was being processed but paused for another, unspecified “higher priority activity” request. It said: “When processing of the aircraft code request resumed, the software defect meant it did not resume correctly and the resulting output was corrupted, and affected some subsequent flight data updates. This happened in the space of a millisecond.”

At 12.32pm the link between the national and London airspace management dropped again and a major incident was declared, with controllers having to conduct some tasks manually. By 12.45pm, Nats was restricting flights as the system continued to glitch, before failing completely at 1.32pm.

At 1.40pm airlines were advised of restrictions, and between 2.50pm and 4.09pm Nats rebooted the system, eventually resuming full operations at 7.30pm – but leaving mass congestion, displaced aircraft and hundreds of thousands of delayed passengers in its wake.

It took more than two days for the backlog of passenger disruption to be cleared, with more than 2,000 flights cancelled in total and hundreds of thousands of people’s travel plans disrupted.

Rolfe said: “The issue has been identified and mitigation is in place while a permanent fix is safety tested and deployed.”

Joan Collins declared the coats “very chic”, and has her eye on a graceful ivory evening dress with caped shoulders. Kemi Badenoch plans to snap up the classic black tuxedo jacket. If the British public are as enthusiastic as the celebrity front row, Marks & Spencer’s first ever London fashion week catwalk looks like a hit.

The show, held at the Design Museum for 310 guests including Ian Wright and Jamie Carragher, was a gamble on both sides. Would snobby fashionistas be traumatised by elasticated waistbands and practical rainwear? Would M&S customers be alienated by a world of £2,000 handbags and shoes you can’t walk in?

The style message was “fashion with a small f, not a capital F”, said the M&S womenswear director, Maddy Evans. The look was new enough to be compelling (sharp kilts instead of flouncy tiered skirts, low-rise slouchy denim replacing mom jeans), but pitched at a before-the-watershed comfort level. A judicious amount of catwalk theatre was added with some sauce (a very short skirt, the odd semi-visible nipple) and a little zeitgeisty styling (faux fur stoles, Charli xcx-adjacent sunglasses).

The real stunner is the price. All the clothes in this collection went on sale as the show began on Friday, with half of the pieces under £50. The most expensive, a leather coat, will retail for £450. The message – that catwalk style is for everyone – is a win for London fashion week, which has struggled to feel relevant to real lives as designer prices have soared during a cost of living crisis.

As a vision of where our wardrobes are going next, the collection will not give Phoebe Philo or Jonathan Anderson any sleepless nights. M&S is not seeking to define the next vibe shift. Instead, they picked up on the currents that make a wardrobe look contemporary: a colour palette of neutrals with pops of red (for men, as well as women) and a shift toward outfits built from separates over dresses. Menswear featured a classic grey office suit – worn, in a witty casting touch, by scowling nepo-rocker Lennon Gallagher – and centrist-dad chore jackets.

M&S are now ranked in second place in style perception, behind Zara. “That’s exactly where we want to be”, said Evans. “Zara are the cutting edge of fashion, and we are fashion for everybody.”

Many pieces felt intentionally familiar, with nods to the archives to celebrate the centenary of fashion being sold at M&S. There was a twinset, reworked as a cardigan over a knitted camisole, and a sage-green lace two-piece set which nodded to the proud history of M&S lingerie. Models of a broad range of ages and body sizes “were chosen to reflect our 23 million customers”, said Evans.

After the show, Wright caught up with Carragher as a fashion week version of an M&S “picky tea” was served: smoked salmon finger sandwiches and champagne on silver trays.

The show was a bold statement about how M&S sees itself, reflecting resurgent style confidence after fashion hits that have included suede loafers that could pass for Saint Laurent and a sellout collaboration with Bella Freud.

M&S is not the only big name giving the London schedule fresh momentum and a renewed sense of occasion this season. McQueen is returning to London after showing in Paris, while Christopher Kane – one of the city’s most beloved and influential designers – is making a keenly anticipated return to the catwalk with a new job at Mulberry.

Singapore is paying people to read books – can it fix the reading crisis?

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 15:26:07 GMT

A government scheme is giving citizens cash for spending time with a good book. We ask behavioural scientists, along with The Anxious Generation author and psychologist Jonathan Haidt, whether it’ll help make the habit stick

Could the solution to the reading crisis lie in paying people to put down their phones and pick up a book? That’s what one government, at least, is resorting to: this month, Singapore launched a scheme promising actual cash to citizens as a reward for logging reading time on a government website.

It’s unlikely to make you megabucks – you have to rack up 50 reading sessions of at least 15 minutes to earn one Singapore dollar (£0.59), with only one logged session allowed per day. But behavioural scientists and psychologists told the Guardian such a scheme could still help boost a habit in precipitous decline.

Jonathan Haidt, a psychologist and the author of the bestselling book The Anxious Generation, about the impact of social media on young people’s mental health, says that some children are highly motivated by money, and “all kids respond to rewards to some degree” – so for young people, the scheme is “likely to have some beneficial effect in setting up a habit of reading”. Lory Barile, associate professor in economics at the University of Warwick, adds that “there is good evidence that repeating a behaviour consistently can help it become more automatic over time”.

If participants find reading “pleasurable in itself”, then the habit may stick, says Haidt. Yet, for some, the monetary reward “will convey to them that they are reading only for the extrinsic reward”, and so when the money stops, the reading will, too. Barile agrees that the most interesting question isn’t whether people read more while they’re being rewarded, but whether the scheme “helps people establish a reading habit that persists once the reward is no longer present”.

While the earning potential of the Singapore scheme is low, this doesn’t necessarily mean it won’t be effective, says Ivo Vlaev, a professor of behavioural psychology at the National University of Singapore. “One of the interesting findings from behavioural science is that incentives do not always work in proportion to their monetary value.”

The scheme shouldn’t be thought of as “paying people to read” in a conventional economic sense – a dollar every few weeks is obviously not enough to compensate participants for the time they’ve invested. Instead, the payment “may be acting more as a trigger than as a wage”, says Vlaev. Logging reading time and accumulating points means participants “receive an immediate signal that the behaviour has been recognised, your streak continues and you make progress towards a goal”. And once someone has actually started reading, “the intrinsic rewards of the activity can take over”, he adds.

We all know reading has long-term benefits, but a key element of the Singapore scheme hinges on introducing a short-term reward for the activity, mimicking the immediate dopamine hit of scrolling. In fact, the “gamified” element may be “smarter” than the financial reward offered, says Patrick Taylor, director of education at the Behavioural Insights Team (which originated in David Cameron’s Cabinet Office, also known as the “nudge unit”). “Having a manageable 15-minute daily goal, built around existing routines like commuting or bedtime, with streaks and tracking to keep progress visible” are the aspects that could make the scheme a success, he says.

Such a scheme may be particularly effective for lapsed readers. “If people are already intrinsically motivated to read, this may be enough to tip them over the edge to read a bit more,” says Katy Milkman, a professor at Wharton business school, University of Pennsylvania. Vlaev adds that “if somebody already intends to read but repeatedly fails to get started, a tiny immediate reward can help bridge the gap between intention and action”.

In the UK, non-monetary reward schemes for reading and other types of learning have long been in place, such as the primary school rainbow certificate scheme, through which “the value comes primarily from recognition and a sense of achievement”, says Barile. The Reading Agency’s Summer Reading Challenge allows children to receive badges and certificates for reading, too.

A UK pilot of the Singapore-style scheme could therefore “compare small financial rewards with symbolic rewards such as certificates or badges, as well as gamification, goal-setting and progress feedback”, says Barile. Others agree that such schemes should be run as trials, “so we find out what works and why”, says Taylor. Haidt suggests a few variations to test: some children could be randomly assigned to be paid in cash, others could be paid in free books of their choice (“so that they see books as a reward, not money as a reward for reading”), and others “are simply urged to read to get points in a competition, no money”. A fourth group “would be a true control, nothing is done, other than measuring how many books they read”.

But the question remains: should governments financially reward what has been traditionally considered something you do for fun? Milkman sees it differently: “We subsidise, and even require, many other forms of education.” So why not reward reading, too?

Judge said Nina Power and her friend’s social media posts had ‘the whiff of threat and antisemitism’

Reform UK’s new mega-donor Ben Delo gave a £350,000 loan to a conservative writer fighting a legal case in which a judge later found she had engaged in online bullying and regrettable conduct with a “whiff of threat and antisemitism”.

Nina Power and her friend, the writer Daniel DC Miller, brought the legal action for defamation against the performance artist Luke Turner, who they had accused of falsely calling them antisemitic. At the same time, Turner brought a counter-claim against the pair accusing them of harassment.

Their libel action failed on the grounds that Turner’s online reach was not big enough to have caused harm to their reputations, while the harassment case also failed on the basis that their conduct was not unlawful.

The loan from Delo to help fund Power’s case before the 2023 trial shines a light on the Reform supporter’s involvement in backing a landmark legal tussle over the boundaries of free speech.

It is understood Delo did not and does not believe Power and Miller held antisemitic views as alleged by Turner, and would never knowingly provide financial or any other support to those who did.

In the case, Miller, who is Jewish, and Power denied promoting fascist or antisemitic views, and said they did not know Turner was Jewish. The judge found there was “no overt antisemitism” displayed by the pair.

But in the counter-claim of harassment, the judge described social media posts by Miller and Power as having “the whiff of threat and antisemitism which they themselves can fairly be held to have created”, although she ruled it was “too occasional, intangible, diffuse and unconsolidated” to have been unlawful.

She said the “radio frequencies of macabre imagery and casualness around antisemitic tropes into which Mr Turner tuned do yield a discernible signal but not one strong enough to be recognised objectively as antisemitic hate speech or a resolved engagement with physical violence sufficient to render this conduct quasi-criminal”.

The judge also said: “Mr Turner evidently had been harassed to a quasi-criminal (or indeed criminal) degree by other people. But what Mr Miller and Ms Power did was not of that order.”

After the failure of the cases, Turner was awarded costs of £1m amounting to 80% of the total, and Power was declared bankrupt. In the course of the bankruptcy proceedings it emerged that Delo had loaned her a sum in the region of £350,000 to help pay her lawyers.

It is understood the loan was made by Delo weeks before the trial started when Power’s conditional fee arrangement with her lawyers collapsed. The loan was made on a commercial basis and secured against the value of a London property she owns, with a repayment schedule.

Delo has been known to be a supporter of the Free Speech Union, run by the Conservative peer Toby Young, and has funded a base known for anti-woke causes.

Power is a former leftwing academic who has written in publications including the Guardian about feminism. She has since described her journey towards being “conservative in the true sense of that word” and wrote a book, What Do Men Want? Masculinity and Its Discontents, in which she argues men have been demonised.

The 2023 high court ruling describes how Miller and Turner were involved in an online incident which emerged from Turner’s involvement in the London arts scene. The artist had risen to prominence thanks to his creative collaborations with the Hollywood actor Shia LaBeouf.

The pair took opposing sides in relation to the London art gallery LD50, which had staged a symposium featuring neo-reactionary speakers and a show advertised online with a quotation from Adolf Hitler, in German gothic font. While Turner described the venue as an alt-Nazi gallery, Miller joined the counter-protest, standing outside LD50 with a placard calling for “the right to openly discuss ideas”.

Miller, who told the court he was of Jewish heritage, is closely associated with the magazine IM-1776, which platforms hard-right views, having previously contributed to the title as an editor and an author. Among the articles published by IM-1776 are pieces celebrating the “Unabomber” Ted Kaczynski and the proto-fascist Italian nationalist Gabriele D’Annunzio.

In the trial, Turner acknowledged he had been wrong to claim Miller was the author of a blog advocating a Hitler-style disability policy.

WhatsApp chats between Miller and Power, disclosed as part of the 2023 trial, did show them dismissing anti-racism as a “psyop”. The term refers to psychological operations used by the military or governments to influence public behaviour.

Power wrote: “The social disapproval for ‘racism’ is a psyop to stop people realising that there *are* alien and fairy races,” and that “black and white were alien races and very different”.

In a later exchange Power brought up Hitler’s autobiographical political manifesto, Mein Kampf, writing “I think … at some point … we need to read Mein Kampf properly …”, adding that she wanted to “understand it”.

In an episode referenced in the judgment, Miller performed at a public event in Athens, delivering a lecture in the persona of the Italian far-right philosopher and antisemite Julius Evola. During the rise of fascism, Evola called for measures to counter “the Jewish menace”. He opposed democracy in favour of a caste-based aristocratic order and was convicted on appeal during the 1950s of trying to revive fascism.

The judge found the pair had between them labelled Turner “low IQ’, ‘sociopathic’, ‘paranoid’, ‘deranged’, ‘obsessive’, ‘paranoid schizophrenic’, ‘dangerously mentally ill’ and so on and on – sometimes accompanied by messages to ‘get help’.” She said in her ruling that Power told her from the witness box that the latter proceeded from genuine and empathetic concern. The judge was unconvinced.

During the trial, Miller and Power denied promoting antisemitic philosophies, describing their interest in the subject as a quest to “critically understand” the issues.

Power and Delo declined to comment. Miller said the story was “based on a systematic distortions of facts”, adding: “I am myself Jewish and proudly Jewish.”

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 15:00:22 GMT

Eighteen-year-old known as Chai was active in networks notorious for their sadistic exploitation of young people

A Swedish teenager known as Chai has been sentenced to more than 10 years in jail for attempted murder, rape and aggravated assault – crimes committed via the internet, including against a teenage girl in Australia.

The district court found that Chai, 18, was active in online networks notorious for their sadistic extortion of young and vulnerable people, coercing them to create sexually explicit material or engage in acts of violence – and for the youth of those involved.

The teenager was between 15 and 17 when the offences were committed.

Chai was convicted of two counts of attempted murder against a young person in Germany, and multiple sexual and violent offences against the Australian teenager, among other offences.

Jenny Östling, a senior public prosecutor at Sweden’s national unit against international and organised crime, said the court had clearly understood the phenomenon of “nihilistic violent extremism” and the Com – an umbrella term for a loosely connected online network that engages in cybercrime, extortion and violence.

“I’m really glad that they realise how serious this is and what it is,” she said.

She noted that the sentence was among the longest possible in Sweden for someone of Chai’s age. The court also found that it was possible for someone to be convicted of violent offences even where they were committed remotely via the internet.

“That is a very important tool for us when we proceed [with] these kinds of cases,” Östling said.

The crimes committed by those involved with sadistic extortion networks, such as one globally known as “764”, often cross borders, with cases in the US, the UK, Germany and Australia, and alleged victims in multiple jurisdictions.

Material is often created and traded among participants to build status and control, lawyers and researchers told the Guardian as part of its investigation into these groups, as well as a means of accessing closed servers and chatrooms.

“These are young people recruiting other young people,” Bjørn Ihler, the founder of the security firm Revontulet, said at the time. “It is a youth phenomenon.”

Chai’s conviction is one of several cases that have resulted in significant terms of imprisonment for young men found to be involved in this ecosystem, including an American, Kyle Spitze, 27, who was sentenced in August to 77 years in prison – the longest federal sentence yet imposed on someone the US government has labelled a “nihilistic violent extremist”.

During the trial, Chai underwent a forensic psychiatric examination that found he was not suffering a serious mental disorder when the offences occurred.

His lawyer, Emily Tovedal, told the Guardian: “The defence’s view is that the court has made an error of judgment regarding a large proportion of the charges.” Authorities internationally have increasingly raised the alarm about sadistic online exploitation of young people, detailing potential warning signs including self-harm and isolation.

“Sadly, I’m confident that … they will probably grow,” Östling said of these networks. “And we will also be aware of more of them, because now we know what to look for.”

Tech billionaires trying to live for ever? That’s a waste of time, says physicist

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 15:00:21 GMT

Exclusive: Prof Jim Al-Khalili says he will offer solution to ‘arrow of time’ problem in Royal Institution lectures

Tech billionaires attempting to live for ever are, quite literally, wasting their time, a leading physicist has said.

While some normal people are turning to unregulated peptide injections, cold plunges and supplements in an effort to defy ageing, the ultra-rich are aiming for immortality with even more drastic interventions: the tech chief executive Bryan Johnson has even tried injecting plasma from his 17-year-old son – although he later said he saw no benefit from it.

Prof Jim Al-Khalili, who will be giving this year’s Royal Institution Christmas lectures on the topic of time, has said people expending their energy on trying to live for ever may be missing out on the here and now.

“We have a finite interval of time in which we exist in the universe. And the more I study the nature of time, the more I think about it, the more I realise that I just want to make the most of the time that I have,” he said.

“We’re [here for] a blink of an eye compared with the age of the universe. If I spend that blink of an eye trying to extend it to two blinks of an eye, I’m not sure if that is actually a worthwhile thing to be spending my life doing.”

Al-Khalili has long been fascinated by time. As a child he was baffled when his father, an engineer, said no one really understood what time was. “I had no idea what he was talking about,” he said. “It was only after training as a physicist you realise that, actually, the notion of time – our commonsense view of time – somehow it is very far removed from the way we think about time in physics in particular.”

Among other examples, Al-Khalili points out that the renowned theoretical physicist Albert Einstein revealed time does not run at the same rate for everyone. “What I might call a second would be longer than a second for you if I was flying past you with my clock in a rocket,” he said. “I’ll say, look, it’s ticking by one second. And you’ll say, no, actually, five seconds have gone by. You’re doing everything in slow motion.”

Gravity, he added, had an effect too. “That for me is the most spine-tingling aspect to it, that time runs at different rates depending on how strong gravity is.”

Einstein’s work may also shed light on a Christmas conundrum: how the ghosts of past, present and future could turn up on the same night to spook Ebenezer Scrooge in Charles Dickens’s A Christmas Carol.

Al-Khalili says that according to Einstein all times coexist – past, present and future – in the same way as all points in space exist. “The problem, of course, is that we only ever experience the present moment,” Al-Khalili said. “So, the idea of the Christmas Carol is a wonderful one that highlights this notion that times maybe aren’t all separate. That maybe we can join with people, someone from the past, someone from the future. But of course, in relativity, that means time travel.”

Time travel is another topic Al-Khalili plans to explore in the Christmas lectures. “Mathematically, it is possible to travel back in time,” he says. The reality, however, is a little more complicated – akin to travelling a rollercoaster’s loop-the-loop.

“You’re travelling forward along the rollercoaster, but what’s happening is you’re doubling back on yourself and arriving back at your starting point. It’s the same sort of thing [with time travel]. What’s called a closed time-like curve in relativity, is somewhere in space-time which is so warped and curved by gravity that you’re travelling what you regard as forward in time, but in fact you’re looping back through space-time to a moment before you started,” he said.

“But the problem, of course, is most physicists think ‘surely that is impossible’, because time travel into the past leads to all sorts of paradoxes.’”

Travelling into the future is, at least in theory, easier. “The way you do it is by slowing time down, either by travelling close to the speed of light or doing what Matthew McConaughey does in Interstellar – you go and orbit around a supermassive black hole whose gravitational field is so strong that, I think in the movie, every hour they spend near this black hole, seven years go by on Earth.”

Al-Khalili will also tackle a conundrum that has bothered scientists for centuries: why time only seems to flow in one direction.

“Things decay, batteries run out, balls roll downhill, we grow older, your children’s bedroom gets more messy, not more tidy – unless you intervene,” he said. “All those things point to a directionality to time, and yet fundamentally our equations say there is no preferred direction in time.”

The problem has kept Al-Khalili up at night for months, if not years. But now he thinks he has the answer: for those who tune in.

“In the lectures, I’m going to give an explanation for how to solve that problem,” he said. “I won’t give any spoilers, that’s for the Christmas lecture. I have solved the problem of the arrow of time.”

The Christmas lectures from the Royal Institution supported by CGI will be broadcast on the BBC and iPlayer in late December

Quentin Bell and Olivia Sterling review – two artists with a magic touch

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 14:32:41 GMT

Charleston, LewesBell’s strange and charming ceramics celebrate a life dedicated to creativity, while next door Sterling’s bawdier, weirder paintings form a critique of race and power

Quentin Bell was not a great artist, but that didn’t stop him. He saw the world as a magical place. The ceramicist (son of the Bloomsbury group’s Vanessa Bell; biographer of his aunt Virginia Woolf) spent his life lost in a world of magic, myth, newts in ponds, levitating women and knights on horseback. He died in 1996, leaving behind decades of pots, plates, figurines and drawings filled with wonder and amazement.

It all started when Bell was nine years old. Taken to a magic show by some relatives, he saw a jaw-dropping spectacle: a beautiful woman seeming to float in the air. It stayed with him throughout his life.

Five sculptures here show bodies caught in mid-air, raised off the ground, stiff as a board. There are rough messy works in wire and wood and plaster from the 1960s, bronze from the 80s and painted ceramics from the 90s; from modern and stark to gaudy and bright, it’s levitation that set him on his creative path and never left his side.

Most of the work here is ceramic: plates, pots and figurines. They’re humorous, brightly coloured, shiny objects. They’re like messy, rough takes on chintzy 18th-century European decorative art, rococo porcelain with its depictions of reclining ladies in voluminous dresses. The figurines aren’t great: they’re basic and poorly rendered, often malformed and pretty unremarkable, if quite funny in places.

His plates and teapots fare better, especially the later cups and jugs, which are colourful and decorative. But his drawings and illustrations are where it really falls apart. He paints Greek myths and biblical scenes, he illustrates the story of Cinderella and his own imagined history of Sussex, but none of it is well executed or particularly interesting. They feel like fun creative projects meant to entertain his kids, which some of them were.

What makes it compelling is that everything here is at odds with the aesthetic trends of his era. There’s none of the austere minimalism of influential contemporary potters such as the amazing Bernard Leach, none of the abstraction or surrealism that was coursing through Europe, none of the grim interwar realism that defined so much English modernism. Instead, there’s something way more anachronistic. This is strange, charming, incredibly English, totally eccentric creativity being expressed on its own terms.

The main takeaway from this exhibition isn’t that Quentin Bell is good at art; he’s not even the best Bell. The main takeaway is that there’s something powerful, even beautiful about dedicating your life to creativity.

Way better is the display of new works next door by the brilliant young English painter Olivia Sterling. She’s taken the magical obsessions of Bell and pushed them to bawdier, weirder, funnier, more critical extremes. Her whole shtick is about using the language of old cartoons and comics, the symbolism of food, the representation of the human body, and twisting it all into biting critiques of race and power dynamics. This is her at her strangest, darkest and filthiest.

You walk into a room-sized painting of vast bodies squeezed into corsets and girdles or flopping about in dressing gowns, like you’ve stumbled into the backstage of some burlesque show. And then the performance starts. A woman has become a dirty dining table in one menacingly red painting, plates of half-eaten cake and glasses of milk strewn across her body. In another work, a pink corpse is littered with ice-creams, a magician’s rabbit scampers over her belly and milk spurts from her nipple. Smaller works show white liquid being squeezed and pulled out of teats and orifices. A huge triptych depicts a white body lying in a magician’s sword box, one black woman pressing down on top of it, another plunging a sword in.

Sterling is drawing a line between magic and power; she’s saying they’re both fundamentally the same thing: an illusion, a world maintained through artifice. It’s clever, political, incisive narrative painting. But, crucially, it’s also fun, ridiculously colourful and totally overblown. If it was miserable, serious and dour, you’d feel like you were getting lectured. Instead, you feel like you’re watching a Tom and Jerry episode about greed and racism, with all the violence and slapstick intact. Now that’s a good magic trick.

At Charleston, Lewes, until 7 March

“We have removed the collection with immediate effect and are reviewing our approval processes to ensure nothing like this happens again. Once again, we would like to put on record our sincere apologies for this error and any offence caused.”

Talk less, listen more and six other top tips on giving good advice

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 14:00:20 GMT

Are you someone who thinks they have all the answers? Is your experience relevant here? Experts on the questions to ask yourself before giving advice

“Often, when people approach you for advice, they just want to talk about how they feel,” says Annalisa Barbieri, advice columnist for the Guardian for almost 20 years. For example, you might vent to a friend about your awful boss, and if they’re shocked it could confirm you’re being treated badly. “I also think people can have a lot of shame when things aren’t working out, and we like to share shame because it’s a hot potato of a feeling.” In other words, not every situation warrants advice. Sometimes, the person just wants to gauge a reaction or to share.

In his Ted Talk How to Tame Your Advice Monster, Michael Bungay Stanier, the author of bestselling book The Coaching Habit, highlights the part of all of us that thinks we can solve people’s problems. “The advice monster looms up when someone starts talking, and you think: ‘Right, I’m about to add value to the conversation,’” he explains. “You think: ‘I have all the answers, and I want to have control and manage uncertainty.’ These are human drivers that are often useful, but can turn into patterns that are less helpful.”

It may sound simple, but ask before giving advice, says Bungay Stanier. Barbieri suggests a phrase she uses, albeit gently, with her children: “Do you want advice, or do you just want to vent?”

As Bungay Stanier puts it in his book The Advice Trap, giving advice is not bad; it’s when advice is your default response to every situation or arrives too quickly that it can become a problem.

The solution? “Understanding that people aren’t looking for a silver bullet, but to be seen, heard and encouraged,” he says. When we move into advice mode too fast, we can send out the message that we think we’re smarter, better, faster. This sets up a power imbalance that makes people resistant to the advice they came for in the first place.

If you’re questioning whether you’re rushing to advice too quickly, do an audit, he suggests. “People don’t realise how fast they move to advice-giving. Even coaches who have been trained to slow down on giving advice can be very trigger-happy, because they want to be helpful. You have to unlearn that.”

Try it: can you let the conversation play out for more than two or three minutes before jumping in?

Listening is important because people are more likely to act on advice they feel they’ve come up with themselves, says psychologist Dr Lee Valls from the London Clinic. But also because, with time and space, they may discover that the presenting problem is not the real problem. “One problem may be masking a bigger, more existential one.”

One way to dig deeper into the real problem is to “stay curious”, says Bungay Stanier. You can ask questions such as: “What’s hard about this for you?” “What’s really going on?” “What have you already figured out?” He explains that “these kinds of questions can encourage agency, but also ensure you’re not giving them stuff they’ve already thought of.”

Barbieri has found that often when people are struggling it’s because their expectations do not match their experience: “Over the last 10 years, I think people’s expectations have become more divorced from reality, particularly with comparing ourselves to others over social media.” With this in mind, if someone says: “My partner is treating me like this,” you might say: “Is that how you want to feel?” rather than “That’s awful, you should do this.” This avoids putting more responsibility on the person when they’re already feeling burdened.

Yitong Zhao of the University of Toronto researches how people help loved ones feel better during stress. In two recent studies, her team examined romantic relationships and friendships, exploring which approaches to advice led to better reported results for the relationship and advice seekers’ mental health.

They studied two approaches. Commitment to the problem involves staying with the person’s feelings rather than dismissing them, and suggesting new ideas, goals or perspectives, such as: “OK, this is hard, but is it also something you can learn from?” Decommitment involved responses such as “It’s not as bad as it seems,” or “It’s out of your hands.”

In highlighting their ability to take control of the situation, commitment led to the loved one feeling more supported and less judged. Decommitment, on the other hand, while an attempt at de-escalation, was riskier. “It can be invalidating – the person may assume you think they’re overreacting, or that they should feel less.”

The key takeaway: how people help is as important as whether they try to help. “When you try to help, it’s not about taking away how someone is feeling; it’s more about expanding what they’re feeling and adding new perspectives,” says Zhao.

We’ve all been there. We’re seeking advice, and the person starts talking about their problems; worse yet, projecting. “We’re all biased,” explains Valls. “Whether we’re a friend or a sibling, the advice we give is shaped by our past experiences, alone or shared. Bias means you feel you know what’s best for the person. Sometimes that’s in their best interest; sometimes it isn’t.”

Valls’ advice: be wary of hijacking the conversation and making it about you. While sharing your own similar situation can be comforting, it’s better to try to hold the space, listen, then maybe share. “But it’s not necessary, and if you do share your experience, always bring it back to them,” says Valls. The dynamic should be like a dance or a game of tennis, where there’s a symbiosis, a back and forth, informing not dictating.

One way to focus the conversation on the person seeking advice is to ask them what their options are. When they go through the options, encourage them to listen to their body, their gut, their instincts, and see where that leads them. This is an approach that therapists and psychologists use. It can help improve the connection between the mind and the body, marrying thought with feeling. “The more there’s a connection there, the more we’re able to make good decisions.”

Child psychologist Dr Margot Sunderland has written several books, including What Every Parent Needs to Know and Conversations That Matter. According to her, the most important thing for parents to know when giving advice to children and teenagers is not to shame. “If they come to you and you get angry or say: ‘That’s a terrible thing you did,’ you will be disqualified as someone to go to for help. Children very quickly decide: ‘Am I going to others for problem-solving or am I going to self-help?’” Self-help may sound positive, but can result in internalising problems and finding coping mechanisms that involve self-harm.

Regulation is important for both parties. “You’re in pain because your child is in pain, so we rush to fix it, rather than wait until you’re both calmer and can think together.” That might mean taking your shock elsewhere by talking to someone else before the difficult conversation. For your child, it might mean letting them run out of the room. “When there’s a problem or distress, we go into survival mode: they might slam a door (fight mode) or hide under the table (flight mode). Allow this to happen first, or they won’t hear your advice anyway.”

A term she comes back to is “hurry slowly”. Sunderland suggests something she did with her own small children: find two nearby toys and suggest that when the child needs help with their feelings, they can let you know by putting the toy cat on top of the Lego house, for example. “They can’t always tell you when they are ready to talk – that would be an adult thing to do – but they can show you.” Another tool for thinking together is drawing out the problem and possible solutions on paper. “It can take the pressure off a face-to-face conversation.”

Last, she reminds us, if a child or teenager comes to you with a problem, you have a child who is help-seeking, not going into self-help. “You should applaud yourself, that means you’ve done something right.”

When Barbieri agreed to become an advice columnist, it was on the condition that she could also consult experts: “I don’t have a problem with saying, ‘I don’t know,’ and I like finding out. I often send people to books or websites, or I go away and speak to a psychotherapist.”

When we don’t have the answers, it’s OK to support a friend in finding them – that’s not the same as saying we don’t want to help. Is there a podcast that might be useful? A way to seek third-party input? Or is it appropriate to ask: “Could therapy or counselling help?”

Often, says Valls, we go to a particular person for advice because they will validate us; what can be more helpful is an objective approach. Besides, there’s no one way to do life “right” – meaning there may not be one right answer either.

Zhao’s research suggests that sharing advice can improve our interpersonal relationships, if approached in a considered way. Other research suggests that responsive, empathetic advice is more likely to increase trust (as opposed to prescriptive advice, which can undermine it).

Today, people can always ask a chatbot for advice, but it doesn’t know us like we know one another. In the 10th anniversary edition of The Coaching Habit, Bungay Stanier reflects on what has changed since he first wrote the book. “ChatGPT can give good advice, with references and extra reading, faster than a person, and without personal entanglement. But the unintended effect of AI getting good at this stuff is people getting more isolated, and that’s a heavy price to pay as a society.”

What AI is also less good at than humans is following up with care. “Advice should not be a one-off conversation,” says Sunderland. Come back to the advice-seeker with: “I’ve been thinking of our conversation the other day – how have things been?”

And crucially, ask for feedback, to become a better advice-giver, advises Bungay Stanier. “Ask: ‘Was any of my advice useful?’ Usually, it’s the thing you least expected to help that has value.”

The definitive guide to men’s shirts: 19 of the best for every occasion

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 14:00:19 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Is an Oxford shirt the ultimate wardrobe staple? Are skin-tight fits ever a good idea? And what’s the perfect fabric for autumn and winter? Our menswear expert has all the answers

The best white T-shirts for men

The photo above stopped me mid-scroll: Harry Styles, before his 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden, dressed in a big white shirt and smart tailored trousers. After a summer spent parked in front of three fans with ice packs on rotation, when wearing actual clothes felt like punishment, here was proof that normal service had resumed.

So, now the rain’s back and autumn’s creeping in, it’s time to follow Harry’s lead and reintroduce some structure to your wardrobe: coats, knitwear, tailoring, all the pieces that make you look forward to getting dressed in the morning. One staple that’s long overdue a comeback? Shirts.

The classic button-up is the shirting equivalent of a white tee – an all-rounder that will hold its own in almost any setting (and it’s perfect for the time of year when a coat’s overkill but a T-shirt’s optimistic). But that’s just one option. You’ve also got the French workwear shirt – the way I’ve seen guys wearing it lately, thrown over a shirt and tie, might be my favourite styling trick of the season – as well as flannels, corduroy, denim and preppy Oxfords.

Before you buy anything new, though, it’s worth raiding your own wardrobe. Shirts never really date, so there’s a good chance you’ve got some solid pieces already. If you do want something new, keep scrolling for the best shirts to buy this season – I’ve broken these down into 10 categories, with a few styling tips for each.

You can’t go wrong with a white shirt. Keep it feeling laid back – poplin, relaxed fit, nothing too formal – and you’ll be able to wear it with almost anything. My go-to combination is blue jeans and black loafers.

Cos pima cotton poplin shirt

Muji men’s washed cotton long-sleeve shirt

My personal favourite (I own nine): this is the white shirt’s more relaxed sibling that feels a touch more “weekend”. Same rules apply: avoid anything tight or dressy and wear it relaxed.

Uniqlo oversized Oxford shirt

Reiss lyocell stripe button-through overshirt

Lightweight needlecord is the gold standard here – anything thicker tends to look stiff and bulky. With that in mind, it’s worth sticking to independent labels like Sunspel or Sirplus that put real thought into their choice of fabric. As this is the kind of low-key wardrobe investment you’ll wear for years, if you can, it’s worth spending a little extra to get it right.

Sunspel fine cord shirt

Sirplus olive needlecord collared shirt

Double denim is still going strong this year – and Drew Starkey’s recent look in NYC is all the proof you need that it doesn’t need to match. Sure, his look is by Dior, but the pieces themselves look like an elevated version of what you’d find at the vintage shop. If you’d rather go matching – a proper Canadian tuxedo – take your jeans with you when you shop to coordinate the shade. Rokit is a good place to start.

Arket regular denim shirt

Charles Tyrwhitt denim shirt, ocean blue

Flannel is the ultimate autumn fabric: it’s cosy, but it won’t make you immediately start sweating the moment you step on public transport. You could go for a check, but it’s not compulsory – a plain, brushed version does the same job without the lumberjack affiliations. See Steve Martin making flannel look cool in the 90s. Just add a cap.

Universal Works brown brushed flannel square pocket shirt

Eton check flannel shirt

Paul Mescal’s never met a boxy fit he didn’t like – and, actually, neither have I. Nothing bunches, nothing rides up – it’s just a clean, straight, slightly cropped hemline that looks sharper than any tucked-in shirt could. The brand to know is Percival, which has a huge selection to choose from, but Asos or Weekday are your best bets for this style on the high street.

Percival Hinsley checked boxy shirt, blue

Sign up to The Filter

Get the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.

after newsletter promotion

Weekday boxy long-sleeved cotton poplin shirt

Whenever you’ve got a dinner reservation at a restaurant with a dress code, this is the kind of shirt you’ll want in your wardrobe. Go for something silkier than your usual cotton – lyocell or viscose – which will drape nicely when it’s tucked in. The key is feeling louche rather than stiff: one button more undone than feels natural, plus a great aftershave.

Selected relaxed fit long-sleeved shirt

A Day’s March clean-cut lyocell shirt

JFK Jr-coded preppy menswear is still going strong and the Oxford shirt is the piece that does the heavy lifting. Look for one with an embroidered logo from one of the OGs – Gant, Ralph Lauren, Tommy Hilfiger – and you’re already on the right track. Keep the fit loose: anything too tight loses the whole off-duty Ivy League aesthetic.

Tommy Hilfiger regular fit button-down Oxford shirt

Vintage is the natural home for this one, though Service Works has the silhouette nailed down, too. Call it what you like – chore jacket, shacket, overshirt – the vibe you’re looking for is old-school French workwear. That means a soft, worn-in fabric with patch pockets low on the hem. Stains, paint splatters or distressed details are welcome.

Service works classic chore shirt

French Chore jacket men’s vintage workwear canvas shirt

Checks were a big part of Jonathan Anderson’s autumn/winter 2026 collection for Dior, so it’s no wonder they’re everywhere right now. The trick is keeping it refined: a microcheck (a small-scale check, rather than anything bold or tartan-y) is usually a safe bet; try to keep the colours to two or three, max.

NN07 Deon casual flannel shirt

Cotton On Richmond long-sleeve shirt

It depends on the occasion, but there’s one golden rule: never go for anything super-tight. Your shirt should always look comfortable and never pull; it’s better to hint at your physique rather than shout it, so skip the “muscle fit”. I think a relaxed fit looks way more stylish too, though if you’re wearing a dress shirt with a suit, it should sit closer to the body. If it’s too loose, it starts to look sloppy.

An Oxford – it’s the most versatile one. Bar formal occasions, it’s an easy fallback that feels smart but never stiff – and it works all year round. Layer it up when it’s cold. Wear it loose when it’s warm. Buttoned up, it’s office-ready but thrown over a vest, it’s sorted for a date. If you want to lean casual, go for a shirt that’s oversized with a low-key embroidered logo – vintage Ralph Lauren is a great place to start. For style cues, check how Paul Newman wore his: relaxed and undone with a preppy edge.

Beyond a classic Oxford, a poplin shirt (white or striped) is your next everyday go-to, followed by denim, flannel and a fine corduroy once autumn properly sets in. For anything dressier – a dinner reservation or party, for instance – try something more flowy: viscose, silk or lyocell.

On the whole, stick to natural fibres – cotton, linen, wool or silk. They come in different weaves and finishes (a cotton could be poplin, twill, Oxford or flannel, for instance) but natural fabrics tend to feel more expensive than synthetics like polyester or nylon. They breathe better, too (although silk is slightly less breathable than other natural fibres).

As with most clothes, the number one rule is washing them as little as possible – most shirts can handle two to three wears before they need a cycle. In between, a spritz of fabric freshener (such as The Lab Co’s Signature fabric mist) and a good airing go a long way. When you do wash them, skip the tumble dryer and hang them up instead – it helps reduce creases and keeps their shape. Deal with stains the moment they happen. Once they’ve set in, it’s hard to shift them.

Peter Bevan is a stylist and fashion journalist covering menswear, womenswear and beauty

‘Eating is my superpower’: Nigella turns up the heat on Bake Off

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 12:00:17 GMT

The domestic goddess is about to be let loose in the Bake Off tent. Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood spill the beans about bonding over dirty martinis, ‘Professor Precision’ – and why they call themselves the Salty Gang

Like the Cleopatra of cake, new Great British Bake Off judge Nigella Lawson reclines on a chaise longue throughout our interview, gently fanning herself. Fellow judge Paul Hollywood chuckles from a nearby armchair. “She’d sit like this between takes in the tent,” he says indulgently. “Reading a book and sipping a coffee while someone fed her grapes.” “Peeled grapes,” specifies Lawson with a grin.

After Prue Leith stepped down from soggy bottom-spotting duties in January – on the unarguable basis that “I’m 86, for goodness sake!” – there was widespread jubilation when Lawson was announced as her replacement. The arrival of the domestic goddess has created serious buzz around Bake Off’s upcoming series. A contest that was at risk of growing stale has become essential viewing again, thanks to the velvet-voiced, spatula-licking doyenne of culinary TV.

“It was lovely to see Nigella come into the tent,” says Hollywood. “We’ve only had two changes to the judging team in 16 years but it’s worked really well. I’ve always been a big fan and she fitted in beautifully – not just with me but with the whole team. She picked up the Bake Off vibe straight away. It was pretty seamless, actually.”

Her TV career was launched with Nigella Bites way back in 1999. Why Bake Off, and why now? “I wanted to do something a bit different,” says Lawson. “I’ve written many books, which I adore, but it means spending a lot of time alone. I was keen to be part of something bigger, part of a team. When I was approached about Bake Off, I instinctively thought: ‘That would be lovely.’ It almost feels too good to be true that you can enjoy something this much and call it work.”

Predictably, there have been tabloid rumours that the judgely duo have been butting heads. Lawson allegedly said that Hollywood arriving on set at Welford Park in a helicopter was “cringe”, which is all the evidence gossipmongers need. Yet there’s no sign of tension on screen, let alone today. Their conversation is full of good-natured ribbing and punctuated by peals of laughter. Hollywood seems enchanted by his new partner-in-cake, while Lawson is endearingly self-effacing, all too aware that she’s joining a long-running hit and simply doesn’t want to “stuff it up”.

Before her appointment was confirmed, the pair had an unofficial chemistry test at a Channel 4 event. “We chatted for 10 minutes and had a great time, didn’t we?” recalls Lawson. “I knew instantly it was going to work. It surprised even us, I think, how well we hit it off. It was lucky that we did get on. Can you imagine if we didn’t? I bet Paul would have said so!”

What does she like about the marquee’s resident master baker? “One of the many lovely things about Paul is that he’s good at being teased. I called him ‘Professor Precision’, then he teased me back and suddenly it all relaxed. He’s much more playful than he looks on camera. He often acts bad cop and does that laser stare but he’s always himself, which encourages other people to be themselves, too. We complement each other. He gets straight to the point and, as you can tell, I’m a witterer. I love talking about food and sometimes can’t stop. When I wittered on in the tent, I did see him go like this once …” She mimes pretending to nod off. He shrugs unrepentantly.

Once she was officially onboard, Lawson hosted separate bonding sessions with her co-stars. “I decided to meet everyone properly before we started,” she says. “I didn’t want the first time we hung out together to be on set.” Hollywood came first. “I went for drinks at Nigella’s house,” he remembers. Oh, to be a fly on the wall. Was there food? “Salami, olives, that kind of thing,” says Lawson. “I wasn’t going to bake for him. That would be madness.” “I was disappointed,” deadpans Hollywood. “I was hoping for a cake on a gingham altar.”

“Play your cards right and you never know,” she shoots back. “No, I wanted it to be as relaxed as possible. Paul brought a bottle of red wine and said: ‘Do you want a glass?’ I said, ‘You’ll have to open it yourself. I’m wearing a white suit!’ And we went from there.” Next came co-hosts Noel Fielding and Alison Hammond. “Noel came round for tea and I did make him a cake,” Lawson confesses. “Oh, thanks very much,” says Hollywood.

“I love Noel,” she continues. “He and I look like two ghouls first thing in the morning.” “Two goths, climbing out of your coffins,” laughs Hollywood. Lawson puts her pale forearm next to his teak-tanned one. “Look! I have to be painted a bit brown, otherwise it’d cause issues for the camera.” And Hammond? “I met Alison at This Morning and we went out to lunch. I hitched a ride to the restaurant in her car and we were practically married by the time we arrived. We have a real laugh together and talked about everything.”

The love affair seems to be mutual. Fielding has compared her to “an Italian film star”, while Hammond says: “We’re obsessed.” As they pose for photos, Hammond whispers: “Doesn’t Nigella look beautiful? She’s a vision!” “Stop it,” scoffs Lawson modestly.

When the casting call came, it wasn’t an immediate yes. “I was apprehensive at first,” she admits. “I wasn’t sure whether I was even qualified and mindful that it was a risk, both for me and the show. So I had a big meeting with the producers and said: ‘Look, these are the things I can’t do.’ They said: ‘That’s OK, that’s what Paul does.’ I didn’t want them to go to the wrong shop, as it were. I’m not a scientist, a technician or a professional baker but what I can do is talk about food, its taste, texture and why I like it. I said: ‘If you now decide you don’t want me after all, I promise I won’t be offended.’ Happily they still did.”

Hollywood previously formed partnerships with Dame Mary Berry and Dame Prue Leith. He refers to their successor in regal terms: “I’ve gone dame, dame, queen. I loved working with Mary. She’s got a lot of bantz, has Bez. We made a good team with Mel and Sue. We’d watch Eurovision, all sitting on the bed in dressing gowns. Prue and I would open a bottle of wine and put the world to rights. Nigella and I have done a very similar thing – not with wine but with a couple of dirty martinis or spicy margaritas.”

Lawson describes her judging style as “pretty direct”. “I assumed I was going to be good cop but realised I just have to be honest. I can’t pretend if I don’t like something. Honesty can feel a bit brutal but you’re not critiquing the person, you’re critiquing the bake. It’s not personal. We’ve all got our own palate and can only speak subjectively.” This double act have their own areas of expertise. “I talk about flavour because eating is my superpower. I’m learning from Paul, though. I’ll start stealing all his lines, going: ‘This needs another three minutes, turn the oven up 20 degrees.’ But on the whole, I talk taste and he talks technique. You’ve got to play to your strengths.”

Sign up to What's On

Get the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every Monday

after newsletter promotion

As an avowed Bake Off superfan – she reels off a list of her favourite alumni, from series one winner Edd Kimber through to last year’s Jasmine Mitchell – how was walking into the fabled tent for the first time? “Oh god, a bit overwhelming,” she confesses. “But I held hands with Alison, which helped. It felt daunting but became cosy within about two minutes.”

This year, the climate crisis came for Bake Off. We’re meeting on one of summer’s most sweltering days, with temperatures hitting 35 degrees. Was it this hot in the tent during filming? “Hotter, like a greenhouse” grimaces Lawson. “Plus you’ve got a mic pack on, which is like wearing a mini radiator. The bakers coped well, considering.” Were there melting chocolate disasters? “It was more caramel that was the issue,” says Hollywood. “There were some sticky moments.” “And that was just Paul,” quips Lawson.

Don’t expect mention of microwaves. Lawson went viral in 2020 when she jokingly referred to her “meecro-wah-vay” – a clip shortlisted as one of Bafta’s TV moments of the year. It was a family in-joke and she’s determined to resist saying it again, instead calling it “the you-know-what”. Bake Off viewers, however, should listen out for a reference to “desecrated coconut”.

Her predecessor Leith had a penchant for boozy bakes. Does Lawson have a similar sweet spot? “It’s not a sweet one, actually,” says Hollywood. “Nigella loves salt.” “I don’t mean over-salty,” she says. “Just that a pinch of salt can balance the sweetness. Similarly, I love anything citrus. A tang of sharp and bitter, rather than unadulterated sweetness. That’s why having raspberries in a vanilla cake is nice. They all tease me, saying: ‘Just add a tablespoon of salt and she’ll like it.’ I’m landed with that now.” “So much so that our WhatsApp group is called Salty Gang,” says Hollywood. Who’s the most active? “Not us,” says Lawson. “It’s mostly Noel and Alison sending funny stuff. We just reply with laughing emojis, like old people.”

The Nigella factor is likely to give Britain’s biggest cookery show a ratings boost. “She’s a breath of fresh air, for sure,” says Hollywood. “Certainly for my male mates. They’ve told me they’ll be tuning in for the first time in 16 bloody years!”

Lawson demurs. “Not trying to be humble but it’s not about me. I’m joining a long-established, deeply loved show. Bake Off is a national treasure with a fabulous audience. It’s been part of people’s lives over many years. I wouldn’t blame them if they thought: ‘Oi, why is she coming on my programme?’ As long as I don’t actively drive people away, I’ll be happy.” Will the viewing figures include the new judge herself? “I don’t like watching myself but I do want to see it because there’s an awful lot of action that we’re not around for. I’ll fast-forward through my bits and watch the bakers.”

During her first time in the tent, the new recruit had a hoot. “We sometimes did a bit too much rabbiting and got told to shush,” says Lawson. “We had so much fun. Even Paul got the giggles. Alison once sent us out of the tent in disgrace. Paul’s very good at remaining poker-faced and then when nobody else is looking, he makes faces at you.” Has Hammond succeeded in her mission to get them all dancing? “I cannot dance on camera, I told her that,” says Lawson. “As judges, we need to retain a modicum of decorum and dignity … we try, anyway.”

Salty and sassy, it sounds like La Lawson is in the tent to stay. “Bake Off’s like Hotel California,” says Hollywood. “You can check out any time you like but you can never leave. And I think Nigella’s here for good.”

The Great British Bake Off returns on Tuesday 22 September at 8pm on Channel 4.

Earl Spencer SLATES the king. Charles DESTROYS Spencer. If only Diana were here to click on it

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 11:19:02 GMT

It’s a battle for hearts and minds – and TikTok, and the ’Gram. Just as it should be. #royalbeef

Reading the extracts from Earl Spencer’s book about his sister Diana, and the king’s two-footed takedown of it, it’s hard to escape the idea that Spencer and the Windsors are just elite content creators now. This entire thing is basically indistinguishable from a blockbuster influencer war, and I honestly won’t be happy till the king puts out a shade TikTok of him driving round the Sandringham estate in sunglasses captioned: “Threatening to release the receipts but never actually releasing the receipts … kinda chic.” Soundtrack: Mariah Carey’s Obsessed.

Meanwhile, perhaps trying to disguise his full descent into the algorithm mines, Charles Spencer has started talking like one of those adverts for twee porcelain plates that you used to see in magazine supplements. You know the kind of thing – “these three little kittens are waiting to steal your heart”. Here is the earl on his Diana book, which he has called Swan Song: “At heart, this is a brother’s simple tribute to an extraordinary sister.” Mmm. And simply bound, very simply, into paginated form as a precious, simple keepsake that also functions as one of Penguin Random House’s lead titles for autumn and the run-in to Christmas. Favourite charming tribute from today’s serialisation in the Mail? Probably the bit when Diana drags Spencer for lunch in the London restaurant San Lorenzo to announce: “My husband is in love with his valet”. Nkay.

But the biggest tea-spill so far has been Spencer’s claim that Charles sounded “giddily elated – like a lottery winner” in a phone call to him immediately after Diana’s death, then hissed: “Rest assured … we’ll forget about her soon enough.” Which definitely sounds like the kind of thing a father of two shockingly bereaved children would say if they were the future king character in a book written by someone quite bad at writing.

By way of rejoinder, Buckingham Palace issued a statement that began with the words “while we do not comment on books as a matter of principle”, and then – hilariously – went on to comment on the book. I mean, what principles? You always see these kinds of royal statements described as “highly unusual”, and yet in recent years their sheer frequency suggests they really aren’t. The royal family – and Spencer – do absolutely everything for the ’Gram. It’s all very Alex Cooper v Alix Earle. I kept reading this week that Charles and William and Kate were “out in force” doing things like playing shinty on Bute and hosting AI summits. Yup, living for the timelines. Posting through it.

And, indeed, posting about it, as that “we won’t comment on books” statement from the king continued in the more-in-sorrow-than-in-anger vein that is so particular to a contemporary social media drive-by. “His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”

Wow. Apart from the pomposity, there is precisely nothing to distinguish this from the same kind of high-horse word salad you see farted out day after day by mid-tier creators involved in online beef about abortive podcast ventures or stolen brand deals. You know the kind of thing: “I’ve stayed quiet till now … But since you want to bring this to the internet, I have receipts. I’m done protecting people. The people who know, know.”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Charles Spencer has, of course, done a whole book of this stuff, probably making him the one the internet is less likely to side with. For just as it is possible to simply get up in the morning and decide not to post something on social media that makes you look like a complete shit, it is also possible to simply not do a whole book of this stuff. Why can’t Spencer just get a turret brand to sponsor his house upkeep like Molly-Mae would? “Loving our new #pediment and #pilasters! What’s one thing you love about your house? Tell me in the comments.”

Instead, here is the earl on his Insta earlier this week: “A month ago I read ‘Swan Song’ out, over three days, for a recording so that it could be available on audiobook. When I finished the recording, I thought: ‘That is exactly what I wanted and needed to say – and she would, I reckon, have approved of every word.’” Oh for sure Diana would have approved. Nailed on. As we know, those who make money off Diana’s memory since she has died tend to do so with the absolute conviction that it’s what she would have wanted. Many of Diana’s indirect financial beneficiaries – her former psychics and energy healers, actors playing her in movies – give interviews announcing that her ghost has visited them to give the seal of approval to whichever commercial venture they’re involved in. Charles Spencer has yet to go down this route with Swan Song, though given the book isn’t actually published till next week – to permit the Mail the best run at the serial rights they paid him a fortune for – we definitely shouldn’t rule out the possibility that he’s keeping something spectral in the bag for the coming days.

Ultimately, it’s increasingly impossible to escape the conviction that the royals and those familially connected with them behave as leading influencers – selling the absolute maddest form of lifestyle that you can still somehow pass off as a gift to your followers. The other day I remembered an interview Prince Harry gave when his own book was out, where he said: “I genuinely believe, and I hope, that reconciliation between my family and us will have a ripple effect across the entire world. Maybe that’s lofty, maybe that’s naive.” Or maybe it’s just the lucrative way they all live now. Either way: #amazing.

Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnist
