An effective ban on disabled people leaving Britain? You read that right, and we will not settle for it

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 11:00:25 GMT

This scandal shows there are many who don’t expect us to live rich lives – and that paternalism lives on in disability services

Disabled people in UK need right to travel abroad, say MPs, after ‘ridiculous’ restrictions

Disabled people are being barred from leaving the country. This isn’t the first line of a dystopian novel but a scandal quietly happening across swathes of England. For the past six months, myself and my colleague Patrick Butler have spoken to disabled people who have effectively been blocked from going abroad on a holiday or to a work event by their local care provider.

There’s 38-year-old Lucy from Oxfordshire who needs to travel internationally as the president of the European Spinal Cord Injury Federation. And Chelsea from Lancashire, a 25-year-old with cerebral palsy who dreams of swimming in Spain again. Then there’s 40-year-old Joel*, who has a muscle weakness and works for a global marketing brand but hasn’t been able to leave the UK for nine years.

Some have live-in personal assistants (PAs) via NHS continuing healthcare, the non-means-tested home support for people with high needs. Others have 24/7 social care through their local authority. But when they try to leave the country, all hit the same wall: they are told they are not allowed to use their care package abroad, sometimes even if they pay any extra costs themselves.

Here’s the plot twist. Some areas of the country are permitting care users to go on holiday or travel for work – while disabled people just a few miles down the road can be stopped. Others are told they can travel but have to pay any extra expenses – effectively still barring them financially from going – while some care boards offer to cover the cost. As there is limited to no national guidance on the issue, disabled people’s right to travel depends on a postcode lottery, with local care officials inspecting their plans for a trip away and having the power to rule “go” or “stay”.

This week, MPs and peers called for national guidelines to end this injustice. Figures such as the work and pensions select committee chair, Debbie Abrahams, the crossbench peer Jane Campbell and the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn told the Guardian that the government must guarantee the rights of disabled people to travel and ensure they have the support they need to do so.

You can practically hear the right preparing to oppose the move with a cry of “Free holidays on the NHS!” But care users going abroad doesn’t cost the taxpayer anything extra in care bills. Disabled people who need 24/7 support for everyday activities already have care funding in place, and in many cases use their own money to pay PAs’ travel expenses, such as accommodation and plane tickets (on top of the already extortionate price of accessible travel). When Lucy was told by her care board she couldn’t take her PAs to a spinal cord conference in Germany this spring, her employer had already offered to pay any additional costs.

The question, then, is why would authorities want to stop disabled people going abroad? If it’s not just about tight budgets, why should it matter to them how an adult chooses to use their care package? You could say that it’s about practicalities: it’s easier not to worry about insurance or visas (disabled people largely sort this themselves for their PAs anyway). But it seems naive not to think there’s some prejudice lurking under the bureaucracy. Blocking disabled people from going on holiday or working abroad goes to the heart of cultural assumptions about disability: that we don’t have careers or families or friends like other, “normal” people.

Sixty years after disabled people left institutions and were able to live independently, alongside the vast gains, the stain of paternalistic control still lurks in disability services. It’s the social worker who suggests you get a commode next to your sofa because it’s cheaper than an accessible bathroom. It’s the care worker who speaks very slowly to you and picks your clothes out on your behalf. It’s the occupational therapist who suggests you get a hospital-style bed that your husband can’t fit in (and is visibly surprised you have a husband).

We’re not supposed to talk about this stuff. There’s an unwritten rule that says disabled people should be just grateful for what they’re given by the state, lest we appear to be scroungers or burdens. I say “unwritten”. It’s written in some newspapers most weeks.

It is uncomfortable, I suppose, in part because it is so ordinary. This isn’t the sort of prejudice that comes with an ableist slur or a violent push. It is the gentle, everyday belief that certain kinds of lives – certain kinds of people – come with low expectations.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Just look at the way much of the political and media class discuss social care. In the rare instances that younger disabled people are mentioned alongside elderly people, social care is still solely spoken about in terms of personal care – say, help to wash or prepare a meal. As Andy Burnham has put reform of the care sector on the agenda in recent months, it’s notable there has been little talk of its role in supporting a disabled person’s family role or career: whether that’s help to drop the kids off at school on the way to the office or to get to the pub to celebrate a friend’s birthday.

That’s understandable. Under the current system, as many as 1.5 million disabled people in England are left without access to even the most basic help. If you are suffering the indignity of sitting in soiled clothes because a care worker hasn’t arrived to assist you to the bathroom, it can feel pointless – delusional, even – to mention you’ve not seen the sea in years.

But to settle for this state of affairs forces disabled people to accept a half-life, to be relieved to at least be clean and fed, and to try to forget the colour that defines being human. It diminishes not only our humanity but the principle that disability campaigners fought for decades for and underpins the modern care system: for disabled people to have choice and independence over our lives, just like everyone else.

When I recently spoke to Campbell, who has 24/7 PAs herself, about the care abroad scandal, she said something telling: “It’s as if those controlling [these decisions] believe disabled people don’t deserve the same experiences they enjoy.”

As pressure for national guidelines mounts, I can’t help but think that is a wise litmus test. Would you expect a non-disabled person to live like this? And if not, why do you think it’s OK for disabled people?

*Name has been changed

Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnist

Drivers ignoring roadwork closures to skip queues ‘wilfully putting lives at risk’

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 11:00:15 GMT

Hundreds of cars driven through cones or barriers in England this year, says National Highways

Drivers ignoring roadwork closures to skip queues are putting lives at risk, National Highways has warned, after recording hundreds of incidents this year where cars were deliberately driven through cones or barriers.

The agency, which manages motorways and major roads, said there was increasing concern about incursions into closed-off roadworks and the danger they posed.

It said its works contractors had reported an increasing proportion of such incidents as deliberate. According to National Highways data, 53% of the 814 incursions reported nationwide in England between January and July this year involved drivers trying to avoid queues, closures or diversions.

Repeated dangerous driving around roadworks has led National Highways to close parts of motorways to protect workers rather than just closing lanes, causing significant delays for road users.

To highlight the issue, the agency released clips showing drivers entering closed-off roadworks areas, which led to successful prosecutions and driving bans. They included footage of the M1 motorway in Hertfordshire, where repeated incursions earlier this year led to it being closed completely to keep workers safe, creating a 10-mile diversion for drivers. There were no casualties in any of the incidents shown.

On average, about 30 incursions a week are recorded across England’s motorways and A-roads. While most are defined as “seeking benefit” – drivers deliberately entering restricted roadwork areas hoping for a short cut – factors including breakdowns or simple driver error also lead to dangerous incursions.

In the latter cases, however, most drivers quickly stop and seek assistance, according to Melanie Clarke, the director of health, safety and wellbeing at National Highways. She said the latest figures showed “a worrying number of drivers wilfully ignoring roadworks to save time, putting road workers and other people at risk”.

Clarke said: “This year alone there have been over 400 incidents of those ‘seeking benefits’ as we describe it. We are definitely seeing a rise. We really encourage our road workers to report these instances so we can understand the level of the risk that they are facing when they are simply just trying to do their jobs.”

She added: “Drivers who just come through to avoid the closure or diversion are often travelling at speed and not necessarily aware of the activities that are going on within the roadworks. Often there’s plant, there’s machinery, the surface may already been treated. Obviously our concern is for our road workers – but those drivers need to understand that they also put themselves at risk.”

At least one fatality had occurred because of incursions this year, Clarke said.

She added that, contrary to occasional driver perception, roads were never sealed off without some activity ongoing or imminent. “If you don’t see people working, that doesn’t mean that there aren’t people working nearby. Or maybe the road surface has been compromised in some way in order to complete the work. So it’s simply not safe for vehicles to travel through that road work session until the work is complete.”

Regardless of the risk, drivers attempting to take a shortcut would normally not make their journey quicker, she said. “It’s simply not worth it.”

Sinead Ryan, a lead traffic management operative for HW Martin, a contractor, said: “People don’t always realise how dangerous our job can be. We work close to live traffic and, while we can do everything possible to keep ourselves safe, we can’t control the actions of drivers.

“When someone ignores a closure or drives into a work area, it only takes a second for someone to get hurt.”

Digested week: BuzzBallz signed by Tory leader builds excitement for conference

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 10:51:20 GMT

Kemi Badenoch-autographed cocktail offered as raffle prize. Plus, Bruce Springsteen’s surprisingly normal nightwear

It’s funny, isn’t it, how many things we take for granted in life? How many things go wholly unmentioned, even wholly unconsidered in any even minutely conscious way – and yet, when they are suddenly kicked away you realise just how much of your internal organisation, your mental integrity, your structural soundness altogether, rested on these unexamined pillars.

One of mine, it turns out, is the belief – no, surely more than that? The sure and certain knowledge, in my bones if never alas vouchsafed by my mere mortal eyes – that Bruce Springsteen does not wear pyjamas.

This is fundamental, surely? The Boss sleeps naked. This is an eternal verity.

But no. According to what I can only describe as reports, he is a loyal customer of the venerable sleepwear shop Schostal in Rome, which was opened in 1870 by two brothers from Vienna. There’s a photo of Bruce hugging the manager, Shirley Braine – to whom he apparently sends regular postcards – and everything.

So. There you have it. The Boss sleeps in pyjamas. Acceptable province of 1950s boarding school boys, your worst boyfriend, and your dad. Please go carefully about your day and from the fragments of your shattered psyche may you rebuild better soon.

Party conference season is almost upon us – I know! Try to contain yourselves! – and the preparations for fun times are gathering pace. News breaks that Blue Beyond, a young Conservatives group (and I always like to know that they’ve found each other rather than roaming free and confused), is offering as a grand raffle prize a BuzzBallz signed by Kemi Badenoch! I said try to contain yourselves! And not only is it signed, but it is a large BuzzBallz! I SAID TRY TO CONTAIN YOURSELVES.

In case you are not as young as a youngster or as cool as a Conservative, I should explain: a BuzzBallz is a spherical plastic container that contains a cocktail, usually of a lurid hue and unsubtle flavour profile (the inscribed orb itself is Berry Cherry Limeade and whyever not?). They come in two sizes – small, which is a bit larger than a tennis ball, and large, which is a bit smaller than a football.

Tickets are available now. The winner will be drawn at the Tory conference and must be over 18 to collect. Rumours that Michael Heseltine will launch it at your head for a small further fee are popular but as yet unsubstantiated.

I find myself unaccountably drawn to the story of the Hyrox poo-er. Not because of any coprophiliac inclinations, you understand, but because the idea of exerting myself to the extent that I might lose control of my bowels is so out of my realm of personal possibility that I am increasingly intrigued by the question of whether Joanna Wietrzyk and I technically qualify as the same species at all.

Again, for the uninitiated/hitherto and possibly blissfully ignorant, a recap: Hyrox Beijing is an intense indoor fitness event and Wietrzyk one of its world record- holding contestants. About halfway through the insanely difficult competition, which comprises a series of horrendous things – I don’t know precisely what, I passed out after reading the word “burpees” – Wietrzyk suffered what was later termed “a severe faecal event”, which went down her leg but didn’t stop her progress round the course.

Cue a roar of outrage against her and the organisers, who didn’t disqualify her immediately before she touched any other equipment, and eventually an apology from Wietrzyk and a forfeit of her points.

To hell with the critics, say I. Biohazardry be damned! You push yourself so hard you crap yourself and keep on going, you’re a winner in my book. Now, someone unwrap this Mars bar for me. Typing is exhausting, you know.

Not all heroes wear capes. Or a light coating of faeces down their legs. Some of them are headteachers who suspend 25 students in the first week back after the summer holidays, including one for the crime of zipping his bag too loudly. The head’s name is Dan Jeffries and, while he denies parents’ claims of suspension for minor infractions, it is clear that whatever measures he has indeed taken, he has no regrets about any of them.

Parents of some of those suspended from Frome college have compared the school to “a military base” and say the strictness demotivates pupils. Whatever, whatever. The world is made up of two types of people: those who want to hear the children’s side of things and those of us who just want Jeffries put in immediate charge of a new government department called The Whole of Modern Life, Starting With Quiet Coaches on the Train and After That I Have a List.

My mother summons me and my sister home. Apparently she needs to clear out the attic before she dies, but ideally before Sunday.

“What’s happening on Sunday?” I ask.

“Sunday,” she replies.

Deadlines by fiat were a mainstay of my childhood and so I ask no more.

My mother has lived in our house for 50 years. We brace ourselves for a hard 48 hours’ work and climb up into the loft.

Three small cardboard boxes of stuff await us.

“There are – there are just three small cardboard boxes of stuff up here.”

“Yes,” she says. “I can’t believe I’ve let it get this bad.”

We bring them down.

My wedding shoes and some papers – including my first book, The Story of Esmerelda, written when I was nine and some letters home from university – are in the first one. The second one contains my son’s baby clothes. The third has my sister’s childhood attempts at making a working model of Sizewell B and some postcards she wrote to Dad when he went on his first trip to America. “Come hom. Shez insane.” On reflection, she shouldn’t have given them to Mum to post.

“Excellent,” Mum says. “We can bin the lot.”

Ah, fiats. Ah, memories.

Sydney Sweeney’s cartoonish provocation has sparked a culture war but let’s just admit sport can be sexy

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 07:00:12 GMT

Yes sport is about effort, sweat and inclusivity – but it also turns elite athletes into magnificent specimens of humanity where the aesthetic is part of the appeal

Have you seen the 40-second video that will change the way you think about women’s sport, women’s bodies, just, you know, women? It’s been unavoidable on social media this week – brazen, unapologetic, dominating the algorithm like an AI kitten hacking a banana-bread recipe while lip-syncing to Cardi B. I for one have enjoyed it at least 50 times already.

It starts with some carefully curated passive-aggression – “Dear Sydney”, “Hey Sydney”, “Respectfully Sydney” – and follows up with clips of what, in its own words, “a woman in sport actually looks like”. It shows its subject pounding the treadmill or powering down the back straight, flooring a rival with a tackle or a roundhouse kick, lifting weights or throwing herself through the air. It is, inevitably, soundtracked by Dua Lipa. Training Season is getting a serious bump this week.

The almighty backlash to the Novig advert that everyone would rather not have talked about at all has generated more montages than we’ve seen since Rocky IV. My own feed is swamped with inspo-insta reels from grassroots and elite athletes alike. Some might argue it’s the best thing to happen to women’s sport this week – unless, you know, they’re the European Solheim Cup team. Either way, a positively cartoonish piece of provocation lit the five-second fuse to the powder-keg stamped CULTURE WAR, and the resultant explosion has enveloped us all in its cloud of colourful outrage and content confetti.

The noisy reaction to an actor posing almost naked with various items of sporting equipment demonstrates the power and importance of solidarity within women’s sport. For decades, being a woman in an incorrigibly sexist sector left you one of two responses. Either you ignored uncomfortable and demeaning situations so you could just get on with the thing you wanted to be doing, or you spoke out, braving either devastating indifference or a cacophony of scorn. These days, we’re privileged to have a far louder voice, and for it to be taken seriously.

There is, however, a danger in taking every piece of deliberate provocation too seriously. And the danger is that it robs us of some of the delight of the thing we love in the first place. Instead of spending this week talking about Lottie Woad’s singles match in the Netherlands, or Chelsea’s 5-0 demolition of Manchester United in the WSL, we’ve surrendered billboards’ worth of brain space to an American celebrity who hasn’t even invested in a Premier League club yet.

Personally I have also, as discussed, spent quite a lot of time scrolling other people’s highlights reels, and I won’t lie that they got me pretty pumped, but then that was very much their goal. From spiralling gymnastic tumbles to grunting deadlifts, all these women look fire. Even a unitedly earnest effort to remind us that sport is about effort and sweat and inclusivity can’t and shouldn’t hide the fact that it’s also, thrillingly, about human bodies and the gloriously impressive things they can be honed to do.

Having to argue that sportswomen aren’t sexual objects, on the other hand, feels as dated as the advert. Part of the problem of the ad is its almost comically regressive throwback to the era of Page 3 girls and 1980s erotica – the kind of aesthetic we now knowingly indulge within the safe confines of a Jilly Cooper TV adaptation. If we’re jumping this far back in the timeline, will we have to revisit, too, whether it’s appropriate to wear make-up on track, or skorts on court, or any other of the subsidiary arguments that determine how sexy or not a female athlete is required – or allowed – to be?

Or can we unclench and leave them in the past where they belong? Might we even skip a bit further into a more confident future and say out loud the thing that we have always had to be extremely careful expressing? Which is that sport is a primarily physical pursuit that tends to turn the people at its apex into magnificent specimens of humanity. And that those aesthetics are a part of what makes it appealing in the first place.

The bulging neck on the rugby pitch and the rock-hard calves on the marathon runner have a functional purpose, as opposed to the fantasy one that prompts today’s Hollywood actors to get superhero-buff. But that doesn’t mean we’re not allowed to admire them. Sport is an environment that invites us to witness and thrill to the power and grace of the human body. It’s not only our tribal allegiances and the dopamine hit of vicarious victory that we’re indulging when we marvel at our sporting heroes: it’s also our appreciation of their physical attributes, whether that’s Rafael Nadal’s arms or Jessica Ennis-Hill’s abs or Serena Williams’s everything.

Sign up to Sport in Focus

after newsletter promotion

And sometimes, when those attributes are in motion, sport can be sexy. Not in the ball-cradling way that Sydney Sweeney’s performance allows delusional men to believe. But in a way that nevertheless holds hostage to the eye and makes the pulse race. It’s rather absurd – and a little self-deluding – for sports fans to pretend either to ourselves or others that we don’t find some of our heroes pretty attractive.

And no, as Amy Hunt so properly pointed out in her own clapback to the Sweeney ad, being an athlete is “not sexy all the time”. If anyone needed proof, the second most notorious viral video of this week was, in fact, a Hyrox competitor soiling herself as she powered to victory. There has, in other words, been plenty of crap circulating on the internet this week. The sanest choice is to avert our eyes.

Slowly then all at once: this emboldened Celtic alliance could spell the end of the UK

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 07:00:11 GMT

It’s something akin to a quiet earthquake: home nations jointly declaring their wish to be freed from English domination. A big move needs a big response

Monday must have been a historical first. Never before have three of the four “nations” of the United Kingdom jointly demanded freedom to vote for its dissolution. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have lost confidence in England. They declared in Cardiff that the unionist government at Westminster is “coming to an end”.

There was no such Celtic alliance against the Normans, Edward I or Cromwell. Celtic MPs have never formed a voting coalition in parliament. The Victorian Liberal party advanced “home rule for all”, but that was not independence and it got nowhere. Ireland rebelled, but it did so alone. When this eventually succeeded, Britain said good riddance, kept hold of Belfast and continued to centralise power in London.

So this is serious stuff. Yet London politics this week treated the declaration as on a par with the Oxfordshire village of Piddington voting to go it alone to ward off the possibility of asylum seekers being housed nearby.

The UK’s only serious geographical devolution came in 1999. It was half-hearted, mostly decentralising the running of the welfare state. But it surged the vote for Scottish and Welsh separatism and fed rather than abated the cause of independence. We can only imagine if ruling parties in Bavaria or Provence or Sicily had opted for independence from Germany, France or Italy – or if California said it had enough of Donald Trump’s US. The result would be political eruption.

What does the Cardiff “memorandum of understanding” actually mean? The answer is not much in detail. There was advocacy of policy collaboration, as on childcare and economic growth. There were hints of moves towards further devolution, of the sort promised by Andy Burnham. But there was no suggestion of a new Celtic state, a British Celtica. The talks seemed to concentrate on self-determination, which Burnham had described as “off limits”, at least in the case of Scotland. Yet this was a man who declared self-determination for the Falklands would be defended even at the cost of tens of millions of pounds a year.

The reality is that these three nations of the union have markedly different relations with England. Northern Ireland’s bipartisan government, a legacy of civil war and the Good Friday agreement, is clearly dysfunctional. As Donald Trump remarked last week, it really should advance toward Irish union.

As interfaith relations slowly improve, a possible majority in favour of reunion also becomes more plausible. Support for union in Northern Ireland is now around one-third, with a majority among the young. Self-determination is not in Burnham’s gift but is written into Northern Ireland’s constitution. Observers accept that it must and will happen one day.

Wales may also have a majority of its under-35s in favour of independence. But only a bare Welsh majority voted for even mild devolution in 1997 and support for independence hovers at 32%. The poor performance of the Welsh health and education services makes self-government ever more alarming, and the generosity of the London Exchequer ever more essential. Perhaps the novelty of the new Plaid Cymru government can transform things, but Welsh independence is at best a distant fantasy.

This leaves Scotland. Here independence is an active issue. The population of 5.5 million puts the country in the 5-10 million band of Europe’s medium-sized states, such as Denmark, Norway, Finland, Austria and Switzerland. “Small is beautiful” appears to suit Europe’s distinctive welfare economies and keeps them ahead of their larger neighbours.

Scottish unionists keep pointing to Scotland’s £25bn fiscal deficit, financed by London’s Treasury and sustaining the country’s struggling health service. But independence is a dynamic not static state. In 1922 Ireland was among the poorest countries in Europe, far behind Scotland. Its economic self-sufficiency seemed hopeless, and for some 30 years it was indeed in desperate straits. Yet by the 1990s Irish membership of the EU and the adoption of a fierce fiscal autonomy had utterly transformed it into the celebrated “Celtic Tiger”. From limping behind Scotland and other poorer European regions, Dublin raced ahead. It has become one of Europe’s richest nations per capita, albeit partly thanks to its status as a base for corporate tax avoidance.

Ireland’s burst of economic vitality in the late 20th century could never have taken place had it remained an adjunct of Britain. Income per head is now ahead of Scotland’s, having once lagged far behind. It grew between 2012 and 2022 by 9% on average, against Scotland’s 1%. Whether Ireland is richer than Denmark is much debated, but the performance of an autonomous Ireland cannot be gainsaid. It is a lighthouse for the macro-economics of smallness.

There is every reason why Scotland could feel held back by longstanding English dominance. Its economy, like the rest of Britain’s, has always been down the queue from London and the south-east. It has long felt cheated of its maritime oil and gas reserves. Trade has been crippled by Brexit. Unionists argue that the Barnett formula subsidy of £50bn a year is fair compensation. But Ireland’s experience suggests that dependence on foreign subsidy is a curse, not a blessing. The most glaring comparative statistic is that health outcomes in both Ireland and Denmark are now well ahead of Scotland’s. The scale of Glasgow’s drug deaths are a horror story.

British loyalist though I may be, if I were a Scot I would have no hesitation. This is a real nation, and has been throughout history. Scotland has a personality and a culture recognised worldwide. Its capital, Edinburgh, is among Europe’s finest cities. Its “Silicon Glen” should be leading Europe’s AI revolution. Tourism is an obvious attraction. That the country should stumble behind its Nordic neighbours is absurd.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Scotland would have a tough transition to self-reliance, as did Ireland. But experience everywhere suggests that small autonomous democracies fare well, witness other relative newcomers such as Slovakia, Slovenia, Croatia and the Baltics. Their governments can concentrate on their own priorities and promote their own virtues.

An independent Scotland would be bespoke. It could retain its royal figurehead and Commonwealth membership. It could even honour a “united kingdom” and the king could stay in Balmoral. Relations with other states, EU and non-EU, would be complicated, as they are at borders across the continent. That is for diplomacy to resolve. The issue is self-determination, not convenience.

Burnham is the first British prime minister to appear sincere in decentralising political power. How far he understands its significance is moot. His beloved “metro mayors” are accountable regionally, not representatives of truly local loyalties. They appear as his agents, enacting his policies and enforcing his planning quotas on subordinate councils. He has shown he will stamp the Piddingtons of England into the ground.

That is why Burnham should welcome any Scottish desire for “independence”. It would be the most exciting constitutional reform of the UK in centuries and one that, on current figures, would save the Treasury around £25bn a year – the cost of the Scottish fiscal deficit. It would also release the Tartan Tiger.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

‘A map is never neutral’: meet the cartographers who took on centuries of western bias

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 05:00:10 GMT

Equal Earth projection, adopted by the UN last week, provides an alternative to 16th-century Mercator display

Three cartographers have spoken of their astonishment at the UN’s near-universal adoption of a map they created to more accurately show the sizes of Africa and Europe, even though they have received a few complaints from some disgruntled diplomats.

The creators of the Equal Earth projection aimed to provide an alternative to the dominant 16th-century Mercator display, which critics have long faulted for giving the impression that northern hemisphere nations are larger than they are – and therefore subtly reinforcing perceptions of where global strength lies.

“It has been a very busy week for me,” said Tom Patterson, a renowned US national parks cartographer who has had to virtually come out of retirement after being inundated with questions from governments on details of the new projection.

Maps are notoriously difficult to make as cartographers need to unfold our spherical Earth onto a flat surface.

To get around this problem, cartographers use mathematical projections. But these can distort shape, area, distance, direction.

The 1569 Mercator projection was developed to help navigators, as each straight line matches a compass bearing.

But this comes at the expense of accurately representing area. These circles, which would look equally sized on a globe, show how Mercator enlarges areas toward the poles, such as North America.

The Equal Earth projection aims to more accurately display the relative size of Africa, Asia and Latin America.

The UN general assembly voted this month to adopt the new map, which more accurately represents the sizes of all continents, particularly Africa. It is hoped the projection will gradually replace Mercator on school walls and government websites.

Put forward by Togo, the proposal was hugely successful, with 164 countries voting in favour. The only “no” vote came from the US, whose UN representative, Yaryna Ferencevych, said resolutions such as the “correct the map” effort were “barnacles on our work here”. The US is one of the countries that appears smaller on the new projection. It also makes Greenland – a territorial prize Donald Trump has openly coveted as a “big beautiful piece of ice” – seem significantly less dominant.

Six other nations abstained from the vote, and Patterson said he had been contacted by diplomats from government embassies in Washington DC looking for clarification.

Japan asked for a revision because it said the map made the disputed Kuril Islands appear to belong to Russia by putting them in the same shade of yellow. Ukraine also abstained, as Russian-occupied Crimea was a different colour to the rest of the country. Ukraine’s representatives at the UN said this opened a “Pandora’s box” and violated international law.

The cartographers see these objections as stemming from something of a misunderstanding. The map voted on at the UN is simply a mathematical projection of the land and sea, without human-made borders or shading. The confusion arose due to a website run by Patterson that offers free Equal Earth projections. He had annotated these with geopolitical lines and the names of countries, and has been rushing this week to update them, including switching colours and changing spellings, such as Turkey to Türkiye.

“I view the Equal Earth maps as living documents and am grateful for the many helpful suggestions that I have received,” he said.

Patterson developed the new projection in 2018 with a California-based software engineer, Bojan Šavrič, the “maths wizard” of the trio, and Bernhard Jenny, an associate professor at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia.

Jenny said people generally believed maps were accurate representations of the Earth, but that logic breaks down because we live on a curved surface. This creates a problem, as a sphere cannot easily be transformed into a flat rectangle.

“It’s like the orange peel analogy,” said Jenny. “You have to tear it and stretch it, and it’s not possible to flatten it out … so you have to make compromises.”

One global map, called the Goode homolosine projection, looks strikingly like a ripped-up orange peel. Its main problems are that it is not very pleasing to the human eye and not very easy to use for navigation – something the flawed Mercator excels at, because north is always up.

For Jenny, cartography is about aesthetics as well as science. “We cartographers say cartography is the art and science of making maps. So it’s kind of the combination of the two.”

Equal Earth is not the first attempt to address Mercator’s shortcomings. Several other projections were developed in the past century, including the Gall-Peters model, which shows the true relative sizes of land masses, but which often appears oddly elongated, almost like the continents are drooping. Jenny said: “There was a lot of backlash from cartographers who said: ‘Well, it looks like clothes are hung up to dry.’”

There are always compromises when making maps. Spend any amount of time with a cartographer and what might seem like fundamental truths quickly break down. “Which way is up?” or “Where is the centre” are not simple questions for cartographers – ancient Islamic maps had a south-up orientation, which put the holy city of Mecca in the eyeline. A London-centric worldview has long dominated how world maps are presented, with Greenwich in the centre.

“You have to make compromises,” said Jenny. The Equal Earth map, for example, would not be useful for getting around, as countries on the edges are squeezed. In fact, if any country had a claim to be upset, it could be New Zealand, which is stretched and distorted, and on the edge of the map.

“A map is never neutral,” said Jenny. “So you cannot please everyone.”

Šavrič, who worked on the mathematical formula, said he never imagined eight years ago that the trio’s research would be discussed at the highest levels.

“What pleases me more is that this creates a valuable opportunity to strengthen map literacy and raise awareness that there is no single map projection capable of providing a completely ‘true’ representation of the world,” he said. “Every map projection involves trade-offs. I particularly appreciate that the [UN] resolution does not completely ban the Mercator projection or mandate a single replacement for all maps.”

Jenny was also thrilled, watching on from Australia. “It’s kind of a cartographer’s dream, right?” he said. “The fact that the UN is debating map projections for an entire hour is already totally thrilling for cartographers, and then it was our map projection. I mean, what else can you ask for?”

He does, however, have a hunch that another factor helped the Equal Earth map: the power of a good name. “I think, definitely, that you know what it is immediately,” said Jenny. If they had called it the “Šavrič-Patterson-Jenny projection”, he joked, maybe it would not have done so well.

Header image is A Correct Sea Chart of the Whole World, According to Wright’s Commonly Called Mercator’s Projection, made in 1728. Courtesy of the David Rumsey Map Collection

Think it’s time for gen Z to ‘grow up’? You’re even more out of touch than the British state

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 05:00:09 GMT

We can’t expect young people to make a seamless transition from childhood to adulthood in this chilly economic climate. Finally, Westminster is catching on

When did you realise you had finally grown up? It’s a trick question, obviously: maturity is just realising that life is full of things you don’t feel old enough for but somehow manage anyway, while getting better at pretending to know what you’re doing. But the question is worth asking nonetheless, because for gen Z the goalposts of grownup life are clearly shifting.

It’s a truism that adulting now comes later than it did to generations who still don’t consider adulting a verb, with 43% of 25-year-olds still living at home and plenty more jobless university graduates boomeranging back there this summer, thanks to a grim labour market. Since they’ll probably be working longer into what were once retirement years, perhaps it’s only natural that they’re taking longer to get started. But there’s a fine line between choosing to grow up more slowly and becoming trapped into a kind of limbo between childhood and adulthood, with nobody to pull you out of the morass beyond parents who aren’t sure how to handle this new life stage either.

If your unemployed 22-year-old is getting rejection after rejection, should you rewrite their job applications for them, or let them figure it out for themselves? What do you do with an 18-year-old too depressed to leave their bedroom, now they’re old enough to make their own GP appointments but not mature enough to know they need one? Kidulthood can be a minefield.

The idea that the state should recognise the years roughly between 18 and 25 as a phase distinct from either childhood or full adulthood, which needs its own tailored policies, is catching on around Westminster. The Nuffield Foundation charitable trust, which has spent two years researching changing journeys to adulthood, held a seminar this week drawing together threads from academia to Alan Milburn’s genuinely thoughtful review of what is causing so many young people to be Neet (not in education, employment or training). As Milburn put it to the Nuffield Foundation’s Carey Oppenheim, councils have to ensure that teenagers are studying or training up to 18, but what happens after that is not their problem. Yet in the Netherlands, the state’s responsibilities extend up to 24 or, in some cases, 27. Guess which country has fewer Neets.

More broadly, he suggested, the British state may be too quick to shrug off responsibility for young people struggling with the transition to adulthood. “We haven’t aligned now with the reality of the transitions that young people are going through in their lives,” he said.

In Australia, Oppenheim points out, the equivalent of Britain’s children and adolescent mental health services runs from age 12 right up to age 25, recognising a growing argument within medicine that adolescence doesn’t end neatly at 19. But in Britain, teenagers still hit a cliff edge, tumbling abruptly out of children’s mental health services into adult ones where the threshold for intervention can be far higher. Even the new social media ban for under-16s assumes teenagers are mature enough at 17 to handle what they couldn’t the day before.

Meanwhile the IPPR thinktank’s State of A Generation project, another deep dive into the coming of age process, warns of a society where “transitions to adulthood are blocked” and young people are increasingly nihilistic about their future.

There’s much we still don’t understand about this evolving life stage, including how far to accept it and how far to push back. If a quarter of 18- to 34-year-olds living with their parents say they’re genuinely happy at home or not ready to leave, rather than feeling stuck, does that imply a worrying failure to launch? Or, as the demographer Prof Ann Berrington argues, a new form of “privileged dependence”, where some young people enjoy a financial and emotional security that ultimately boosts them into adult life, and it’s the young people who can’t go home in a crisis we should worry about?

There’s an obvious danger here of over-babying young people, potentially making them even more anxious in the process, or of the state intruding too far into the lives of twentysomethings who are coping fine. As the parent of a 19-year-old, I’m well aware that gen Z are often far more resilient and competent than they get credit for.

But a significant minority do seem to be falling into a gap between childhood and adulthood, and in a chilly economic climate they look increasingly exposed. Maybe the real mark of having finally grown up is feeling ready to help someone else do the same.

The spectre of ‘remigration’ is haunting Europe. Slovenia in 1992 gives us a blueprint for this state terror

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 04:00:09 GMT

In February that year, the Slovenian government officially deleted 25,000 citizens, turning them overnight into illegal immigrants

So much of your daily life – your job, your health, your home – hinges on the fact that your name is in a government database. Are you a legal citizen of your country, with everything that entails? You are, until an anonymous bureaucrat hits a key one night and strips it all away, turning you into an illegal immigrant. It happened in Slovenia in 1992.

“I took my son to register for secondary school. The clerk rifled through the papers, then stared at me as if refusing to see the boy standing right next to me. Finally, she said: ‘But you don’t have a son. He doesn’t exist.’” I can’t forget the look on the face of the woman who was telling me this story. It was a mixture of deep hurt and bewilderment, with a pause after every sentence, as if she were walking through a minefield. During the research for my book Erased, I compiled countless stories like this: stories I once would have thought impossible.

On 26 February 1992, the Slovenian government quietly deleted 1.3% of its citizenry overnight. The criterion was frighteningly simple: anyone born in another part of the former Yugoslavia who was a permanent resident of Slovenia (regardless of whether they considered themselves naturalised) suddenly lost their citizenship, their right to reside, their healthcare, their pension: everything. They were transformed into illegal immigrants overnight, without prior notification, and with no right to appeal. The goal was to cleanse Slovenia of a Balkan “fifth column” and pivot closer to Europe.

I have long felt this dark piece of Slovenian history to be an ugly stain on the conscience of my nation; but its spirit is spreading across Europe and beyond. The horrors of migrant deaths in the Mediterranean and the English Channel are regularly witnessed and documented, the victims dying at the very gates of “fortress Europe”. But even if you are already inside the fortress, even if you consider yourself fully naturalised, you are perhaps no longer safe. In an age of constant video surveillance, there is nothing fantastical about an official refusing to renew a permit, or unearthing a minor “offence” committed decades earlier, to strip away your citizenship.

The spectre of “remigration” is haunting Europe, and its shadow looms ever larger. What Slovenia did in 1992 has become a blueprint for a quiet, bureaucratic form of state terror.

The woman who told me about her son lived in a village equidistant between two towns. During her pregnancy, she had to choose between two maternity hospitals. After the collapse of Yugoslavia, the town she had picked was across the new border in Croatia, while her village remained in Slovenia. And so, on that fateful day in 1992, her son ceased to exist. His story had a happy ending: Slovenia is a very small country, and if you have a wide enough network, you’ll eventually find someone who knows someone. So the boy emerged from the ranks of the disappeared and was able to attend school. But for those without friends in high places, things rarely ended happily.

One man was rushing to work, speeding, when he was pulled over by the police. Unable to find him in the registry, they took him to an asylum centre. He had been born in Serbia, but Slovenia’s only border with the former Yugoslavia is with Croatia. So they deported him there instead. Croatia was at war with Serbia at the time, and the man was treated as a prisoner of war. He was lucky: had he been born in Croatia, he would have been conscripted and sent straight to the frontlines.

For six years, 1.3% of the population hid and survived however they could. They worked illegally for subsistence wages, at the mercy of bosses and landlords. One man locked himself in his flat, eating old canned food, refusing to open the door to anyone. It was a wise strategy. There were cases of the erased returning home to find their locks changed: someone had simply claimed and occupied their flat, realising the victim would have no recourse to call the police.

There were also stories of profound kindness: a citizen who officially contracted every disease imaginable because he kept lending his healthcare card to the erased; a waitress who walked out of her shift with a first aid kit to treat an injured, erased man who had just been thrown out of the hospital. Relying on the kindness of strangers, however, is a lottery I wouldn’t wish on anyone.

In 1998, the Slovenian constitutional court ruled the erasure unconstitutional, and the immediate threat subsided. But the long road to restoring rights and securing measly compensation for the victims turned into a gruelling odyssey that, for some, continues to this day.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

A monument has since been erected for the erased in Ljubljana, and a park named after them. But it is always easier to build a monument than to issue an apology, let alone settle dues. The UK has its own unresolved equivalent in the Windrush generation – and their monument is standing, too.

Many of the erased never doubted their status because they considered themselves Slovenians. Overnight, they were expected to deport themselves to countries they had no meaningful connection to. I was reminded of their fate when reading about the US administration’s “operation second look”, which entails ICE agents scavenging decades-old files for minor administrative discrepancies in the hope of stripping people of their citizenship.

As it so often does, Europe follows America’s lead. Gregory Bovino, the former US Border Patrol “commander-at-large”, was recently in Europe and treated like a rock star. At a rightwing gathering in Portugal he noted that he and the Austrian ethnonationalist Martin Sellner are “on the same sheet of music”. Perhaps the original Slovenian experiment in “remigration” was indeed exactly what it was claimed to be back then: a step closer to Europe, but a meaner and more sinister version of Europe.

Miha Mazzini is a writer, film-maker and anthropologist

How Trump Is Wielding Power to Stifle Speech

The New York Times September 12, 2026

Trump Administration

News Analysis

President Trump has harnessed agencies across the government to curtail press freedoms, a sweeping campaign that free speech advocates say will have lasting effects.

News Analysis

President Trump has harnessed agencies across the government to curtail press freedoms, a sweeping campaign that free speech advocates say will have lasting effects.

Credit... Doug Mills/The New York Times

Supported by

By Jim Rutenberg and Maggie Haberman

Jim Rutenberg writes about the intersection of media and politics. Maggie Haberman covers the White House.

The Justice Department has sent F. B. I. agents to reporters’ homes to serve subpoenas and, in at least one case, flashed a warrant to seize devices. The Pentagon has fired the editor and publisher of its traditionally independent newspaper, Stars and Stripes, and blocked access to other journalists who refused to sign pledges that would limit their reporting.

Regulatory agencies are using their powers to pressure media organizations over their content. The administration has stripped funding from public television and radio. Angry over stories he does not like, President Trump has sued major news organizations and the White House has taken control of the previously independent press pool that tracks the president, deciding which outlets can participate.

Almost 20 months into Mr. Trump’s second term, his long-running media clashes have grown into a sweeping campaign to control speech in America that stands out for applying so many levers, so fast, all at once.

Driven by personal pique, fury over leaks and a determination to shape the political narrative to his advantage, Mr. Trump is deploying the might of the federal government and filing personal lawsuits — targeting not just journalists and liberal critics, but also comedians and talk show hosts, and the corporate entities behind them.

To the president and his allies, he is simply demanding accountability for what he casts as biased, unfair and sometimes inaccurate coverage and criticism — an effort that has been welcomed by longtime conservative press critics like those at the Media Research Center.

Aides noted that the White House has this year expanded who gets invited to cover events, such as the off-the-record presidential lunch with network anchors that precedes the annual State of the Union address.

In a statement, the White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said that “biased reporting from the media is a disservice to the American people.” Pointing to Mr. Trump’s heavy rotation of question and answer sessions with reporters as evidence of “unprecedented access,’’ he added: “We utilize every tool available to ensure that accurate reporting is provided to the public and the stain of those who knowingly peddle false information is held accountable.”

Free speech advocates say the president’s intent is apparent: to punish, intimidate and silence dissenters.

“There’s not a week that goes by where they’re not taking a new step to curtail press freedom in the country,” said Clayton Weimers, the executive director of the North America division of Reporters Without Borders. “We have measured a substantial diminishment of press freedoms.”

When challenged in court, the president and the administration have frequently lost, confronted with strongly worded rulings from judges affirming First Amendment rights.

Still, even the path to legal victory can have severe financial and reputational costs for those he views as adversaries, which have included The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the BBC. And each time the president assails what has long been considered protected speech, media analysts say, he is eroding norms and undercutting the role of an independent press.

Reporters Without Borders maintains an index that tracks press freedom in 180 countries, clocking governmental threats, subpoenas and the vindictive use of regulations against journalists. The United States now ranks at its lowest since the organization started the index in 2002 — 64th, just above Panama and just below Botswana. The trend is the same at similar indexes kept by the Freedom of the Press Foundation and the V-Dem Institute of Sweden.

There is a long record of U. S. presidents taking steps to curtail speech. President Woodrow Wilson imposed strict censorship and forced dissenting publishers out of business during World War I. Richard M. Nixon kept an enemies list, and his aides threatened F. C. C. action against broadcasters. More recently, the George W. Bush White House expanded government secrecy and the Obama administration went after the sources of journalists through leak investigations.

Mr. Trump had inveighed against the Biden administration for what he and his supporters portrayed as draconian pressure on social media companies to censor disfavored content often at their expense, promising at his second inauguration to “stop all government censorship.”

Now his administration is breaking new ground in stifling dissent with personal lawsuits and novel uses of executive power, longtime First Amendment lawyers say, with implications that extend far beyond Mr. Trump’s presidency.

“We live in a different world under this administration because the threats are so grave,” said Floyd Abrams, who has worked on free speech cases for 60 years. “It’s one thing to say there’s an extraordinarily powerful First Amendment, but unless and until courts rule on these matters, the threat is very real.”

Long before he took office, Mr. Trump was well known for his media feuds. As a developer and reality TV star, he was quick to threaten defamation suits against those who challenged his assertions about his business successes and his wealth.

Mr. Trump has been candid about his aim: to inflict pain, even if it was fleeting. After bringing a failed libel suit against the former Times reporter Timothy L. O’Brien, whose book “TrumpNation” estimated Mr. Trump to be worth far less than he claimed, the president gloated about forcing the publisher to spend money. “I did it to make his life miserable, which I’m happy about,” he said.

In his first term, the president branded journalists as “fake news” and crudely attacked reporters, especially women.

In his second term, Mr. Trump is now imprinting his pugilistic approach across the machinery of the federal government. Those who once might have checked him have been replaced by loyalists who often use their power to fulfill Mr. Trump’s desire to punish perceived enemies.

Soon after his inauguration, the White House banned The Associated Press from the Oval Office and Air Force One, ostensibly because the wire service would not call the Gulf of Mexico by Mr. Trump’s preferred name, the Gulf of America. Another reason for the ban: The A. P. would not give the Trump team rights to its photo of Mr. Trump, bloodied with a raised fist, after he was shot in Butler, Pa., in 2024. At a private lunch with Mr. Trump and network anchors last year, White House aides tied the A. P. ban to the denial of the rights to the photo, according to two people briefed on the event.

Mr. Trump’s team is unapologetic about its goal of achieving firmer control over the national information environment — what Mr. Cheung, the communications director, has dubbed in a social media post “Full Spectrum Dominance.”

Brendan Carr, the chairman of the Federal Communications Commission and one of the most aggressive supporters of Mr. Trump’s efforts, has said that the president is “reshaping the media landscape.”

Citing the big broadcast networks, Mr. Carr told an interviewer for CNBC last year that “for years government officials just allowed those entities, with executives sitting in Hollywood and New York, to dictate the political narrative.” Mr. Trump, he added, has “fundamentally changed the game.”

One of the Trump administration’s strategies appeared to take root in a dispute between Elon Musk and the liberal press watchdog group Media Matters for America.

In 2023, Mr. Musk was furious about a Media Matters article that showed pro-Nazi posts were running on his social media platform X alongside promotional posts from major consumer brands, contributing to an advertiser exodus from the site.

A longtime Trump adviser, Stephen Miller, took to X to pointedly note that Republican state attorneys general had the power to consider civil and criminal fraud charges against the group. In short order, Mr. Musk sued Media Matters for allegedly manipulating the X algorithm to produce its results, the Texas attorney general’s office opened an investigation into deceptive trade practices and the Missouri attorney general followed with its own inquiry.

Media Matters won court injunctions blocking the Texas and Missouri investigations. But soon after Mr. Trump took office again, the Federal Trade Commission, newly headed by the conservative lawyer Andrew Ferguson, began its own investigation, demanding internal documents related to Media Matters’ methodology for evaluating media sources and its finances.

The investigation was part of a broader F. T. C. inquiry into whether several groups that work to identify online disinformation were colluding with advertising firms to direct money away from disfavored outlets. Conservatives saw the issue as central to what some labeled a “censorship industrial complex.”

A federal judge in Washington ultimately determined that the F. T. C.’s investigation of Media Matters presented “a straightforward First Amendment violation.”

But the fight was costly for Media Matters. In addition to paying legal fees, the group said it had self-censored articles to avoid further scrutiny from the agency. (It is still defending itself against Mr. Musk’s suit.)

The F. T. C. also investigated NewsGuard, a site that rates the reliability of online information. It is avowedly nonpartisan in its approach; Fox News, for instance, rates above MS NOW.

In court papers, NewsGuard said it drew attention in part because it had given a low rating to the conservative site Newsmax, which is run by an ally of Mr. Trump’s, Chris Ruddy. Mr. Ruddy had complained that ad agencies were relying on NewsGuard ratings to withhold money from right-leaning outlets like his.

The F. T. C. took another tack that NewsGuard said affected it directly, related to the merger of two of the country’s largest advertising holding companies, Omnicom and Interpublic Group. The F. T. C. entered into a consent decree with the newly joined company barring it from broadly using ratings like those published by NewsGuard to withhold ad spending from certain sites, among other things. (It could still follow individual clients’ requests to do so.)

In a lawsuit filed in February, NewsGuard said the provision effectively placed it on a blacklist, immediately causing it to lose business.

The F. T. C. ultimately dropped its investigations into both NewsGuard and Media Matters, saying it had achieved its goal of defending free speech through agreements with ad firms. It said it was fulfilling its mission of protecting consumers from anticompetitive behavior that “distorted the marketplace of ideas,” as Mr. Ferguson put it.

Dan Schneider, vice president for free speech at the conservative watchdog group Media Research Center, described the actions by the F. T. C. and the F. C. C. as a correction against abuses under the past two Democratic presidents. “Please, let’s not forget history and rewrite everything that went on before,” Mr. Schneider said.

But Rebecca Kelly Slaughter, a Democratic F. T. C. commissioner fired by Mr. Trump last year, said in an interview that the agency’s actions were “a perversion of the F. T. C.’s authorities in order to punish the speech of perceived enemies and reward perceived allies.”

Much of the administration’s action has been led by Mr. Carr. The longtime F. C. C. lawyer is known to frequent the president’s golf clubs when Mr. Trump is there on weekends and often speaks to the president directly about his grievances with news outlets, according to people briefed on their conversations.

He has bent the F. C. C. to the president’s will, investigating the major broadcast networks by reviving largely dormant rules, like those against so-called news distortion — meant to punish the deliberate staging or distortion of a news event. Mr. Carr has also pursued networks for their diversity, equity and inclusion practices, inquiring whether they violate federal law and agency regulations, a tactic the administration has used to significant effect against universities and law firms.

Early on, Mr. Carr extracted extraordinary concessions from Skydance, the company run by the studio executive David Ellison, the son of the billionaire Trump ally Larry Ellison, as it sought to purchase Paramount, the parent company of CBS. To secure F. C. C. approval for the merger, Skydance agreed to end CBS’s diversity policies and appoint a monitor for news bias. (Mr. Trump has since shown a rooting interest in the Ellisons’ attempt to buy Warner Bros. Discovery, which owns CNN.)

Critics, among them F. C. C. chairs from past Republican administrations, have said Mr. Carr is exceeding his authority. Mr. Carr says he is simply following the law by requiring broadcasters to serve the public interest in ways that he says his predecessors had failed to do.

Mr. Trump is clearly pleased with Mr. Carr’s effort to solve the so-called fake news problem, as he put it in a speech in April at a private White House event ahead of the celebrations for America’s 250th anniversary.

“He’s keeping these crooked networks honest,” Mr. Trump said as he spotted Mr. Carr in the crowd, describing his appointee as “the most powerful man in the world.”

After Mr. Trump recently called for punishment of the NBC host Kristen Welker for reporting he did not like, and suggested F. C. C. action against the airing of “fake polls,” Mr. Carr responded by saying the agency was considering “a lot of actions,” including on “fake polls.”

No network has borne the brunt of the president’s ire as much as the Disney-owned ABC network.

Mr. Trump’s animus against ABC grew in 2024, when he sued over the anchor George Stephanopoulos’s characterization of the verdict in the defamation case brought by E. Jean Carroll, who accused Mr. Trump of sexual abuse. ABC settled the suit for $15 million.

In the president’s second term, his anger has increased as the ABC late-night comic Jimmy Kimmel has made him the regular butt of jokes.

Last year, the F. C. C. opened an investigation into the network’s diversity and inclusion hiring policies and revived a conservative group’s complaint over ABC’s 2024 presidential debate.

Early this year, the agency sought to require its talk show “The View” to follow so-called equal-time rules for political candidates, even though the F. C. C. previously agreed that the show qualified for an exemption.

In April, after Mr. Trump and the first lady demanded ABC fire Mr. Kimmel over a joke he made about her being an “expectant widow,” the F. C. C. started an early review of the federal licenses that ABC stations need to operate, years before they are set to expire.

The agency had never brought such a mass challenge to a major network’s station licenses. It said it was doing so because ABC was deficient in its responses to the diversity and inclusion inquiry.

ABC is now fighting the agency’s actions, which it called “deeply un-American.”

The network has asked a federal court to intervene immediately, arguing that Mr. Carr was effectively using the agency’s enforcement process to wage a “retaliatory campaign” that is already negatively affecting its programming decisions.

Out of fear of retaliation, ABC decided to carry live online a prime-time speech that Mr. Trump gave on election security, which it would not have otherwise done, and avoided certain bookings and video clips on “The View,” the network said in court papers.

It also reported onerous F. C. C. demands for documents, including staff communications from inside “The View” and internal ABC News editorial policies.

“It’s unprecedented to seek these records because they are part of the editorial decision-making,” Anna Gomez, the lone Democratic F. C. C. commissioner, said in an interview. “It’s all a strategy, and tools, to intimidate broadcasters into submission.”

Mr. Carr has called ABC’s suit meritless. This month, the F. C. C. moved to get the case dismissed, arguing ABC was simply trying to short-circuit an agency investigation while exaggerating harms to its speech rights.

Trevor Timm, the executive director of the Freedom of the Press Foundation, a nonprofit group that tracks press freedom violations in the United States, said that the administration’s moves “have certainly risen to the level where they’re kind of off the charts.”

Government efforts to subpoena journalists and chill their reporting through threats are at the highest level since the foundation started tracking incidents in 2017.

And as a private citizen, Mr. Trump has filed lawsuits against a wide range of targets including the Guardian newspaper, the journalist Bob Woodward and the Pulitzer Prize board — legal battles often financed by his donor-funded political action committee.

Many of the moves have also drawn stern rebukes and concern from judges.

That was the case after the F. B. I. served a search warrant in January at the home of a Washington Post reporter and seized several of her devices, as part of an investigation into a contractor’s handling of classified material. In February, Judge William B. Porter chastised the government and forbade officials from immediately reviewing the reporter’s materials, saying to do otherwise would be “the equivalent of leaving the government’s fox in charge of The Washington Post’s henhouse.”

While weighing a suit Mr. Trump has personally brought against The Des Moines Register for a poll it published showing him behind in Iowa in 2024, a judge worried that allowing the suit to proceed could have “a massive, chilling effect.”

After a judge harshly questioned government lawyers in July over subpoenas for phone records and testimony from Times journalists who reported on the security capabilities of the new Qatari-donated Air Force One jet, the Justice Department withdrew the subpoenas.

At the time, David McCraw, the paper’s top newsroom lawyer, called the outcome “an important affirmation of our country’s commitment to a free press,” but added in a statement that the subpoenas “should never have been issued in the first place.”

In siding with The Times in a challenge to restrictions for reporters at the Pentagon, Judge Paul Friedman of U. S. District Court for the District of Columbia wrote in March, “Those who drafted the First Amendment believed that the nation’s security requires a free press and an informed people and that such security is endangered by governmental suppression of political speech.”

After The Times initially prevailed in court, Pentagon officials sidestepped the ruling to again limit the access of journalists to the building. The Times sued again. This time, an appellate panel allowed a key new restriction to stand, at least temporarily — reporters must have escorts inside the Pentagon where they once roamed freely.

The rule remains in place while the legal fight presses on.

Jim Rutenberg is a writer at large for The Times and The New York Times Magazine and writes most often about media and politics.

Maggie Haberman is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

New Species of Cat Discovered for First Time in a Century

The New York Times September 18, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The species, called a tilcayo, is smaller than a house cat and lives in the cloud forests of the Andes Mountains in Bolivia.

By Kate Golembiewski

A three-pound wildcat with leopardlike spots from Bolivia who once lived briefly as a house pet isn’t just adorable. He is also, scientists say, the standard-bearer for the first new feline species discovered in a century.

The cat himself is named Tigrino, and his species is called tilcayo.

Several other cat species have gained official recognition after previously being considered subspecies. But the tilcayo, found in the cloud forests of the Andes Mountains in Bolivia, is the first brand-new feline species added to the cat family tree since the pampas cat was described in 1923.

The diminutive tilcayo, officially Leopardus tilcayo, resembles its closest relatives, the so-called tiger cats, found in Central and South America. After DNA analysis, the scientists whose study was published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology say the species split from its closest relatives 1.4 million years ago.

Still, little else is known about the new species, including its behavior and the number of cats in wild.

The biologist Paola Nogales Ascarrunz first met Tigrino nearly a decade ago at the Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary in Bolivia. The cat had been kept as a house pet for a year, before the family realized it was a wild animal, ill-suited for domestic life, and brought it to the sanctuary around 2017.

The sanctuary staff assumed that he was an oncilla, part of the species Leopardus tigrinus, and nicknamed him “Tigrino” based on the species name. But Dr. Nogales Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and the founder of the conservation organization Programa de Investigación Félidos Bolivia, was struck by Tigrino’s size.

“I couldn’t believe how small it was,” Dr. Nogales Ascarrunz said. “I thought that this must be a young cat, or maybe a kitten.” At a year old, Tigrino was fully grown but smaller than a typical adult oncilla, which can weigh more than seven pounds. Initially, Dr. Nogales Ascarrunz did not think too much of the discrepancy, though.

That changed in 2019, when she was working on a guidebook of local Bolivian wildcats. She noticed subtle differences between a reference photo of an oncilla and her photos of Tigrino. In addition to being smaller than the oncilla, Tigrino’s spots were bigger. “It didn’t really match,” Dr. Nogales Ascarrunz said, so she began a study of Tigrino’s DNA, comparing it with other members of the Leopardus genus, colloquially known as “tiger cats.”

At the time, another team of scientists, Eduardo Eizirik and Jonas Lescroart, was studying other tiger cat species from elsewhere in South America, particularly drawing upon preserved specimens in museum collections. After discussing their shared research interests, Dr. Eizirik and Dr. Lescroart joined forces with Dr. Nogales Ascarrunz.

“There were assumed to be two to four species, but the exact number wasn’t really settled yet,” said Dr. Lescroart, a biologist at the University of Antwerp and a co-author of the study with Dr. Nogales Ascarrunz.

“We decided to join our two data sets together, analyze everything together, and it came out to be five different species of tiger cats, with this new Bolivian one being completely unexpected at the time.”

The differences among these five feline species are subtle and often difficult to discern without the help of DNA analysis. However, what might seem like academic hairsplitting about species delineations has real conservation implications. Tiger cats’ habitats are threatened by deforestation and fragmentation, and their populations are scattered by the illegal pet trade.

“If one supposedly widespread species is actually several more restricted lineages, each may have a much smaller geographic range,” said Samantha Zwicker, an ecologist and co-director of the conservation nonprofit Hoja Nueva, who was not involved with the study.

Dr. Eizirik, the study’s senior author and a researcher at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul, said the discovery of the tilcayo had resulted in the most attention to small cats that he has seen in the 30 years he has studied the group.

He expressed hopes that this attention would translate into conservation efforts that would help both the tilcayo and other less cuddly-looking species it lives alongside. “Who knows what else is undiscovered in those Bolivian jungles?” Dr. Eizirik said. “The tilcayo may actually save a lot of things.”
