Russia Holds Stage-Managed Elections

The New York Times September 18, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

Also, a new kind of cat was found. Here’s the latest at the end of Friday.

By Matthew Cullen

Russians began voting today in the country’s first parliamentary elections since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But as my colleague Ivan Nechepurenko walked through Moscow in recent weeks, he was struck by the utter lack of campaigning. It was yet another sign, Ivan said, that the elections were by no means free or fair. In his latest article, he explains how the Kremlin gets the vote it wants.

Even by Russian standards, this weekend’s vote is shaping up to be unsurprising. The only antiwar party, Yabloko, was barred from the ballot. And hundreds of thousands of people have fled the country, including most of Russia’s vocal opposition leaders and activists.

You may be asking, what’s the point? Why would an autocrat even bother to hold an election? Analysts say it’s largely because Vladimir Putin can use the results as a source of legitimacy for himself and his policies.

That has many Russians worried about what might come next. Rumors of a military mobilization have filled online information spaces and are discussed in cafes, on trains and in smoking areas near offices.

Related: Classified U. S. intelligence assessments determined that the Kremlin is, once again, seeking to undermine confidence in the upcoming U. S. elections.

Early this month, the F. B. I. temporarily halted some cooperation with its northern counterpart, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, after Canada’s public broadcaster reminded its journalists not to refer to the Sept. 11 attacks as “terrorism” without attributing it to experts, under a longstanding policy about the word.

The move by Kash Patel, the F. B. I. director, appears to have been short-lived. The two agencies, which typically work closely together on issues like terrorism and cybersecurity, resumed cooperation about a week ago. The Canadian broadcaster, which is editorially independent from the government, also reversed its stance.

In other administration news:

President Trump said that he was banning journalists from CNN, Politico, and MS NOW from reporting at the White House.

The F. A. A. requested that the president put an eternal flame atop his proposed arch.

The president made clear this week that he is an A. I. optimist: He described the fear that A. I. could lead to mass extinction as a “HOAX,” and criticized the large portion of Americans who oppose data centers. Inside the White House, as my colleagues reported today, the debate is far more complex.

People who have discussed the issue with him say the president fears that if the A. I. boom slows, a recession could follow. But some voices in the president’s ear urge caution, some of whom — particularly in the National Security Council and the Energy Department — share the growing concern that it could be dangerous to continue charging ahead with A. I. development without limits.

For more:

Our White House reporter Jonathan Swan explains how Trump became an A. I. evangelist.

Iran, China and some groups in Israel have used A. I. to create influence campaigns on social media.

We answered several frequently asked A. I. questions.

Scientists announced this week that they had identified a new feline species, called tilcayo, living in the cloud forests of Bolivia’s section of the Andes Mountains. They have leopardlike spots and are smaller than most house cats.

The discovery came after a family took in an adorable three-pound wildcat named Tigrino, which they brought to a wildlife sanctuary after realizing it was ill-suited for domestic life. His diminutive size raised the curiosity of a researcher, resulting in the first species added to the cat family tree since the pampas cat was described in 1923.

Business: Warren Buffett, the 96-year-old investor, stepped down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, where he will be succeeded by his 71-year-old son Howard.

Immigration: A hotel in Equatorial Guinea, a small African autocracy, has become a nightmare prison for deportees from the U. S.

Clancy trial: The lone holdout from the deadlocked jury released a statement saying he did not have doubts that Lindsay Clancy was guilty of killing her three young children.

Politics: Trump has called the $400 million super PAC run by his political advisers “my money that I control.” In response, a campaign watchdog group filed a complaint.

Los Angeles: The driver who killed two people by crashing into a bus — coverage of which led to a fatal news helicopter crash — was charged with murder.

Nepal: The flash floods that left more than 8,000 dead or missing have raised alarms about melting glaciers and how to prepare for the next catastrophe.

Canada: After a survey indicated that an overwhelming majority of residents were in favor, Manitoba decided to stop adjusting its clocks for daylight saving time.

Obituary: Duncan Sheik, a pop heartthrob turned Tony-winning composer, died at 56.

Our newest list of recommendations from my colleagues at the Book Review includes China Miéville’s 1,246-page novel, “The Rouse.” After reading our review by the author Jeff VanderMeer, it’s not hard to see why.

VanderMeer describes “The Rouse” as an intimate epic and a maturation of the fantasy novel. “I felt it in my bones, the undeniable power of a jagged masterpiece,” he wrote.

On this day in 1851, the New-York Daily Times published its first issue, by candlelight.

To mark the anniversary, we are looking back at the history that this paper has chronicled. Today, I want to direct your attention to a moving story about Samuel Wilkeson Jr., a Times reporter who, in 1863, filed a report from the battlefield at Gettysburg, then went looking for a Union officer, his son. (We made the article free for all Evening readers.)

For more: Take our quiz to see how well you know The Times, and try our special anniversary-edition crossword.

Audrey Hobert became a pop music phenom after one eccentric album. She sat down with my colleagues to talk about what it’s like.

After 21 years of calling Mets games, Howie Rose still believes in miracles.

Missy Mazzoli is pushing opera into the future with dance beats, kazoos and Abe Lincoln.

If you had $1.8 million to buy an Irish house, which would you choose?

Bake this elegant Earl Grey pear and almond cake.

Watch the 1986 film “True Stories,” or one of our other free-to-stream picks.

Plan a trip to Toronto. We mapped out a food lover’s tour.

Simplify your life with a “novelty audit.”

Treat yourself this fall. Here are some ideas.

Take this week’s news quiz.

Play today’s Connections, Spelling Bee and Mini Crossword. Find all our games here.

A few years ago, a friend told James Purcell and Andrew Taeger about Campaign for North Africa, a 1979 board game so complex that no one is believed to have ever completed (including its creator). Naturally, they agreed they needed to give it a shot. So they’ve been practicing and studying the rules for two years, planning to begin playing next month.

The objective of the game is to win control over the territory, as the Allied powers did in World War II. But in order to do that, players must keep detailed logs for every piece on the board: Italian units, for example, require more water because they need to make pasta. Playing four to five hours a week, Purcell and Taeger estimate that it will take them about 20 years to complete, if it doesn’t drive them mad first.

Have a committed weekend.

Thanks for reading. My colleague Evan Gorelick will fill in for me on Monday. I’ll be back on Tuesday — Matthew

Keith Bedford was our photo editor.

We welcome your feedback. Reach us at evening@nytimes. com.

Matthew Cullen is the lead writer of The Evening, a Times newsletter covering the day’s top stories every weekday.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Weary of the heartthrob label after his 1996 hit “Barely Breathing,” he pivoted to musical theater and won two Tonys for composing “Spring Awakening.”

Duncan Sheik in 1998. Credit... Joanne Chan/CA-Redux

Supported by

By Alex Williams

Duncan Sheik, an introspective singer-songwriter whose alt-pop hit “Barely Breathing” became a Generation X touchstone, but who squirmed under the label of MTV heartthrob and eventually decamped to Broadway, winning two Tonys for composing the smash musical “Spring Awakening,” died on Thursday in Manhattan. He was 56.

His death, in a hospital, was confirmed by his mother, Suzanne Sheik, who said that the cause was organ failure.

Soft-spoken and cerebral — complete with a degree in semiotics from Brown — Mr. Sheik seemed like a long shot for fame when he arrived in Los Angeles in 1992 with a demo tape and a deep unease with the spotlight.

Though he had played guitar for the future hitmaker Lisa Loeb in college, he “could barely sing in public to save my life at that point,” he recalled in a 2011 interview with the site Pop Dose.

Yet in just a few years, he was a rising star. In 1996, Rolling Stone called his first album, “Duncan Sheik,” a “defiant debut — beautiful and benevolent of spirit” and praised his “raw and articulate singing.”

The single “Barely Breathing,” an unvarnished sketch of a dying relationship that was propelled by candy-sweet hooks, saturated the radio airwaves. It earned a Grammy nomination and rose to No. 16 on the Billboard Hot 100, remaining on the chart for 55 weeks — at the time, the fourth-longest run ever.

In the decade of Nirvana and Soundgarden, Mr. Sheik intended his artfully crafted record “as a reaction against the existing alternative music,” he said in a 1997 interview with The Palm Beach Post, complaining that alt rock had become “this kind of monolithic distorted guitar chord.”

With a grounding in classical composition, and influences as diverse as Joni Mitchell, the Cocteau Twins and the Estonian composer Arvo Pärt, Mr. Sheik mixed heart-rending melodies with lyrics that mined Buddhist philosophy and brimmed with existential angst.

In a review of his second album, “Humming” (1998), in The New York Times, Stephen Holden wrote that Mr. Sheik’s “beautifully orchestrated meditations suggest that pop can still aspire to a lofty, searching classicism.”

Fans embraced him as a tortured troubadour, like Jeff Buckley or Elliott Smith. Critics often noted his musical similarities to Nick Drake, the haunting and haunted British singer-songwriter of the late 1960s and early ’70s.

But Mr. Sheik — with looks that called to mind the Gen X dreamboat John Cusack and a female-tilting fan base — was also cast in the news media as a sensitive, soulful sex symbol. The Palm Beach Post noted his “name straight out of a romance novel and the face of a GQ model.”

“Don’t hate Duncan Sheik because he’s beautiful,” the critic Ann Powers wrote in a review of a 1998 concert in The Times. “He is trying very hard to distance himself from that fact.”

Duncan Scott Sheik was born on Nov. 18, 1969, in Glen Ridge, N. J. By the time he was 6, he was learning piano from his grandmother, who had studied at Juilliard. After his parents divorced, his mother moved to Hilton Head Island, S. C., where Duncan got his first electric guitar and played in a band that performed Def Leppard and Van Halen covers.

After graduating from Phillips Academy in Andover, Mass., in 1988, he enrolled at Brown, where he holed up in the campus recording studio working on his own material, when he wasn’t playing with Ms. Loeb, a fellow student who in 1994 would hit No. 1 with “Stay (I Missed You).”

It took a few years of living in Los Angeles after college for his career to take off — but once it did, he found fame to be at times overwhelming.

“I was put in situations that I didn’t have the experience to handle,” he recalled in a 2003 interview with University Wire, adding that he had performed on David Letterman and Jay Leno’s late-night shows when he had “just made one album and I had played maybe 30 or 40 shows in my life. And I’m sure I sucked.”

An adherent of Nichiren Buddhism, rooted in 13th-century Japan, since he was 19, he found that daily chanting helped him to be “just a bit more positive about life in general,” he told The Palm Beach Post.

Despite critical plaudits, “Humming” sold modestly. Mr. Sheik’s somber third album, “Phantom Moon” (2001) — a collaboration with the poet and playwright and his fellow Buddhist Steven Sater — was, according to Mr. Holden’s Times review, “the most entrancing collection of pop dream songs since Nick Drake’s 1969 album, ‘Five Leaves Left.’”

That, Mr. Holden added, was “not to suggest that this hauntingly melancholy suite is poised to hurtle up the charts anytime soon.”

By that point, Mr. Sheik said in a 2015 interview with HuffPost, “the ‘authenticity’ of the alt-rock era of the early and mid-90s was over and the music business took a hard right turn back toward artifice and the more overtly pop sound of Britney, Christina, ’N Sync and Backstreet Boys.”

He scored an unlikely dance hit in 2002 with the percolating “On a High,” from the album “Daylight,” but he was growing ever more weary of the industry hustle.

“I thought, I’m not going to win in this game of trying to be Justin Timberlake,” he recalled in a 2022 interview with The Houston Chronicle. “Maybe I should try and do something different.”

Mr. Sheik met Mr. Sater through the Buddhist association Soka Gakkai, and in 1999 Mr. Sater broached the idea of working together on a musical based on “Spring Awakening,” Frank Wedekind’s 1891 play exploring the tormented inner lives and flowering sexuality of a group of teenagers.

After initial doubts, Mr. Sheik ended up feeling a kinship with the material. “Being a recording artist who tours and performs and who has never had a normal job or anything, I have never really evolved past my 17-year-old self,” he said in a 2014 interview with Broadway World.

In development for years, the rock-meets-folk-meets-emo musical — striking for its raw treatment of topics like abortion, abuse and suicide — ran Off Broadway at the Atlantic Theater Company starting in spring 2006, before opening on Broadway that December.

“It was really about ‘Can we make a musical score that sounds as cool as the music that any alternative rock kid is listening to on their iPod?,’” Mr. Sheik recalled in a 2020 interview.

Before the show premiered, he coached the cast — which included future stars like Lea Michele, Jonathan Groff and John Gallagher, Jr. — to steer clear of traditional Broadway bombast.

“Imagine that you’re Thom Yorke,” he said he told them. “Imagine that you’re a young David Bowie. Imagine that you are Fiona Apple. And please forget about all the vocal training you’ve ever had.”

In a rave review in The Times, the critic Charles Isherwood praised Mr. Sheik’s “ravishing rock score,” calling the show a “brave new musical, haunting and electrifying by turns.”

“Spring Awakening” won eight Tony Awards, including best musical, with Mr. Sheik taking home two, for the score — an honor he shared with Mr. Sater, who wrote the book and lyrics — and for his orchestrations. The show ran for over two years on Broadway, where it was revived in 2015; a new production opens Off Broadway in November.

Mr. Sheik wrote the scores for several other musicals, including “Alice by Heart,” a version of “Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland” set in London during World War II, and “American Psycho,” an adaptation of the blood-soaked Bret Easton Ellis novel, which flopped on Broadway in 2016.

Information about his survivors was not immediately available.

Along the way, Mr. Sheik continued to release non-theater albums, including a 2011 collection of covers of songs by British acts of the 1980s like Depeche Mode and Tears for Fears. His final album, “Claptrap” (2022), wove his trademark delicate melodies into an ambient electronic soundscape.

In interviews over the years, his Buddhist outlook came through as he described fame, critical success and even life itself as capricious and beyond anyone’s control.

“I subscribe to the death-of-the-author theory,” he said in a 1997 interview with The Orange County Register, “that once a cultural product has been created and sent out into the world, it no longer has any attachment to its author.”

Alex Williams is a Times reporter on the Obituaries desk.

Russia Aims to Inject Chaos Into Elections, U. S. Intelligence Finds

The New York Times September 18, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Kremlin is once again seeking to undermine confidence in American democracy with online influence campaigns, U. S. officials said.

By Dustin VolzJulian E. Barnes and Steven Lee Myers

Dustin Volz and Julian E. Barnes cover U. S. intelligence agencies and reported from Washington. Steven Lee Myers is a former Moscow bureau chief who writes about disinformation and reported from San Francisco.

The Russian government has been targeting Americans with covert online disinformation operations seeking to undermine public confidence in November’s midterm elections, using a familiar playbook in an attempt to inject chaos into the voting season, according to U. S. officials familiar with the matter.

Classified U. S. intelligence assessments from recent months have determined that the Kremlin has again authorized a digital influence campaign to peddle content across social media in hopes of seeding or amplifying domestic divisions around the election season, the officials said.

The assessments did not find evidence of attempts to take aim at voting machinery in a way that could compromise the actual voting process, the officials added. The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss classified information, did not specify the efforts to influence attitudes online. But experts in Russian disinformation have spotted some social media campaigns in recent weeks that use artificial intelligence to create fake videos of Hollywood celebrities talking about key battleground Senate races.

The disinformation campaign appeared to be less extensive or coordinated than at least some of Russia’s prior efforts in American elections, some of the officials said. Since 2016, the Kremlin has initiated online influence operations in every American federal election cycle, according to previously declassified assessments. The officials added that U. S. spy agencies see Moscow as less interested in midterm races than in presidential contests and as distracted by its grinding war with Ukraine.

Still, the push to inflame the electorate comes as President Trump has repeatedly sought to challenge the integrity of American democracy. In July, Mr. Trump gave a televised prime-time address on election security in which he claimed there were severe vulnerabilities in U. S. voting systems and accused American officials of a yearslong “cover-up” to conceal efforts by China and others to influence elections.

He has instructed a task force to declassify documents purporting to support his narratives of rampant voter fraud and foreign tampering, but those files, which were heavily redacted, did not reveal major new weaknesses in the country’s election systems or show that foreign governments had manipulated any votes.

Some of the officials said the main goal of the Russian influence operations appeared to be to sow chaos rather than aid one particular party, though the examples that independent disinformation researchers in recent weeks have attributed to Russia have exclusively attacked Democratic candidates in swing states.

The White House, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the Russian Embassy did not respond to requests for comment. Russia has historically denied U. S. allegations of election meddling.

Some intelligence assessments have also found that Iran, too, may engage in influence operations around the November election as well, the officials said, though little activity had been documented in classified channels that traced to Tehran. The country, which has been locked in a war with the United States since February, sought to spread propaganda undermining Mr. Trump in the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections, and officials said it was reasonable to expect the regime to do so again.

Last month, Meta released a report highlighting a small network of accounts on Facebook and Instagram originating in Iran that focused on U. S. politics. The network’s content, some of which was generated with artificial intelligence, included “anti-Republican views,” Meta said.

The U. S. intelligence findings also said China could be willing to engage in influence operations by targeting individual congressional races or members of Congress whom Beijing sees as adversarial to its interests, officials said.

That approach, too, would echo its activity in past election seasons, but the U. S. intelligence assessments found that Beijing may ultimately steer clear for fear of blowback, the officials said. In general, China is more careful in order to avoid being caught, while Russia and Iran are seen as less bothered about being discovered, current and former U. S. officials said.

In 2016, President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia ordered a multipronged interference effort that sought to denigrate Hillary Clinton, the Democratic nominee, and bolster the electoral prospects of her Republican rival, Mr. Trump, U. S. spy agencies concluded. Multiple audits of those intelligence findings, including a multiyear investigation by the Republican-led Senate Intelligence Committee, corroborated those conclusions.

Researchers in Europe and the United States who track Russian disinformation campaigns have seen recent signs of Russian activity. In two separate waves over the past week, a network previously linked to Kremlin trolls posted a series of videos on X and BlueSky that appeared to rely on A. I. to churn out baseless claims against Democrats running for Senate in closely contested races. Elements of the campaign were reported earlier by MS NOW.

The posts attacked the candidates using themes that Mr. Trump and the Republican Party have relied on to disparage Democrats, including accusations of corruption, antisemitism and support for gay and transgender rights.

The posts included false or unsubstantiated claims in videos devised to seem as if they came from prominent news organizations, including CNN, the BBC and The New York Times.

Among those targeted were Senator Jon Ossoff, who faces re-election in Georgia, and other challengers who have a chance of giving Democrats a majority in the Senate: Sherrod Brown in Ohio, Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Troy Jackson in Maine, Chris Pappas in New Hampshire, Mary Peltola in Alaska, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, James Talarico in Texas, and Joshua Turek in Iowa.

Graphika, a threat analysis company, attributed the blitz to a Kremlin-linked operation that experts have called Operation Overload or Matryoshka, which often impersonates real news organizations to spread fabricated content.

A post that appeared on Thursday mimicked a Times video featuring an image of the actress Jamie Lee Curtis with subtitles criticizing the Democrats for their policies on transgender issues. “There’s not even a scintilla of truth in that,” the actress’ publicist, Heidi Schaeffer, said in an interview.

By the end of the day, the post had been viewed nearly 200,000 times, according to X’s count. X, which did not respond to a request for comment, removed some of the posts that appeared earlier in the week, but many remain online.

The posts employed Russian tactics familiar from previous elections in the United States and Europe.

Jean Le Roux, a senior researcher at Graphika, noted that the American content appeared shortly after elections in Germany and Sweden concluded.

“We’re definitely expecting it to ramp up,” he said of the Russian effort. “I don’t think they’re going to stop. I think that we’re seeing the initial kickoff of the U. S. election focused campaigning.”

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

Steven Lee Myers covers misinformation and disinformation from San Francisco. Since joining The Times in 1989, he has reported from around the world, including Moscow, Baghdad, Beijing and Seoul.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

The 300,000-square-foot so-called entertainment zone has scaled down capacity for horse race spectators, but added spaces for concerts and other performances.

Credit...

Supported by

By Joe Drape

Visuals by Lexi Parra

Reporting from Elmont, N. Y.

The new Belmont Park, just outside New York City, reopens Friday not merely as a racetrack but also as a host for a range of events, including large concerts and intimate performances. At least that is the vision of the New York Racing Association, which bet $550 million on its makeover.

The organization could not have rebuilt it without a $455 million loan from the state that was championed by Gov. Kathy Hochul. She intends to be at a ribbon-cutting ceremony Friday morning about 14 hours after watching her hometown Buffalo Bills in their new $2.1 billion Highmark Stadium.

“From Buffalo to Belmont we are investing in sports, which is a point of pride for New Yorkers,” Governor Hochul said in an interview. “Live racing in a world-class, cutting-edge structure I thought was a smart use of land.”

Horse racing is surging as deep-pocketed owners are setting records for spending at horse sales, thanks to a tax break in President Trump’s major spending and tax bill that was signed into law last year. The provision — called a bonus depreciation — lets businesses immediately deduct the full cost of certain assets, like machinery and equipment, to enhance their cash flow.

It now applies to racehorses, and it is helping turn these animals into a hot investment for wealthy people. Last year, owners spent nearly $1.5 billion in North America in pursuit of fast racehorses, a nearly 21 percent increase from 2024.

New construction and renovation have also been done on signature racetracks in Kentucky and Maryland. But at a time when horse bets can be placed with a few taps on a phone, the big question is whether people will go out to spend a day at the races.

In its heyday, more than 20,000 people filled the Belmont Park building on weekends and the Belmont Stakes, the third leg of the Triple Crown, often drew more than 100,000. It was considered the grand old racetrack on Long Island with its mile-and-a-half oval and imposing grandstand.

The new Belmont Park was designed for a thriving sport with a more modest hold on the public. The five-story, 300,000-square-foot building accommodates 10,000 people in its seats, suites and restaurants, but can be expanded with temporary structures to handle the demand for the Belmont Stakes, which in recent years was held at the Saratoga Race Course and capped at 50,000 attendees. It offers a smaller, more European-style experience, with plenty of green space. And the building is ringed with balconies overlooking the paddock and the racetrack that also offer views of Manhattan.

While everyday horse players can still get general admission tickets for as little as $7, the prices get steeper for more premium experiences. Box-seat memberships go for $36,000 to $72,000 a year and include hospitality. Ninety percent of those seats have been sold, according to N. Y. R. A. officials. More than half of the 32 Champion Suites, which can fit 16 to 50 people and start at $175,000 annually, have been sold on a multiyear basis. They also include food and drink and are equipped with flat screens and betting windows.

Marc Holliday, chairman of the N. Y. R. A. board of directors, said the association’s goal was to “right size” Belmont Park with a modern design and to offer best-in-class hospitality and experiences. He said he wanted it to be different from Saratoga, which is one of the nation’s oldest sporting venue.

“Saratoga will always be known for its history and the nostalgic day of racing,” said Mr. Holliday, who is also chief executive of SL Green Realty Corp. “ I wanted downstate to be something completely oriented towards the future and kind of a new beginning for horse racing.”

David O’Rourke, the chief executive of N. Y. R. A., said the old Belmont Park, which opened in 1968, had been built strictly for gambling on horses. At the time, there were no competing casinos, and legalized sports betting was half a century away.

He said the downsized Belmont Park had been designed to be an “entertainment zone,” hosting big concerts in its infield or smaller performances, like plays, in the track’s paddock where horses are prepared before a race.

Mr. O’Rourke said the new Belmont would benefit from its neighbor, the UBS Arena, home to the New York Islanders of the National Hockey League. The two now share a backyard, where the new Big Red’s sports bar offers easily accessible pregame hospitality for both venues.

“Now the intention will be to see how the patrons interact with it,” he said. “Is it the backyard where we’re going to have playgrounds and a kid’s zone? And as people start to experience it and use it, that’s how we’re going to move forward with the investment and the things that we’ll add to it.”

Still, for 10 months a year, Belmont Park’s main attraction will remain horse racing. The $455 million loan was given on the condition that N. Y. R. A. return Aqueduct racetrack in Queens and its more than 100 acres of land to the state. With the financing, the association razed the old Belmont and built four new racing surfaces: a renovated 1.5-mile oval along with two new grass tracks and a synthetic one that will host winter racing.

N. Y. R. A. will repay the state $25.8 million annually for 20 years with money from its video lottery capital funds — a designated percentage of revenues from downstate facilities such as Resorts World New York City Casino at Aqueduct — to pay for race purses, capital improvements and operational support.

On Friday, the equine star of Belmont Park is Forever Young, a Japanese racehorse widely considered the best in the world. He has won more than $31 million in purses, racing in Japan, Saudi Arabia and the United States, and is the favorite to win the Jockey Club Gold Cup on Friday.

Forever Young’s handlers are impressed with the new facilities.

“Belmont Park is the best complex for training now in North America,” said Hiroshi Ando, racing manager for the horse’s owner, Susumu Fujita. “We have a lot of options with main track, training track, Tapeta track, small track.”

Joe Drape is a Times reporter writing about how the intersection of money, power and sports impacts our culture.

Lexi Parra is a photojournalist for The Times, based in New York. She is a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

At Gettysburg, a Reporter Captured a Nation’s Loss, and His Own

The New York Times September 18, 2026

Samuel Wilkeson Jr. filed a report for The Times from the battlefield. Then he went looking for a Union officer, his son.

Credit... Matt Dorfman

Supported by

By Dan Barry

Dan Barry, a Times writer since 1995, went to the battlefields of Gettysburg for this story.

This story is part of a series marking 175 years of eyewitness journalism from The New York Times. Read more here.

After the battle the heavens above Gettysburg wept, the rain falling hard upon the blood-dappled fields, the bullet-shorn trees, the tens of thousands of dead, dying, maimed. It was the Fourth of July, the foundational anniversary for a nation now at war with itself, and all was mud.

A war correspondent for The New York Times named Samuel Wilkeson Jr. trudged through the violated Pennsylvania landscape on a solitary quest. The weary journalist was searching for one particular Union soldier who was said to have had his leg blown off. His teenage son.

Wilkeson believed the end of slavery could be achieved only through the Union Army’s defeat of the Confederacy, but the human cost of the war he deemed necessary was now strewn before him. The corpses in blue and gray bloating in the July heat. The wounded begging for the mercy of death. And here, in the muck at his feet, the bold lieutenant of Battery G, Fourth U. S. Artillery, his son Bayard.

In that moment the mourning of a father could have eclipsed the duty of a journalist, just as deadline pressure might have kept the raw pain at bay. Instead, grief and duty melded into a singular force, and Sam Wilkeson began to write.

Two days later, The Times published his eyewitness account, regarded now as a singular piece of American reportage: a dispatch entwining the intimate and the universal, laced with an eloquence that may have informed the Gettysburg Address delivered four months later by President Abraham Lincoln.

The front page of that New York Times edition, July 6, 1863, is kept in the company archives, safe and preserved. The dimpled impressions left by the typesetting process in the bone-white newsprint lend a tactile urgency to every word, as if Wilkeson were reaching through the folds of time to shake us by the shoulders and share what he had witnessed and felt.

“My pen is heavy,” wrote the journalist and father.

In the raucous pantheon of 19th-century American reporters, Sam Wilkeson stood out. He had a sly facility with words, a mercurial disposition — he had at least one fistfight with a colleague — and a gift for insinuating himself into the inner sanctums of power.

Having connections came naturally to Wilkeson. His father, Samuel the elder, had been a successful merchant and politician who helped to establish the city of Buffalo. His wife, Catherine, was the sister of Elizabeth Cady Stanton, of the women’s rights movement.

After giving up the practice of law to become a newspaperman, Wilkeson rose to become a star reporter for The New York Tribune, founded and edited by the renowned Horace Greeley. His promotion to Washington bureau chief, in 1861, prompted a competing newspaper to describe him as a “fanatical, impertinent, revolutionary fellow who will bear watching.”

When the Civil War broke out that same year, Wilkeson became a must-read, undaunted in questioning government policies, holding generals to account, decrying press censorship — and using his journalistic role in ways that would be unacceptable today.

“He cultivated access to people in power not only to record events, but to try to shape them,” wrote Chuck Raasch in “Imperfect Union,” his 2016 book about the Wilkesons at Gettysburg. “He used that access to inform and contextualize his reporting, but also to protect and reward his sources and punish his enemies.”

Determined to bear witness to the war, Wilkeson left Washington to follow the action, sleeping outdoors and wearing the same clothes for weeks. He scorned the dilettante journalists he encountered along the way.

“No man who in any way talks about his living — alludes to it as a subject which rests on his mind, is fit to follow an army in an enemy’s country,” he wrote. “Reporters must be earnest and devoted.”

The war first scarred the Wilkeson family at the Battle of Seven Pines in the spring of 1862. In the mayhem of that engagement in Virginia, Sam Wilkeson aided the Union Army by rallying the rattled troops and serving as a go-between among the officers. Military officials later commended him for his bravery.

After writing his account of the battle, the journalist tracked down the body of a beloved nephew, a Union soldier killed in the conflict. After that shattering experience, he came down with dysentery, and the required months of rest at his upstate New York home came as a blessing. Throughout his recuperation, Wilkeson’s thoughts must have turned to another young soldier: his oldest son, Bayard. The gangly boy he had once watched plowing the family field with such dedication of purpose was now just as determined to join the fray.

Bayard had presented his well-connected father with a difficult choice. Either watch his son enlist as an Army private or help him secure an appointment as a second lieutenant. For the concerned father and journalist, the latter option seemed less dangerous.

In October 1861, young Wilkeson sent a letter to the Army to accept the commission, his earnestness evident in every handwritten loop and curl. “I am 17 years and six months of age,” he noted.

A series of battles pulled the young man northward through Virginia, drawing him closer to his fate. Fredericksburg, in December 1862. Deserted House, in January 1863. Chancellorsville, in the spring of 1863, where his battery, a tactical artillery unit of six cannons and 10 dozen men, took part in a devastating Union Army defeat.

Bayard Wilkeson, now a first lieutenant, often felt on the periphery of meaningful action. In a letter dated June 22, 1863, he begged his father to call in more favors to get him reassigned.

“I want to have a name at the end of this war,” he wrote.

Nine days later, the Union officer known to his family as Bay sat on a white horse, exposed to the enemy. It was cloudy the afternoon of July 1, and all around him raged the beginning of the war’s bloodiest conflict: the Battle of Gettysburg. He was 19 years old.

Following orders that would later be questioned, Lieutenant Wilkeson had positioned his battery on a knoll overlooking the fields where the Confederate infantry and artillery were bombarding an undermanned Union line of defense. The Union soldiers wheeled into position their Napoleon cannons, capable of shooting 12-pound balls nearly a mile. But the enemy had them as well, and in greater number. Cannonballs rocketed through the air, tearing through field and flesh.

Tall in his saddle to inspire his inexperienced men, Wilkeson moved back and forth, calling out commands and assurances, urging his gunners to shoot straight and true. A little more than a half-mile to the northeast, Confederate soldiers aimed their barrels toward this conspicuous target, who almost seemed to be daring them to fire.

A shell tore through the white horse and mangled the lieutenant’s right leg below the knee, sending wounded man and dead animal tumbling to the ground. He was carried to a spot between two cannons where, remaining composed, he continued to issue commands.

What happened next lingers in that mysterious space between fact and legend. According to a display at the Gettysburg National Military Park Museum, Wilkeson then “tied a tourniquet with his sash and used a penknife to amputate what remained of his shattered leg.” But family letters and military reports do not refer to a self-amputation occurring in a harrowing scene in no need of embellishment.

The one-legged lieutenant maintained a cheerfulness perhaps rooted in shock. Cradled in a blanket, he was carried a quarter-mile to a building on the grounds of the county almshouse, where the poor, disabled and mentally unwell were given shelter. He was placed beside other wounded soldiers on a damp basement floor, in the cool of imminent death.

Hour by hour, he lost blood and strength as the Union forces, including its surgeons, retreated south through Gettysburg town. Two women, their identities lost to time other than that one was Black and the other Irish, tended as best they could to his needs.

The Irishwoman would recall how beautiful the wounded officer looked as she wiped blood from his face, while the Black woman would say she could tell that he was a gentleman. They would both remember hearing the faltering young man call for his mother and father.

Sam Wilkeson did not arrive in Gettysburg until late that night or early the morning of Thursday, July 2. He was greeted with the news that his son had lost a leg in battle and was out there somewhere in the summer darkness, wounded and unlikely to be under medical care. Possibly a Confederate prisoner. Possibly dead.

But the elder Wilkeson had a job. He was now covering the war for The Times and an editor he admired, Henry Raymond, who had co-founded the newspaper in 1851. Wilkeson was following the Union general George Meade, commander of the Army of the Potomac, who had set up headquarters at a farmhouse just two miles south of where his suffering son lay.

The shedding of blood continued through Thursday, as Gen. Robert E. Lee failed to capitalize on the Confederacy’s first-day success. In once-obscure places now part of Civil War lore — Little Round Top and the Wheatfield, the Peach Orchard and Devil’s Den — an estimated 15,000 soldiers were killed, wounded or missing.

In the stifling afternoon of the next day, Friday, July 3, Wilkeson and other exhausted correspondents collapsed on the grass outside the farmhouse being used as Meade’s base. He had already filed brief dispatches for The Times, describing the erratic rhythms of gunfire as “slack and scattering for a while, and then heavy and continuous.”

Birdsong coming from a peach tree was suddenly overtaken by a screaming shell, Wilkeson later wrote, “followed by another, and another, and in a moment the air was full of the most complete artillery prelude to an infantry battle that was ever exhibited.” The barrage killed 16 horses, wounded several officers, splintered parts of the farmhouse — and sent the correspondents scrambling for safer ground.

General Lee’s army began to bombard the Union stronghold in hope of securing victory, but the battle — and the war — was taking a turn. In midafternoon, the Confederate general George Pickett led a mile-long stretch of more than 12,000 soldiers on an audacious gambit to break through Union lines, their central target a slight rise appropriately called Cemetery Ridge.

The Confederate calamity known as Pickett’s Charge played to its blood-soaked conclusion, with thousands of the South’s soldiers mowed down in open fields and overwhelmed in hand-to-hand combat at the Union line along the ridge. General Lee soon retreated to Virginia, leaving the North to celebrate a pivotal victory.

A late-afternoon thunderstorm augured the heavy rain to come, its rumbling a pale echo of the din of artillery fire that had defined the day. As dusk was settling, Wilkeson filed a four-paragraph dispatch. “While I write the ground about me is covered thick with rebel dead, mingled with our own,” he wrote.

The journalist’s duty done for the moment, the father set out at the dawn of the Fourth of July to find his son.

Wilkeson made his way through transformed Gettysburg, past the fields of dead. Past the shattered cemetery monuments, the obliterated fences, the sheared trees, the spent shells and bullets so numerous they would be found for generations to come.

At some point Wilkeson’s brother John, whose own son had been killed at the Battle of Seven Pines, arrived in Gettysburg to join the search for Bayard. Toward the end of a long day’s hunt, he encountered Sam, who, it appears, had finally found what he had been looking for, yet hoped not to see.

“What a picture of grief and despair he presented,” John Wilkeson later wrote.

Bayard Wilkeson had died around 10 on the night of July 1. After some time, his body was wrapped in a blanket and buried in the shallow mud. When it was exhumed, John Wilkeson wrote, there was a cotton bandage wrapped around the right knee, one he imagined Bayard had tied with “his own hands in the vain hope of stanching the flow of blood.”

Somehow, at some point, Sam Wilkeson began to compose an extended dispatch from Gettysburg. He wrote both as a journalist providing an eyewitness account and as a believer in the Union cause now reckoning with the profound expense of that belief. He began:

“Who can write the history of a battle whose eyes are immovably fastened upon a central figure of transcendingly absorbing interest — the dead body of an oldest born, crushed by a shell in a position where a battery should never have been sent, and abandoned to death in a building where surgeons dared not to stay?”

Wilkeson proceeded to deliver a vivid, almost impressionistic account of the three-day battle, providing “such details as I have the heart for,” he wrote.

The “marvellous outspread upon the board of death of dead animals — of dead soldiers in blue, and dead soldiers in gray.” The “silence as of deep sleep” that fell upon the battlefield between breaks in the fighting. The shells that “shrieked, whirled, moaned, whistled and wrathfully fluttered over our ground.” The Union soldiers who “died with the peculiar yells that blend the extorted cry of pain with horror and despair.”

In his final paragraph, Wilkeson stepped back once again, briefly removing the reportorial mask to note that “I rise from a grave whose wet clay I have passionately kissed.” But he never mentioned Bayard Wilkeson by name, choosing instead to channel the North’s communal grief and communal resolve.

“My pen is heavy,” he wrote. “Oh, you dead, who at Gettysburgh have baptized with your blood the second birth of Freedom in America, how you are to be envied!”

Wilkeson’s dispatch, probably sent by telegraph from the nearby town of Hanover, appeared on the front page of The Times on Monday, July 6, and was widely reprinted, including in pamphlet form. It is conceivable, even likely, that Lincoln read the essay, as he was familiar with Wilkeson and his reporting.

Four months later, Lincoln would famously refer in his Gettysburg Address to “a new birth of freedom” — perhaps in echo of Wilkeson’s “second birth of Freedom in America.” For Matthew Pinsker, a Civil War scholar and the director of the House Divided Project at Dickinson College, it is “the most inspiring paraphrase in American history.”

I stood one late spring afternoon on the ground where Bayard Wilkeson had once commanded from atop a horse. The grass was lush, the air still. A few monuments sprouted like small trees from the raised spot now known as Barlow’s Knoll, after the general who had ordered Wilkeson’s battery to take position here.

Beside me was Tim Smith, a local historian who knows more about the Battle of Gettysburg than just about anyone alive. He motioned southward down the hill. Past that Weis supermarket and across from that bank building, he said, was the almshouse, long gone, a county building dedicated to agriculture in its place.

We headed northeast about a half-mile, past plowed fields and stands of trees, across Old Harrisburg Road. There, beside a Lutheran retirement village, part-replica cannons marked the spot where the Confederates had taken aim.

“He would have been exposed a mile away,” Smith said of Bayard Wilkeson, before indicating that he did not hold Gen. Francis Barlow in high regard.

Neither did Sam Wilkeson, who never stopped believing that his son’s death resulted from military mismanagement. He ended his journalism career not long after Gettysburg, eventually becoming a railroad executive and, later, a real estate entrepreneur who helped to establish the city of Tacoma, Wash.

In 1889 he returned to the state of his birth, New York, and died soon afterward; he was 72. His wife, Catherine Cady Wilkeson, died a decade later, at 79.

They are buried on a small rise in a bucolic Buffalo necropolis called Forest Lawn Cemetery, their graves flanking a monument depicting a cannon barrel aimed heavenward. It marks the gravesite of the ambitious young soldier who called for them as he faded away on a damp Gettysburg floor.

While researching the Civil War story of Times journalist Sam Wilkeson and his son Bayard, I realized that it touches on many themes, including the cost of war, the need to bear witness, the bond between parent and child, and the anguish of loss. Their story is timeless.

Dan Barry is a longtime reporter and columnist, having written both the “This Land” and “About New York” columns. The author of several books, he writes on myriad topics, including New York City, sports, culture and the nation.

The Kennedy Center Is Trump’s Most Grotesque Obsession

The New York Times September 18, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Robin Givhan

Ms. Givhan is a contributing Opinion writer. She wrote from Washington.

I’ve lived in Washington since 2009 and have come to love the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Not all of the time, but most of the time. It has a distinctly retro vibe — not in a cool way, but in a slightly out-of-date way. It opened in 1971 and has been described as a living memorial. It’s enmeshed in the life of the city, even if it’s not that easy to get to: it’s not close enough to a Metro line, and it’s sandwiched between the Potomac River and a daunting traffic circle.

But it’s been a place of delight. For years it welcomed the crowd-pleasing Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater for its annual Washington residence, and I’ve seen the troupe perform “Revelations” so many times that I feel as if I could join in with my white parasol held high. I’ve celebrated the holidays there at concerts of Christmas carols. I’ve watched the Martha Graham Dance Company, and I’ve laughed with the comedian Trevor Noah.

It was home to the National Symphony Orchestra and the Washington National Opera — where both Justices Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Antonin Scalia would go. It showcased jazz concerts and lectures. And its Millennium Stage hosted freebies: drumming troupes from Africa, classic films and all sorts of creative diversions to keep kiddos amused. And every year, there was “The Nutcracker.” (OK, I kind of hate “The Nutcracker.”)

Now President Trump is out to destroy the Kennedy Center, and the magnitude of my rage startles me. After all, Mr. Trump has done so many other cruel, brutal things that have upended people’s lives, this democracy and its place in the world. But his determination to take over, and his threat to demolish, the Kennedy Center of all things? Nothing has so thoroughly highlighted his indefatigable petulance.

Because Mr. Trump wants his name on the building. That’s it.

Mr. Trump briefly tasted success. In December, his name was added to the building’s facade. In May, a federal judge ordered its removal, noting that only Congress can alter the name. The legal protest was led by an ex officio Kennedy Center board member, Representative Joyce Beatty, a Democrat from Ohio who is a Black woman. This last fact has, I suspect, added to the president’s determination to have his way.

When I was engulfed in reporting for a recent book, I celebrated the completion of a particularly challenging chapter by taking myself to a Marvin Gaye tribute by the National Symphony Orchestra. It was June 2023, and I paid $79 for an orchestra seat.

I arrived early and walked around the sprawling campus and took a picture of “Blue,” the jaunty sculpture by Joel Shapiro that Mr. Trump’s henchmen recently had removed. I bought a little bottle of prosecco from the bar and sat outside enjoying the view of the Potomac River until it was time for the show to begin.

Mr. Trump would have people believe that the Kennedy Center was some kind of incubator of anti-American esoterica. But it was not that at all, sometimes to the frustration of those who long for the sort of experimental fare you’d have to take the Acela up to New York City to see.

Instead, it’s a place that has welcomed touring musicals and exuberant dance companies. It’s a place that has gone out of its way to treat its audiences — locals and tourists, adults and children — with respect, having faith in their intelligence and curiosity, without making a night at the theater feel like watching someone defend her dissertation.

It was a place where, as Francesca Zambello, the longtime artistic director of the Washington National Opera, told me, political views weren’t discussed. (The opera ended its affiliation with the Kennedy Center in January.)

The Kennedy Center is part of a cultural ecosystem in Washington that stands apart from places like New York and Chicago. The arts are accessible here to anyone — and by that I mean a good deal of it is free. Anyone can stop by the National Gallery of Art just to commune with the Rothkos without having to shell out 20 or 30 bucks. A tourist can visit the original Star-Spangled Banner at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History. Free. The Kennedy Center offered many gratis performances, too.

The artists began canceling as soon as Mr. Trump stuffed the board with his loyalists and installed himself as chairman. Ticket sales were down; the donations slowed. Soon enough, the newly reconstituted board declared the building a rundown hellhole.

No one disputes that the Kennedy Center needs repairs, particularly those backstage areas that the public rarely sees. I have always found its lobby bar to be less than glamorous. Mr. Trump’s minions on the board and in the administration tell us that mercifully, he — and only he — could save it.

The president’s obsession with the Kennedy Center is in keeping with his desire to remake the nation’s capital — the White House, the parks, the wide boulevards and open spaces — to his own gilded, tarty, self-aggrandizing taste. “The president works all day, every day, and there are two things that he does for enjoyment,” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said. “He plays golf on the weekend and he builds. He loves to build.”

“It’s fun for him,” Lutnick added.

I live less than four miles from the Kennedy Center. I drove over Wednesday morning, in part, to make sure it was still standing. I approached it from the side, walking up the path near the Watergate apartments. The building looked especially beautiful in the clear morning light, even though its once-gold pillars have been painted white. A landscaper was clearing leaves from the plaza. A few joggers dashed by. Dogs were out for their morning constitutional. It was quiet.

The inscription on the front of the building bearing the center’s name was still obscured by elaborate scaffolding. A security guard told me the building was “closed until further notice.”

If President Trump should succeed in this tantrum, his name will be inscribed on a memorial to another president. Or he could tear it down, as his Department of Justice has threatened. On Wednesday night, Mr. Trump was photographed through the windows of Air Force One studying a poster board emblazoned with the words “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED.”

Will his presidency be remembered more for his foolishness or his failure? Either way, everyone loses. And that most certainly includes Mr. Trump.

Yes, Robin - I share your rage about the Kennedy Center as a former Washingtonian and arts administrator. I am heartbroken. The Kennedy Center was built using gifts from other countries who were touched by JFK - the Carrara marble a gift from Italy for example. What would it mean to tear this facility down and destroy those gifts? Every design decision in a performing arts facility needs to be considered based around the needs of the performers. There is a reason why the details of the Concert Hall for example have been chosen - to perfect the acoustics. Designing these facilities takes a team of specialists, not a real estate developer. I have no confidence that the KC board has assembled any such team of experts. I had the honor of raising funds to build a world-class performing arts facility in another city. The lead donor - a woman - insisted that her name should not be on the building because she wanted the community and the artists to feel a sense of shared ownership. Her generosity and modesty always inspired me.

Kind of a frightening dynamic - if he can’t own it, he will try to destroy it. Is this his not quite subconscious relationship to the whole country?

Robin Givhan is a Pulitzer Prize-winning fashion critic and a former senior critic at large for The Washington Post.

F. A. A. to Roll Out New A. I. Tool for Washington Airports

The New York Times September 18, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The tool, called SMART, will crunch scheduling and weather data to predict and avoid delays. It will be deployed in the Washington region’s three major airports next week.

By Aishvarya Kavi and Karoun Demirjian

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration plans to roll out a new A. I. air traffic control tool designed to predict and prevent flight delays in the Washington region starting Monday, as the opening step of an eventual nationwide deployment.

The tool, called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routing and Trajectories, or SMART, is designed to analyze airline schedules, weather patterns and other potential air traffic interruptions to “predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur” and recommend alternate flight routes to avoid compound delays.

While the $875 million system is expected to be deployed nationwide by 2028, Monday’s rollout will be limited to the Washington region, affecting three airports: Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, Dulles International Airport and Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport.

Washington’s congested airspace, one of the busiest in the nation, has drawn particular scrutiny following the January 2025 midair collision between a commercial jet and an Army Black Hawk helicopter that killed 67. The National Transportation Safety Board placed the blame for certain failures leading up to the crash on the Federal Aviation Administration.

The phased rollout is a chance for the administration to assess how well the new technology helps airlines and air traffic controllers avoid flight delays, and whether artificial intelligence can help those responsible for managing airline traffic circumvent potential interruptions more efficiently than they can on their own. The rollout comes amid a national uproar over the rapid development of A. I. models and bipartisan calls to rein in the industry, which President Trump and several of his deputies have flatly rejected.

Against that background, Transportation Department officials stress that the SMART system will not replace human operators or direct any changes to flight routes, but merely offer recommendations that controllers can choose to heed or ignore. The system will be located at the F. A. A.’s Air Traffic Control System Command Center in Warrenton, Va., which manages airspace traffic; officials will disseminate the A. I. recommendations to controllers at the regional towers and other air traffic facilities.

Transportation officials also pointed out that SMART is designed to analyze scheduling and congestion data over a month in advance to help predict when airports and airlines might be vulnerable to delays. But the rollout will begin modestly at first, with the A. I. system offering alternatives to avoid only same-day delays, such as those caused by weather, before being scaled up to its full potential.

“We’re excited to launch SMART and take another major step toward improving air travel for the American people,” the F. A. A. spokeswoman Hannah Walden said in a statement, calling SMART “a new tool that will fundamentally change the way we manage our skies.”

Yet the progress to this point has not been wholly smooth.

Federal transportation officials announced in June that they had awarded the contract to develop SMART to Air Space Intelligence, a Boston-based software company. At a congressional hearing this week, Bryan Bedford, the F. A. A. administrator, asked Congress for billions more dollars to fully modernize air traffic control systems, arguing that new technologies are needed to “supercharge our ability to safely grow traffic and reduce the workload and strain on our controllers.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and other administration officials have criticized current air traffic control systems as outdated and touted new programs, including the new A. I. tool, as “a huge, massive build and upgrade.”

For a rollout to begin only a few months after the contract was awarded is uncommonly fast, according to officials and experts, some of whom stressed that the F. A. A. had to engage in extensive conversations to allay concerns among airlines and controllers that the A. I. system might prove more problematic than helpful.

Robert Mann, a former airline executive who is now an aviation industry consultant, said that SMART may suggest better flight plans, but it is unlikely to address the major problems associated with delays, which happen after a flight plan is filed.

“Whether it’s on the ground or in flight or in the terminal area,” Mr. Mann said, “you’re up against a whole bunch of other traffic which arrives roughly the same time, and that’s because they’ve experienced the same sort of random delays on the ground, en route, and in the arrivals area that you are.”

While airlines might cooperate with the program initially, he added that they might come to view it as an intrusion from the F. A. A., because they carefully plan and manage their flight schedules well in advance and changes are costly.

“We’ll see how long that acquiescence lasts,” Mr. Mann added.

The rollout also comes as the F. A. A. has struggled to solve a chronic shortage of air traffic controllers. While the agency has insisted that the new A. I. system will not displace or replace human employees, the Trump administration and the union representing air traffic controllers are currently locked in a dispute about how many controllers the F. A. A. needs to hire to make up staffing shortfalls.

A year ago, the F. A. A. published a report suggesting that it would need 14,633 controllers to be fully staffed; this spring, it revised that estimate down by more than 2,000 positions, stressing that more efficient scheduling could offset the need for more hires. As of this April, the F. A. A. reported having more than 11,000 fully certified controllers.

A spokesman for the National Air Traffic Controllers Association said in a statement that the union “believes any new technology should complement and not replace the experience, training and professional judgment of air traffic controllers who are responsible for the safety of the National Airspace System.” It added that the group had not been part of the design or testing process of the system.

Aishvarya Kavi works in the Washington bureau of The Times, helping to cover a variety of political and national news.

Holdout Juror in Lindsay Clancy Case Says He Didn’t Doubt Her Guilt

The New York Times September 18, 2026

Lindsay Clancy Trial

Advertisement

Supported by

The juror, Michael P. Desronvil, defended his decision not to join other jurors in voting for Ms. Clancy’s acquittal.

By Nicholas Bogel-Burroughs

The lone juror who had wanted to convict Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman who was on trial this month for killing her three young children, said on Friday that he had no doubt that she was guilty.

In a statement, the holdout juror, Michael P. Desronvil, said that other jurors repeatedly cut him off during deliberations when he tried to propose his theories about the case. He defended himself against accusations from some of the other jurors, who said he refused to follow the law regarding reasonable doubt.

“Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presented, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned,” Mr. Desronvil said of Ms. Clancy.

Mr. Desronvil, 48, released the statement through his lawyer, Edward Paltzik, who specializes in defamation litigation and has represented President Trump in lawsuits against CBS News and The New York Times.

Mr. Paltzik also released a statement on social media that called his client an American hero, and said they would share more information in the coming days. He declined to signal what, if any, legal actions may come from Mr. Desronvil, who received both withering criticism and outspoken support in the wake of his jury service.

The trial of Ms. Clancy ended this month with the jury deadlocked, 11 to 1, in favor of acquitting her on murder and manslaughter charges. Jurors deliberated for roughly 38 hours across seven days before the judge declared a mistrial.

Ms. Clancy had admitted to strangling her three children, in January 2023, but her lawyers had argued she was in the throes of postpartum psychosis and should be absolved of criminal responsibility.

The case horrified and divided the country and prompted discussions of postpartum complications.

Prosecutors have not said whether they will retry Ms. Clancy, 36, who remains in custody in a state-run psychiatric center.

Following the mistrial, national attention turned to the jury of nine women and three men, and in particular to the holdout. The court has not revealed their identities — their names remain under seal — but several jurors have spoken publicly about their experience.

Identifying details about Mr. Desronvil began to emerge in the news media, including the fact that he had been charged, in 2021, with misdemeanor domestic violence after his then-partner said he had grabbed her throat and thrown her against a dresser. That charge was later dismissed.

Then, last year, a teenage family member asked a judge for a restraining order against Mr. Desronvil. The yearlong order expired last month, during the trial.

Mr. Desronvil was not prohibited from serving on a jury. Massachusetts law bars only people who have been convicted of a felony in the last seven years. But the charges raised questions about how Mr. Desronvil had responded when asked, on a juror form, about whether he had ever been charged with a crime, as well as whether Ms. Clancy’s lawyers had made a mistake by not trying to have him removed.

On Friday, Mr. Desronvil said in his statement that he “didn’t have any doubts” about the case.

Mr. Paltzik, his lawyer, described him on social media as a “HERO holdout” and said that he was “safe and sound at an undisclosed secure location” in rural New England. He also asked people to stop calling his client and to stay away from his home.

The lawyer also said that Mr. Desronvil “supports our amazing leader, President Donald J. Trump.” (A lawyer for Ms. Clancy previously called on Mr. Trump to pardon his client, though the president has no power to wipe away state charges.)

Mr. Paltzik had previously noted that Mr. Desronvil, who is Black, was the only nonwhite person on the jury, and said he had been “viciously attacked” in public comments by several white jurors who served with him.

In addition to representing Mr. Desronvil and Mr. Trump, Mr. Paltzik also recently began representing three young men who were friends with Nolan Wells, a Black man who died after spending time on an island with friends on July 4 in Mississippi.

The friends, who are white, had come under social media scrutiny following Mr. Wells’s death, which the authorities said was a suspected drowning but remains under investigation. Mr. Paltzik has said that the friends were unfairly defamed and has started a fund-raiser for them.

Nicholas Bogel-Burroughs reports on stories across the United States, including natural disasters, protests, unsolved mysteries, high-profile criminal cases and more.

Why Israel Fears This Searing New Documentary

The New York Times September 18, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Michelle Goldberg

By Michelle Goldberg

Opinion Columnist

Israel is treating the new documentary “NAZA,” by the Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, less like bad publicity than a national security crisis.

Eyal Zamir, chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, pledged to use “every tool at our disposal” against the documentary, which features anonymous interviews with 24 intelligence officers and soldiers, most involved in remote strikes in Gaza. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has called for legislation that would let the state strip Abraham and Szor of their citizenship. Israel’s culture minister has asked the Interior Ministry to investigate them for treason. Activists and staff members from the far-right party of Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir protested outside Szor’s parents’ house, where a speaker called for Abraham and Szor to be executed and their families’ homes demolished, as often happens to the homes of Palestinians.

The official calls for persecution of Abraham and Szor, who previously made the Oscar-winning documentary “No Other Land” with two Palestinian filmmakers, seem strategically unwise, since they’re spurring heightened interest in “NAZA.” A press screening I went to on Wednesday, at New York’s 268-seat Walter Reade Theater, was at capacity, and I was told to arrive a half-hour early to get a seat. This is, in my experience, very unusual for documentaries of any sort, even those that, like “NAZA,” win the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival.

After seeing it, I can understand why Israel finds it so threatening. Its subjects described factory-scale targeting, enabled by artificial intelligence, in which little effort was made to avoid enormous numbers of civilian casualties. “The goal was quantity, not quality,” said one of the speakers. According to the sources in the film, the military chose to target members of Hamas, some low-level, at home at night rather than when they were out during the day because it was easier, even though it meant killing their families and neighbors. One man told of hacking into the phone of a 12-year-old girl to learn when her father arrived home, and then ordering a bombing in which she was killed.

“NAZA” is Hebrew military shorthand for nezek agavi, or collateral damage. One of the speakers described a computer interface showing how many people would be killed if a particular site were bombed. Typically, said one, “20 NAZA” was a benchmark — meaning it was OK to kill 20 civilians for one Hamas target. (That figure was previously reported by The New York Times.) An interviewee said that for one bombing, a NAZA figure of 500 was approved, which the I. D. F. has denied.

Part of what makes “NAZA” so devastating is the way it shows that mere indifference to civilian deaths can shade into deliberate mass killing. To Israel’s defenders, after all, the fact that the military puts limits on acceptable collateral damage shows that it’s not trying to kill as many people as possible and thus can’t be genocidal. The Israeli journalist Ariel Oseran argued, for example, that the very word NAZA is exculpatory, writing, “If Israel’s specific objective were to destroy the Palestinian population, Palestinian deaths would not be categorized as collateral damage; they would be the intended goal.”

But “NAZA” suggests that the system Israel created had mass death built into it. In the frantic days after the Oct. 7 attacks by Hamas, Israel was full of calls to annihilate Gaza, and the murderous rhetoric has persisted. After 50,000 Gazans had already been killed, the former head of Israeli military intelligence said, in leaked audio, “For every one person on Oct. 7, 50 Palestinians must die. It doesn’t matter now if they are children.” In this atmosphere of rage, grief and total self-justification, the Israeli military made a series of choices that ensured Gaza would become a killing field, whatever the specific motives of everyone involved. “When people talk about ‘flattening Gaza,’ what do you mean if not executing people?” asked one of the subjects in “NAZA.”

At one point in the film, as an interviewee explained the rules of engagement, Abraham said, “But if you can kill 20 people per junior member, and there are tens of thousands of members …” To which the man responded, “You end up with all of Gaza, yes.”

Of course, we don’t know who these sources are. They were filmed on Tel Aviv rooftops at night, their faces shadowed, their profiles and voices digitally altered. Journalistically, the use of anonymous sources for explosive allegations isn’t unusual, but it makes some of the documentary’s claims impossible to check. The I. D. F. has emphasized the whistle-blowers’ anonymity in disparaging the film. At the same time, it’s opened a leak investigation to find out whether classified material was used in the production, a strange thing to do if the revelations are false.

Ultimately, Israel’s fury at “NAZA” — which has its U. S. premiere at the New York Film Festival on Sept. 26 — is almost certainly not about journalistic ethics. Part of the uproar is simply Netanyahu and his allies demagoguing ahead of next month’s parliamentary election, trying to cast the Israeli left as traitorous enemies of the military. (One Haaretz writer called the controversy a gift to Israel’s “fascist-nationalist bloc.”) But there’s also a broader sense of a taboo being smashed, of Israel being confronted with something it desperately doesn’t want to see.

“Israel has been in a state of denial now for close to three years,” said the Israeli American historian Omer Bartov, author of the recent book “Israel: What Went Wrong.” Until “NAZA,” he said, there had been little debate in the country about the leveling of Gaza. Now, he said, people are “actually speaking about the issue of what happened in Gaza rather than refusing to speak about it.”

But it’s a conversation many cannot face. “In Israel you may be on the left, but your children go to serve in the army, and often you are proud of them being soldiers,” said Bartov. “And then you’re told they maybe were involved in a criminal war. That’s very difficult for people to accept, and they will find all kinds of ways to resist it.”

It’s hard to tell whether Israelis are enraged by “NAZA” because they think it’s full of lies, or because they know or fear it’s true.

Ms. Goldberg writes, "It's hard to tell whether Israelis are enraged by 'NAZA' because they think it's full of lies, or because they know or fear it's true." Israel has been the target of numerous lies over its existence, but the scorched-earth reaction is so different in degree it may have become different in kind. If the documentary were simply false, why not expose its falsehoods and move on? The Israeli government seems to be calling for the total destruction of the mirror because they can't live with the reflection.
